Recent advancements in single-cell transcriptomics have greatly enhanced our understanding of tissue biology. However, digitizing tissue sections for single-cell analysis remains a complex and time-consuming process, largely holding back the full potential of single-cell data in tumor tissue studies. A new method utilizing deep learning and MaZel, an algorithm for automatic cell detection and segmentation within whole-slide images of cancer tissues, facilitates rapid analysis of tissue sections at a cellular level. When integrated with single-cell transcriptomics, this method allows for highly accurate computation of cellular and tissue characteristics. In a series of experiments, this approach demonstrated superior performance compared to other available techniques, yielding reliable estimates of tumor cell density, lymphocyte infiltration, and clonality. Furthermore, this method revealed novel insights into the distribution of clonal cells within individual tumor tissues. Notably, it was discovered that clonal cells often form distinct patterns within the tumor, and that the size and distribution of these patterns can be predicted from the cell trajectory in a three-dimensional model. These findings highlight the potential for automatic tissue analysis to reveal previously unknown aspects of cancer biology. A pre-trained version of the model has been made available for research purposes. Further details are available at https://github.com/ai4health-ucd/MaZel_SCC/tree/main/model. Additional information about the dataset and code used in this study can be found at https://github.com/ucd-ai4health/Cancer_Tissue_Analysis. MaZel's performance was evaluated using comprehensive metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, mean IoU, mean surface IoU, Matthews correlation coefficient, frequency-weighted Matthews correlation coefficient, and adjusted Rand index. These calculations were performed using the tools available at https://github.com/ai4health-ucd/MaZel_SCC/tree/main/utils. The source code for the study was maintained at https://github.com/ucd-ai4health/Tissue_Analysis_SCC. The research was supported by the funding from the SFI, HSE, and UCD. This work introduces a unified framework for generating gaits in quadrupedal robots
through reinforcement learning. The method empowers these robots to adapt their gait
patterns in response to diverse and dynamic environments without requiring fine-
tuned control algorithms. Within this framework, the robots learn a universal policy
that can be activated in various situations. Moreover, due to the policy's inherent
generalizability, it is feasible to create customized gait controllers by pruning the
unessential information accumulated during the policy's training. Our approach has
been successfully validated through simulations and practical tests on the Spot robot. 
Notably, models trained on a specific robot platform can be transferred to other
quadrupedal systems with minimal adjustments. Our research has achieved gait
performance comparable to that achieved using deep reinforcement learning on the
same platform, but with significantly reduced model complexity. Ultimately, this
framework holds great promise for enabling the effective deployment of reinforcement
learning in the development of scalable and adaptable control systems for legged
robots. Our code is publicly accessible at: https://github.com/Control-Labs/rl-gait. 
Additionally, the dataset utilized in this research is available at: https://www.embodied.ai/rl-gait-dataset.

This dense star cluster is situated near the center of the galaxy and is home to multiple stellar populations, which we've identified through multiwavelength observations. A particularly metal-rich and chemically enriched population was detected in a specific star cluster, evident from various spectral features analyzed in detailed spectroscopic studies. Analysis of multiple elements revealed a high metallicity comparable to that of the most metal-rich stars within the Milky Way's globular cluster system, while also exhibiting an unusually high abundance of certain elements relative to others. This unusual pattern sets this population apart from typical high-metallicity globular clusters within the Milky Way and suggests a distinct origin for this dense cluster in NGC 300. This discovery is significant as it represents the first known example of a dense, highly metal-rich and chemically enriched globular cluster system within a nearby spiral galaxy and sheds new light on the complex formation history of these clusters through extensive galaxy mergers and interactions. A novel approach to finding anomalies is by dividing an image into various regions based on differences in pixel values and identifying irregular areas within each section. However, this method has limitations in accurately pinpointing unusual areas since it divides the image into uniform sections regardless of the content. To overcome this, we've created an improved algorithm that dynamically sections an image into content-based areas and accurately detects irregularities. We've tested our method against a standard benchmark and compared it to other top-notch algorithms, achieving superior results. Recent advances in programming task models have shown significant improvements when fine-tuned with pre-trained language models, achieving nearly human-level performance in some cases. However, the process is costly due to the need for extensive data and computational resources, making it inaccessible to many programmers, especially those in developing countries. In response, we've adapted a novel technique that enables the creation of effective task models from limited data, and we successfully tested it on a basic programming challenge. Notably, our results show that task models can be efficiently trained and achieve comparable success when the dataset is a tiny fraction (1% of the standard size) of what's typically used in the field. We've made our training code and other resources available for public use.

The coexistence of distinctively different shapes in nearby galaxies - discs and spheroids - has long been a notable phenomenon. These shapes are often associated with different environments and are thought to result from distinct formation processes. While spiral galaxies form through gradual disc formation, ellipticals are proposed to have originated from the merger of smaller components. We aim to investigate the influence of environmental factors on galaxy morphology using a simulation tool. By employing an advanced hydrodynamic model that accurately replicates the behavior of cold dark matter and gas, we simulate the growth of galaxies in diverse environments. Notably, our results indicate that galaxies exhibiting a disc-like structure tend to reside in peaceful environments, whereas those with a spheroidal shape are more commonly found in dynamic environments. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the merger of smaller components can also contribute to the development of disc galaxies, particularly those with less massive central black holes. These outcomes imply that environmental factors have a profound impact on galaxy morphology and shape. While simulations have achieved significant success, discrepancies between simulations and observations persist. Notably, blue spheroids were found, which are thought to be underrepresented in the simulations. To resolve this discrepancy, a more in-depth analysis of the feedback mechanisms is necessary. Additionally, the simulations failed to replicate the intricate details of galaxy morphologies observed in the central regions of massive galaxies. To overcome this limitation, incorporating the effects of feedback and magnetic fields is essential. Overall, our research suggests that environmental factors have a profound influence on galaxy morphology and shape, with further refinements to the feedback mechanisms and the inclusion of magnetic fields necessary to achieve greater accuracy. We've developed a novel technique for determining the vertical aerosol optical depth by utilizing photometry from a broad field of view, paired with satellite angular resolution. This approach enables aerosol height profile retrieval without the need for absolute instrument calibration and can be applied to existing ground-based networks with minor modifications for space-based data analysis. We applied this method to observations from the OMNI satellite at 7.4 micrometers during the 2006 biomass-burning event in Western Canada, resulting in aerosol height profiles that were then used to calculate the vertical distribution of aerosol optical depth with an accuracy of 10-20% across different latitude bands. These findings were validated by comparison with satellite imagery from the MODIS satellite and in situ measurements from aircraft. We found that our technique produced a more detailed and spatially extensive aerosol profile than the standard omni-directional averaging method, particularly at low altitude ranges. We also observed that aerosol height decreased exponentially with distance from the Earth's surface, with the turn-over point occurring at approximately 1-2 km above ground level. This study demonstrates the potential for wide-field photometry to contribute valuable information about aerosol cloud complexity and structure to existing ground-based and space-based monitoring networks. Future applications of this technique could enable the identification of aerosol cloud shapes and sizes, ultimately enhancing our understanding of atmospheric phenomena and improving retrievals of geophysical parameters from satellite data. Additionally, this approach could facilitate the analysis of future satellite missions with broad field of view instruments, such as the Lucy and the Habitable Exoplanet Imaging Mission, by providing accurate and detailed planetary surface properties. Furthermore, this research may also be applicable to future terrestrial exoplanet imaging missions by enabling the identification of clouds, clear skies, and planetary features. Finally, we suggest that this method could be adapted for use in future ground-based and space-based spectroscopic monitoring missions by utilizing broad-band photometry as a reference for accurate and precise retrieval of gas and aerosol species from spectral data. This approach has significant potential to enhance the performance of various atmospheric monitoring missions. In conclusion, this research presents a novel, efficient, and versatile technique for determining aerosol cloud complexity and derive accurate vertical aerosol distributions from wide-field photometry, paving the way for new applications in planetary science and exoplanetary research. This method is expected to contribute to future monitoring missions by enabling the identification of clouds, clear skies, and geophysical features on exoplanets and planets in our solar system. This paper enhances the Graphical Largo (GL) model by accounting for unobserved factors, resulting in a Latent Graphical Lasso (LGL) algorithm. LGL incorporates techniques from multiple imputation and posterior inference to maximize the likelihood of the models parameters. Our approach can be applied to complete and incomplete data sets, and includes a metric to assess the convergence of the latent variables. Simulation studies demonstrate the superiority of LGL in estimating precision matrix sizes and network structures, particularly when dealing with missing data. Furthermore, LGL is used to construct a brain connectivity network from the fMRI dataset NIBS, and a gene expression network from the lung cancer dataset lung.tar, in comparison to the standard GL method. We've developed a disk model that accounts for the free-free emission from both the inner and outer regions of a disk, taking into consideration the X-ray emission from its center. In our analysis of the starless core IRAS 15398-3359, we found that the inner free-free emission significantly outweighs the contribution from X-rays, and as a result, the star's X-ray luminosity was underestimated by a factor of 1000 in previous studies of similar objects. Our data suggest that the core's temperature is approximately 28 K, and based on our calculations of thermal and radiation pressure-driven diffusion, we estimate a disk mass of 1.2 millimasses for an assumed outer radius of 0.1 parsecs. This model is particularly relevant for studying starless cores with high central densities and temperatures, and could also be applied to other astrophysical objects such as protoplanetary disks and cometary comae. Given its broad applications, we believe this model has the potential to make significant contributions to the field of low-mass star formation research. Finally, we propose that future studies of disk emission should be approached with caution if they rely solely on spectral index and radius, and instead suggest combining this method with other approaches such as statistical mechanics and chemical modeling. These additional perspectives could offer valuable insights into the physical properties of the disk. Ultimately, further observations are needed to confirm our findings and gain a more comprehensive understanding of the disk structure in low-mass star-forming regions. Based on our analysis, we predict that future radio interferometers with greater sensitivity will be able to detect free-free emission from disks around 1 solar mass objects, and may potentially reveal the presence of disks around even lower-mass stars. This discovery could have significant implications for our understanding of the disk evolution and planetary formation processes. In conclusion, our study highlights the importance of accurately modeling complex physical processes in the formation of stars like our solar system. Background noise significantly affects speech detection, with pitch values often masked, leading to inaccurate results. This research proposes a noise estimation and removal method that utilizes non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) and feedback from a neural network, enhancing the recovery of pitch values. Experimental comparisons reveal the superiority of this proposal over current techniques in retrieving pitch values from noisy backgrounds. Additionally, this study introduces a new evaluation metric to assess the accuracy of pitch value detection. Furthermore, this method may be adapted for extracting pitch information from other sound types. Implementing this approach yields a practical solution for an effective pitch extraction algorithm that withstands a variety of background noises. All the source code is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zhengyu-chen/Pitch-Extract-Without-Clean.

The DWIFOB algorithm, an improved version of the Anderson acceleration method for fixed points, shows robustness in a variety of direct numerical simulation challenges. Within the context of turbulence modeling, it outperforms the underlying method it enhances and is comparable to a more advanced approach known as quasi-compressed gradients. In certain situations, it even surpasses them. Our analysis using a simplified model reveals that DWIFOB's reliability is largely a result of its ability to produce trustworthy estimates from earlier iterations. These estimates act as a solid foundation for guiding the algorithm's convergence. Furthermore, we have successfully applied DWIFOB to a challenging flame structure problem and observed significant enhancements over the standard method. Although it occasionally diverges in some difficulties, our research aims to refine the algorithm to boost its reliability. This is accomplished by introducing an innovative strategy based on the concept of virtual iterations. This strategy has the added benefit of enhancing the robustness of the DWIFOB algorithm and making it more versatile. By combining theoretical and experimental methods, we have analyzed the convergence properties of this new approach and found that it is comparable to the original method in terms of computational cost. Nevertheless, it offers notable improvements in terms of robustness and is more adaptable. Our research has also applied this new technique to a range of challenging tasks, including a modified version of the Anderson acceleration test suite and a turbulent combustion problem, in which it consistently outperformed the original method and showed promising potential. Ultimately, it is hoped that this new technique will contribute to the development of more efficient algorithms for solving fixed-point problems in the broader field of computational fluid dynamics. This includes turbulence modeling and the simulation of complex multiphase flows. In pursuit of highly efficient neural networks, researchers have extensively explored
network architecture search (NAS). Recent breakthroughs have revealed connections between
network architectures and their program properties. This study delves deeper into uncovering
program-based explanations for neural architecture performance. To this end, we comprehensively
evaluated the performance of 560 distinct neural architectures, as well as their program attributes,
within a space of 4.2 trillion possible variants. Our analysis indicates that integrated program
properties can accurately forecast top-performing architectures in both search-based and transfer-learning
scenarios. Moreover, we discovered that neural architectures excel due to a combination of efficient
control flow and well-balanced module architectures. To facilitate future research, we introduce
the first open-source, general-purpose neural program execution framework called ProSE. Our findings
and tool are expected to foster significant contributions in the nas segment. Our code and data can be
accessed at https://www.facebook.com/research/nas/ and https://github.com/facebook/prose.

This research explores the capabilities of mmWave multicasting when using multiple antennas at the receiver end. We focus on developing an optimal beamforming technique that takes into account both the broadcast nature of the wireless communication and the limitations imposed by receiver antenna count. This problem is framed as an integer programming issue, which is then resolved using a computationally efficient algorithm based on the successive lower bound method. We also introduce a data-driven approach to enhance the performance of this technique over large frequency ranges in practical scenarios. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that this proposed method yields substantial improvements in overall system performance, with gains of 90% and 40% in comparison to single-user and multi-user MISO systems, respectively. Notably, this method achieves near-optimal performance with minimal computational complexity. Finally, we evaluate the effectiveness of this technique in scenarios with varying levels of antenna count at both the transmitter and receiver ends. Our results indicate that our proposed method remains highly effective even when antenna count is low, specifically when below 4 in the receiver case and below 6 in the transmitter case. These findings suggest that our method is well-suited for practical applications with limited antenna count. To facilitate this, we introduce a tool called mmWaveSim, which enables the simulation of mmWave wireless networks in a realistic manner. This tool is available for public use at https://github.com/asharif/mmWaveSim. Some of the included features in mmWaveSim pertain to the optimization of beamforming techniques, while other key features include the integration of automatic channel modeling, dynamic user movement, and the ability to switch between different system configurations through a graphical user interface. This tool is designed to support a wide range of wireless system configurations spanning from 28 GHz to 70 GHz frequency ranges and covering various antenna counts from 1 to 16 per device. It is capable of handling simulations involving up to 200 users on a single core of a high-performance CPU. Some of the key simulation outcomes include optimized beamforming vectors, channel gain values, user association information, and network topologies that can be visualized in 3D. A novel communication-efficient technique, Compressed Federated Distillation, is proposed in this paper. Firstly, FD is distinguished from FED and other federated learning methods by sharing compressed models instead of averaging them. Theoretical analysis confirms that CFD achieves a similar classification performance as FD, using a fraction of the models required by FED. Experimental results across three datasets demonstrate CFD's efficiency in reducing communication costs, particularly in scenarios with limited data availability. The proposed method also demonstrates the potential for long-term collaboration without sustained data access. The code for this research is openly accessible at the following link: https://github.com/alexeydg/cfd.

1.  A formal description of Compressed Federated Distillation and its comparison to existing techniques.
2.  Theoretical proof of CFD's performance equivalence to FD with reduced communication costs.
3.  Empirical evaluation of CFD's efficiency and its potential applications in scenarios with limited data access.

A thorough evaluation revealed that SDADO outperforms alternative solutions by achieving substantial improvements of up to 25% and 30% in end-to-end delays and increased throughput, respectively. We focus on a nonlinear vibrating model of a star-shaped metric graph with multiple branches, where the absence of elasticity at the junction has significant implications for the stability of the system. Under certain geometric constraints, we establish exponential stability of the entire graph's dynamics, building upon a specific canonical structure near the junction. Furthermore, we introduce a dissipation function and, with the aid of a complete differential characterization, along with some advanced inequalities, prove that the system's energy function is sublinearly convergent. Moreover, we demonstrate that the absence of elasticity at the junction contributes to unique stability properties, distinct from analogous linear systems, which we obtain via a novel time-scale invariance property alongside standard time-invariant methods. Ultimately, our findings are complemented by illustrative examples and the introduction of novel concepts within the context of geometric graph theory. In particular, a new concept of outer-helicity is presented, which may find applications in the analysis of more complex graph structures in the future. In addition, we establish a unique stability property for a system of coupled Schrödinger equations on a star-shaped graph, which marks a new direction in research. By leveraging techniques from nonlinear Schrödinger equation analysis and applying them to a time-discrete setting, we achieve exponential stability of the entire graph's dynamics while preserving canonical structures near the junction. This approach also enables the extension of our results to more general star-shaped graphs through a systematic construction of reference systems with preserved rotational symmetry. Furthermore, we demonstrate the existence of unique stability properties in various other graph configurations, which lays the groundwork for future research in this area. In the interest of clarity and conciseness, some of the intermediate steps and additional findings are presented in the appended discussion section. In particular, a novel concept of outer-helicity for a Schrödinger equation on a graph is introduced, which may contribute to new insights in geometric graph theory. In addition, the ideas presented can be applied to the analysis of nonlinear equations on more complex graphs, which holds significant potential for future research. In the final section, we explore the connections between our results and the broader themes of geometric graph theory, nonlinear equation analysis, and the Schrödinger equation in particular. In the process, we identify existing research gaps and propose potential avenues of investigation for future study. In the interest of completeness, we also outline the necessary prerequisites for pursuing original contributions in this area. The research explores the behavior of inhomogeneous matter in terms of $G_2$ symmetry, focusing on the $0^{++}$ channel. Using a linearized fluctuation analysis, it's discovered that the $0^{++}$ channel exhibits instability. This analysis further considers how this matter could formulate into variously shaped soliton configurations, with initial findings indicating that, due to energy increase, compact ring-shaped solitons may be the most feasible option to form in nature. Additionally, the study investigates how this matter could be observed in neutron star crusts and, through various calculations, concludes that neutron star crusts could potentially host $G_2$-flavored density waves. This study also speculates on the possibility of observing these matter formations through future astronomical observations. Finally, potential future research directions are suggested, including examining the role of vector mesons in $G_2$-flavored density waves and exploring the feasibility of $G_2$-flavored quarkyonic matter. This could potentially lead to new discoveries and a deeper understanding of complex matter in astronomy.

MTlTe3 was initially studied as a 3D topological insulator with unusual properties 
and as a material with an unusual crystal structure, characterized by four interconnected 
thallium atoms in a square arrangement, exhibiting anomalous electronic behavior. 
Recent research revealed that this arrangement of thallium atoms displays four-fold electronic 
behavior rather than the usual two-fold behavior seen in typical insulators. 
This unique property allows MTlTe3 to seamlessly transition between a three-dimensional 
topological insulator and a two-dimensional insulator or even a superconductor. 
This unique transformation makes MTlTe3 an ideal material for use in spin torque equipment and 
other spin devices due to its ability to easily modify its electronic properties. 
This study delves deeper into the electronic and magnetic properties of MTlTe3 by using 
first principles calculations to simulate different configurations of the material. 
These simulations have shown that MTlTe3 naturally develops a magnetic structure 
comprised of stripes running in two different directions, exhibiting unique properties 
such as a significant internal magnetic field and an unusual electronic behavior 
characterized by the absence of electronic carriers. 
This research further explores how external factors such as pressure can modify the material's 
crystal structure, resulting in various electronic and magnetic configurations, 
including the disappearance of the material's magnetic stripe structure and the emergence 
of a two-dimensional insulator or superconductor state. 
This study has also identified several transition metal dopants that can be used to make MTlTe3 
a permanent magnet, a property that could be useful in the development of advanced spin devices. 
Overall, this research has shown that MTlTe3 has a wide range of electronic and magnetic properties 
that can be easily modified through the use of external factors such as pressure or chemical doping. 
This versatility makes MTlTe3 an ideal material for the development of advanced spin devices, 
including those used in the production of precise and efficient magnetic sensors. 
This research has also identified several potential applications of MTlTe3, 
including its use as a component in the development of advanced spin logic circuits and as a material 
for the creation of precise and efficient magnetic field patterns in spin devices and equipment.

Optimizing a utility function offline with the help of expert knowledge allows for preferences to be incomplete, as expert insights supplement limited data, unlike pairwise result comparisons which are complete but rely solely on local preferences. We investigate a utility learning problem where we take advantage of expert insights to learn a utility function offline. The problem involves choosing a utility function from a parameterized utility class based on expert-provided utilities for specific features. We find that this problem is hard when the utility class is restricted to Boolean functions, as it's equivalent to solving the P vs NP problem. However, we successfully reduce the complexity of this problem when the utility class is limited to polynomial functions, providing a computationally efficient solution. We further demonstrate that this offline utility learning problem is applicable in real-world scenarios, as seen in our example of learning a utility function to rank search results based on user features. Our work also includes a study of what happens when we allow a slight discrepancy in offline preferences, discovering that this leads to a more efficient solution but with limitations on utility class restrictions. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings with experiments using synthetic and real-world data. Our code is available at https://github.com/alexbosch/offline-utility-learning. Recurrent sequence-to-sequence models have been successfully applied to forecasting future actions of reinforcement learning agents, but the utility of attention mechanisms in this context has been uncertain. To clarify the inherent properties of such models, we examined the relationship between past inputs, future outputs, and the projected future trajectories. Our experiments demonstrate that while future outputs are directly influenced by past inputs, future projections are only indirectly affected, thereby justifying the use of dedicated models for precise future trajectory forecasts. We introduce a novel, compact architecture that outperforms baseline models in this area. Notably, our design also enables the recovery of past agent trajectories with minimal information, highlighting its potential for data compression and privacy enhancement in reinforcement learning training and deployment. Ultimately, our work showcases the value of analytical assessments in informing the development of more efficient reinforcement learning methods. All source code is publicly available on our project website.

perturbations to the Hamiltonian allows the exploration of an extensive range of electronic 
properties, encompassing different types of metallic, insulating, and superconducting behavior. 
A key feature of the model is its susceptibility to complex and nonlinear electronic behavior, 
demonstrated through the emergence of multifractal states resulting from self-organization within the 
lattice. Utilizing the Kondo lattice model as a basis, we incorporate wave function-based hybridization 
fields to mimic thermal effects, thereby inducing a transition between distinct phases. A thorough 
investigation of the model's behavior yields a comprehensive understanding of the phase diagram, along 
with identification of critical phenomena marking the boundaries between different states. Moreover, 
we calculate the critical exponents governing the behavior of these critical phenomena. Lastly, 
considering the potential for experimental realization, we assess the feasibility of replicating the 
model using a specific type of atomic chain and highlight the significance of accurately controlling the 
interactions between adjacent atoms in order to access the intricate electronic states characteristic of 
the herringbone lattice model. Ultimately, the intricate nature of the model's electronic properties 
demonstrates its potential as a unique framework for understanding complex matter. Furthermore, the 
application of external stimuli to modify the lattice's properties offers a promising pathway for 
controlling and accessing the intricate electronic states essential for discovering novel phenomena.

simulator devices. Conversely, the complexity of replicating the model using atomic chains presents a 
significant challenge that must be overcome in order to successfully realize the model's unique features.

We investigate whether restart-based algorithms are inherently robust to changes in their learning environment. We focus on risk-sensitive reinforcement learning and find that existing algorithms are not necessarily capable of adapting to shifts in their environmental dynamics. Consequently, this led to the development of new risk-sensitive restart-based algorithms that are globally convergent and effective in adapting to changes in reward functions or transition matrices within a set of possible variations. Notably, our globally convergent results differ significantly from previous work in this field. The global convergence of our new algorithms is achieved through the use of a globally convergent version of the EXPLORER algorithm and a new variant of the global optimization algorithm for risk-sensitive reinforcement learning. The performance of these algorithms is validated through numerical experiments, with our risk-sensitive restart-based EXPLORER algorithms demonstrating superior performance compared to other risk-sensitive restart-based algorithms and existing risk-sensitive algorithms that are adapted to changing environments. The numerical experiments also reveal that our algorithms are capable of adapting to complex changes in environmental dynamics while maintaining efficient sample complexity in comparison to existing methods. The performance of our algorithms is further illustrated through their application in a real-world problem, that is, playing a variant of the game of Connect Four. The results show that our algorithms are capable of successfully adapting to changing strategies of an opponent while improving their performance relative to a benchmark algorithm. Building upon the proposed WPM, a distributed stochastic gradient descent based method is formulated and its convergence rates are rigorously evaluated under specific conditions. Notably, it is observed that WPM outperforms traditional linear aggregation methods in certain situations, with empirical validation provided through comprehensive numerical experiments. Additionally, it is demonstrated that WPM can effectively handle data with irregular patterns of communication. Importantly, the developed method is successfully applied to distribute non-negative data across incompatible networks of nodes. Overall, the proposed WPM offers a versatile and efficient aggregation tool for distributed machine learning algorithms. Furthermore, a detailed examination is conducted to understand when communication patterns lead to data valuation and the potential of WPM is explored in parallel regularization of machine learning models. Lastly, an innovative approach is introduced to utilize the collaborative power of WPM in promoting smooth learning curves and mitigating overfitting in distributed machine learning systems. We have developed a novel inference technique for polymers that reconstructs their molecular structure from a dynamic simulation of the macromolecule in a fluid state. Our method, which works without regard to topology, represents a polymer as a connected sequence of monomers and efficiently identifies unique, physically feasible configurations. In place of a complex graph representation, our method employs a compact, easily parsable sequence that streamlines the identification and comparison of polymer configurations. Additionally, our method employs an optimized clustering algorithm that group configurations based on their visual appearance and physical properties. Our results show that this new method significantly outperforms previous topologically-based approaches, achieving faster processing speeds and improved accuracy. For example, in a test simulation involving a 1000-monomer polymer, our method required only 1.7 seconds to identify unique configurations, a task that other methods accomplished in 10-20 seconds. When applied to a 500-monomer polymer, our method reached speeds of up to 60 frames per second. Our method demonstrates a substantial improvement in efficiency, enabling the detailed study of polymer behavior on a much larger scale. With our method, researchers can simulate and analyze macromolecules composed of thousands of monomers, shedding new light on polymer dynamics and behavior. Our work has significant implications for the simulation and study of biological molecules like DNA and proteins. During the COVID-19 pandemic, there has been an intense shortage of ventilators, leading to a critical need for rationing a single device among multiple patients while maintaining individualized ventilation volumes. This challenge has sparked an interest in ventilator sharing, a process that is inherently difficult to control due to variables affecting airflow dynamics. To address this issue, we have developed a closed-loop ventilation system that can effectively regulate and optimize air supply to each patient while ensuring they receive their prescribed tidal volume. This innovative approach combines real-time video monitoring with deep learning algorithms to continuously track patient airflow dynamics, and uses model predictive control to calculate and adjust the ventilator rate and duration based on real-time feedback. In simulations involving two and three patients, our system demonstrated high accuracy and reliability, successfully delivering the prescribed tidal volume to each patient. This ventilator-sharing method has the potential to be easily translated to clinical settings, and we are currently conducting in-vivo tests to further refine and validate the system. From a frequentist perspective, fast posterior contraction is a desirable property. Researchers have previously established contraction rates for Bayesian models with known error variance, but little is known about the case where error variance is unknown. This study fills this gap by considering a typical Bayesian linear regression model under both standard and relaxed assumptions. The results show that uncertainty about noise magnitude increases the speed of posterior contraction, outperforming a related frequentist estimator. The study also provides a solution to an open problem in the field by demonstrating that standard Bayesian model selection is possible even when error variance is unknown. The results are validated through simulations and illustrated with data from a study on the effect of income on lifespan. The findings have implications for the use of Bayesian methods in applications with unknown error variance. The study offers a new approach for establishing contraction rates in models with unknown error variance, opening doors to future research in this area. A machining operation's outcome is heavily influenced by the cutting tool's surface condition. This study investigates the impact of various factors on the roughness of a machined surface. An experiment involving a double three-roll bowl design examined the effect of five variables: the ratio of follower to leading diameters, the angle of the follower, the position of the supporting roller, the depth of the depression, and the surface roughness of the tools. The study found that the variables were correlated with surface roughness values ranging from 2.62 to 10.57 micrometers. Analysis of the data using the Taguchi method and principal component regression revealed that the surface roughness is primarily determined by the ratio of follower to leading diameters, the angle of the follower, and their interaction. The results indicate that increasing this ratio or angle leads to a significant decrease in surface roughness. Additionally, the models developed in the study are capable of accurately predicting surface roughness values with an average error of 0.78 percent. Comparing the performance of the models to other studies, it was found that the current models outperform them in terms of prediction accuracy. However, it was observed that the models are susceptible to overfitting, which may affect their performance when testing unknown conditions. Therefore, it is recommended that the tools be used in a variety of different configurations to verify the applicability of the models in predicting surface roughness values. Ultimately, the study's findings can guide the selection of cutting tools based on their surface condition to achieve desired surface finish qualities. Furthermore, the research suggests that the Taguchi method and principal component regression can be effective techniques for analyzing complex systems characterized by numerous correlated variables. While the study's models can effectively predict surface roughness values, they are primarily intended for educational purposes and may have limited practical applications in cutting tool design. Potential avenues for further research include investigating the correlation between surface roughness and mechanical properties, exploring alternative regression techniques that can handle correlated variables, and developing models that can accurately predict surface roughness values over a wider range of cutting conditions. Additionally, it is suggested that future studies examine the feasibility of using the supporting roller's position as a control parameter to minimize surface roughness values. If successful, this could enable the development of a control strategy to produce desired surface finish qualities. Finally, it is recommended that future research investigate the system's behavior when subjected to various cutting conditions characterized by multiple parameter combinations. This could involve integrating the study's models with existing knowledge to develop a predictive system for surface roughness control.

This research focuses on creating more robust templates to enhance the effectiveness of forgery detection systems, particularly when dealing with tampered images. Given the limited data available for training, increasing the diversity of created templates is a key concern. We investigated various methods to compare the authenticity of different templates and discovered that incorporating metrics like distinctiveness, complexity, and repeatability is crucial for achieving high accuracy. Our findings also reveal that bi-directional CNN architecture is better suited for template creation and that using a cross-channel correlation filter yields superior results compared to traditional boundary-based image matching methods. We further developed a two-stage forgery detection system, starting with automatic template creation and integration, and demonstrated significant improvements in performance with our proposed approach. Notably, this system achieved impressive accuracy of 96.5% on the widely-used DIBS dataset. Our method and additional testing data are available for download on our website at https://www.iiitbd.edu.in/~vision/iiitforgery.html. In contrast to previous single-zone models, which assumed a fixed nitrogen-to-oxygen ratio, this model reveals how this ratio changes over time, depending on a galaxy's metallicity. This study introduces a computational framework for complex systems that combines graphical representation of networked data to analyze complex biological systems. The framework utilizes an advanced method of Dirichlet Process Mixtures to model the relationship between node attributes in a graph topology. It then applies a dynamic optimization technique to extract meaningful patterns or cycles in the data. The framework's effectiveness was demonstrated in two real-world scenarios, one involving the discovery of regulatory cycles in protein expression data and the other in the identification of meaningful cycles in a simulated molecular interaction network. The results showed that it is capable of identifying known cycles to a high degree of accuracy as well as discovering novel cycles. Further analysis revealed the biological significance of the detected cycles. Additionally, the framework shows flexibility in operating on a variety of graph structures and it is possible to improve its performance by incorporating domain knowledge. The GPA innovates by improving upon existing graph models and outperforms them in real-world image classification tasks. This research explores how statistical entanglement in quantum mechanics affects the concept of entropy. Building on previous models of thermal systems, we extend this investigation to electromagnetic radiation. We demonstrate that entanglement, a quantum property, has a significant impact on entropy balance equations, causing it to follow non-intuitive paths that differ from typical thermal behavior. Notably, our analysis shows that entanglement can lead to negative entropy rates under certain conditions, even reversing the conventional increase towards equilibrium. Furthermore, we consider the possibility of propagating entropy waves and find that these non-local patterns are feasible within certain speed limits set by the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle. Finally, we examine the potential applications of these models in studying heat transfer between small particles, which are often treated as point sources of radiation. Our investigation reveals that taking entanglement into account can result in substantial errors, which are particularly significant when the distance between particles is comparable to or smaller than their size. Overall, our findings indicate that quantum statistical entanglement has a substantial effect on entropy behavior, which is most pronounced in the radiation of high-energy particles. Importantly, our research shows that this effect can be attributed to the inherent speed of light being greater than any possible entropy propagation velocity, which is a fundamental characteristic of quantum mechanics. This research delves into enhancing the accuracy of predicting user influence in social networks by exploring the potential of augmentation methods both during training and testing periods. We examine the influence of various graph sizes on the efficacy of these techniques, revealing that both train- and test-time augmentation exhibit declining performance trends as graph size increases. Notably, our empirical findings on two large datasets reveal that test-time augmentation is the dominant factor contributing to prediction errors. Based on these insights, we develop a streamlined influence prediction model that omits test-time augmentation, yielding significant improvements and demonstrating comparable or even superior results to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Collaborative coding environments, such as Integrated Development Environments, play a crucial role in supporting group work throughout the software development lifecycle, but our understanding of how members interact with these environments is limited, particularly regarding maintenance practices. To fill this gap, we conducted an in-depth study of how developers use a shared folder feature in a collaborative IDE used widely in software development. Our survey revealed that while repository owners typically handle maintenance tasks associated with shared files, other contributors rarely engage in these activities. Notably, when multiple owners shared the same repository, the workload for maintenance was even more dispersed. Interestingly, despite the existence of several available tools, many developers still use the repository for file sharing and do not utilize more advanced features offered by these tools. Our findings suggest that providing educational resources could help improve awareness of available capabilities and, ultimately, promote more effective collaboration on software projects. Based on our results, we propose a research hypothesis for further investigation. Specifically, we hypothesize that promoting best practices in collaborative workspace maintenance could lead to improved team productivity in software development projects. To test this hypothesis, we plan to investigate the impact of a maintenance adoption strategy, such as encouraging developers to utilize all available features in their repositories, on the quality of software development processes. By exploring this potential correlation, we can gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between collaborative workspace management and software development processes. This knowledge can be utilized to design more effective collaborative tools and strategies to boost team performance in software development. Ultimately, by promoting best practices in collaborative workspace management, we can contribute to improved team productivity in software development. The primary objective of any laboratory is to produce reliable and accurate data, achieved by minimizing human error through efficient data management and documentation automation. This process involves creating automated reports by linking experimental results to predefined templates, thereby streamlining document creation and saving personnel time for more critical tasks. Moreover, by reducing manual documentation burdens, laboratories can allocate more resources to other important activities, ultimately leading to enhanced productivity and better results. This case study examines how modern automation tools can be applied to a typical biochemical laboratory's daily operations, including sample analysis, testing procedures, and quality control processes, as well as other complex experiments, to prove their substantial benefits in both large and small laboratories. By successfully implementing these tools, laboratories can achieve significant cost savings, leading to a positive impact on their overall budget. This chapter presents an innovative solution for a laboratory's data management and documentation, showcasing its application to an experiment using an HPLC instrument as an example. This solution was designed using a Visually Unified Model Driven Architecture (VUMDA) approach, emphasizing the integration of various systems through a unified model to facilitate seamless data exchange and automated processes. As a result, this implementation has greatly improved the laboratory's efficiency, productivity, and data quality by eliminating human errors and facilitating fast and easy data analysis. Furthermore, this chapter also explores the potential for scaling this solution to accommodate a variety of instruments and experiments in a typical laboratory setting. Finally, the chapter discusses the potential for this solution to be adapted in other domains, demonstrating the universal applicability of modern data management and documentation best practices. Ultimately, the main goal of this research is to promote model-driven data management and documentation in the knowledge domain, as well as in industry, through its presentation at conferences and publication in relevant journals. The $T_{CC}$ particle, recently discovered by LHCb, is a $D^{\ast} D^{\ast}$ bound state that decays into $\Xi_{c}^{+} \pi$ with a significantly larger than expected cross section. This work investigates the contributions of final state interactions in the decay process, specifically examining the influence of $D^{\ast} D$ and $D^{\ast} \Xi_{c}$ final state interactions within a nonrelativistic quark model framework. The calculations reveal that the former contribution dominates, yielding a cross section that aligns with the experimental findings, whereas omitting this effect while including the latter results in a cross section that significantly exceeds the experimental data. Additionally, the study explores the influence of different kernels used in the $D^{\ast} D$ final state interaction, indicating that the UZA kernel produces a cross section that is in better agreement with the experimental data. The analysis also examines the influence of different binding energies of the $D^{\ast} D$ bound state within the range of 50 to 200 MeV, revealing that the cross section increases with lower binding energies. Furthermore, the study examines the influence of $D^{\ast} \Xi_{c}$ final state interactions, demonstrating that the cross section remains relatively low compared to the $D^{\ast} D$ contribution. Finally, the study explores the potential for measuring the $D^{\ast} D$ phase shift through the $T_{CC}$ production at a higher energy level, specifically examining the influence of a 5.5 GeV/c quark momentum, which reveals a significantly larger cross section at this higher energy level. This study provides valuable insights into the $T_{CC}$ production mechanism, highlighting the significance of $D^{\ast} D$ final state interactions within the decay process. The findings of this study also underscore the potential for utilizing the $T_{CC}$ production at a higher energy level to measure the $D^{\ast} D$ phase shift. This paper introduces a novel application of graph neural networks in the realm of subspace learning where traditional linear transformations are typically employed. By reimagining dimensionality reduction as a graph partitioning task, we leverage GNNs to develop an innovative method called GNN-based Subspace Learning (GSL). GSL utilizes two primary components - a graph construction module and a GNN encoder - to divide the data into distinct clusters based on density. We test GSL across three diverse dimensionality reduction techniques and compare its performance to existing linear subspace learning approaches using standardized datasets and evaluation metrics. Notably, our experiments demonstrate that GSL outperforms baseline methods, with comparable performance in some cases, and offers several advantages over traditional linear transformations. Additionally, this framework facilitates the integration of multiple data types and encodings into a unified subspace, making it particularly beneficial for multi-modal learning. A comprehensive codebase is available at https://github.com/alexeydudik/gsl for reproduction of the results. Further details can be found at https://dudik-lab.github.io/gsl-paper/index.html. This research investigates how various sampling methods, particularly in the context of binary matrices, influences the solutions obtained for the minimum weight codeword problem when using a greedy algorithm. Our studies reveal that random sampling methods, including those using a non-uniform probability distribution based on minimum weight codewords, can yield better performance than uniform sampling alone. Furthermore, we developed a sampling method that dynamically adjusts the probability of selecting each codeword according to its weight, resulting in a more efficient use of computational resources. Our results show that non-uniform sampling leads to significantly faster minimization of the weight of sampled codewords, with a notable improvement in running time of up to 60 times, compared to uniform sampling, achieving a minimum weight of 2 after an average of $0.45\cdot n$ iterations, where $n$ is the length of the codewords. We also explored extensions of this approach to estimate the minimum weight codeword and proved that it is accurate in most cases, while providing a worst-case error rate of at most $1-\frac{1}{p}$. We demonstrated the applicability of this research to decode binary linear codes, comparing it to the standard Gomory-Hu algorithm and the minimum weight codeword search approach. Our experiments using standard codes from the MAGMA software package showed that our sampling-based approach is more efficient in terms of computational speed, while maintaining high accuracy. We also applied this research to the minimum weight codeword problem, achieving a notable success rate of over 99% in finding codewords with a weight of 3, and over 90% in finding those with a weight of 4, in a large dataset of binary linear codes. We further extended this research to estimate the minimum weight codeword, achieving an error rate of at most $1-\frac{1}{p}$, while demonstrating its applicability to decode binary linear codes efficiently. Our results show that our approach is more efficient in terms of computational speed, while maintaining high accuracy. We also analyzed the running time of this research, revealing that it is directly proportional to the number of codewords, as well as their average weight, making it a scalable solution. This research presents a sophisticated method for solving the DGLAP equations in a comprehensive framework that incorporates a variety of PDF fitting techniques. The basis of our approach is the DAPTHOD program, which offers an innovative solution to the DGLAP problem by utilizing a combination of analytical and numerical methods. In this article, we outline a novel strategy for integrating the DAPTHOD program with existing PDF fitting tools. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through simulations using the NNPDF40 analysis as an example. Furthermore, we describe a new set of variables derived from Chebyshev polynomials that enhances the precision of PDF fits at different scales. Our results indicate that this new variables significantly contribute to the accuracy of the fit, allowing for a more rigorous testing of the DGLAP hypothesis. This integration has enabled the development of a new family of PDF sets, known as NNPDF40_DAPTHOD_nnn, which are uniquely suited for validating the DGLAP evolution at different scales. With these PDFs, we have conducted an exhaustive comparison with various datasets, including those from LHC experiments, and found that the fit remains robust against perturbative corrections up to five-loop order. Our analysis also reveals that the uncertainty in the PDFs is largely insensitive to the choice of renormalization group equation (RGE) kernel, while perturbative corrections up to three-loop order adequately describe data at very high scales. We have further developed a novel method to investigate the asymptotic behavior of parton distribution functions at extremely high scales. Using this approach, we have derived an important constraint on the asymptotic behavior of the gluon distribution function, which is universally applicable to different analysis methods and is independent of the choice of RGE kernel. This new understanding provides a significant advancement in the knowledge of parton distribution functions at extremely high scales. Finally, we have used our approach to investigate the asymptotic behavior of parton distribution functions at extremely high scales in a family of PDFs derived using the DAPTHOD program, which are uniquely suited for this purpose. Our results indicate that the gluon distribution function in the NNPDF40_DAPTHOD_nnn PDF set exhibits a power-law behavior at extremely high scales, with an exponent that is in agreement with predictions from effective theories of massless QCD. This analysis provides a significant advancement in the understanding of the asymptotic behavior of parton distribution functions at extremely high scales. This paper introduces ELKI, an open-source data mining framework, designed to surpass existing solutions such as Weka in terms of speed, scalability, flexibility, and ease of use. By leveraging multi-threading across various processing units, including CPUs and GPUs, via the Java Virtual Machine, ELKI achieves remarkable performance gains. Furthermore, the platform's modular architecture and abstract data types enable the efficient addition of new techniques and operators, resulting in a substantial enhancement of processing speeds. In comparison tests, OLAP tasks with high densities are executed up to 100 times faster on a single PC, while density-based clustering methods exhibit improved scalability through load balancing and partial data transfer. All source code is freely available under the Simplified BSD license at http://www.elswark.com. Additionally, a comprehensive tutorial is provided to facilitate the easy integration of novel techniques into the framework. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of this approach in achieving outstanding performance and flexibility. In fact, the source code has already inspired over 20 new data mining algorithms within the community. In this paper, we will detail the design of the platform, present benchmarking results, and highlight the benefits and limitations of this approach. Ultimately, we aim to foster a collaborative environment where users can contribute to, and benefit from, the ongoing development of the platform. To date, the community has created over 150 new algorithms, datasets, and other resources, which are freely accessible through the website http://www.elswark.com/wiki/index.php/Contributions. As the community continues to grow, we anticipate that the platform will remain an essential and dynamic tool for data mining applications. In fact, the recent success of the 12th Challenge has yielded an impressive 34% success rate, with 19 out of 56 participants using the platform in their research. In this paper, we will outline the history and evolution of the platform, highlighting key milestones and achievements in Section II, before presenting our methodological approach in Section III. In particular, we will discuss the underlying architecture, shared memory data types, thread management, and research applications driven by the community. In Section IV, we will delve into performance optimization techniques, including loop unrolling, data parallelism, and partial data transfer. In addition, we will outline future development directions in Section V, before concluding the paper in Section VI. This spectrum exhibits properties of weak mixing and spectral faithfulness. Similarly, subgroups of the solvable affine group $A_n(\A)$ also possess abelian, nonequivalent subgroups $R$ with the same spectral characteristics. Notably, these findings differ from previously established cases where the subgroups in question were cyclic, although they shared some similarities with the present research. It is also shown that the proposed subgroups $R$ offer a method for detecting irreducibility in representations of the solvable polynomial and affine groups. Lastly, it is proven that the solvable polynomial and affine groups cannot be expressed as the product of a finite abelian group and a finite non-identical simple group. This paper investigates the properties of quasi neural networks, which are constructed by aggregating random features derived from Gaussian processes. Our findings reveal that quasi neural networks exhibit a range of statistical properties analogous to those of standard neural networks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the neural tangent kernel acts as an efficient tool for generating these random features, thereby significantly reducing the computational requirements of training quasi neural networks. Our theoretical analysis shows that the eigenvalues associated with the neural tangent kernel decay exponentially, which in turn enables the training of quasi neural networks with an exponentially large number of parameters. In support of our theoretical findings, we include numerical simulations that validate our conclusions. Notably, we observed that the performance of quasi neural networks constructed using the neural tangent kernel was comparable to those built using standard gradient descent, despite the former having a significantly reduced computational overhead. Our research suggests that quasi neural networks offer a computationally efficient solution to standardization challenges in statistical learning tasks. For instance, we successfully applied quasi neural networks to address the problem of independent component analysis, which resulted in performance comparable to that of established methods such as nonparametric mutual information minimization and deep autoencoders. The monogamy of mutual information in quantum information theory quantifies how information about one subsystem is restricted once another subsystem is known. This principle has been extended to cover entanglement measures like entropy, yet applying it rigorously requires precise definitions of 'bulk' and 'boundary' regions in spatially configured quantum systems. This challenge has hindered the application of the principle to entropies, which are less sensitive to spatial configurations than mutual information. In our research, we define the bulk and boundary of a quantum system through local unitary equivariance and develop a unified proof of the monogamy of entropies, mutual information, and other related quantities like quantum correlation. Furthermore, our findings reveal that boundary entropies must adhere to specific minimum values, which can be seen as a derivative of the monogamy of mutual information itself. Additionally, our work shows that strong monogamy of mutual information implies strong monogamy of entropies, a relationship previously unknown. These outcomes provide a comprehensive framework for applying the monogamy of mutual information to entanglement measures like entropy, offering novel insights into quantum correlation and its regulation within spatial systems. In addition, our research delves into the properties of quantum correlation, revealing that it can reach its maximum under specific conditions and establishing a connection between it and entropy, which cannot exceed its mutual information. Finally, our work explores the connection between information paradoxes and the monogamy of mutual information, highlighting the key role it plays in resolving such conundrums. Ultimately, our research provides a unified framework that clarifies the relationships between different concepts in quantum information theory and provides a potential solution to information paradoxes. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the strong monogamy of mutual information could serve as a criterion for identifying local unitary equivariance as the correct bulk boundary, a previously unknown relationship. In addition, our research provides a novel method to compute boundary entropies without relying on the bulk boundary itself, a previously unknown connection. Advanced astronomical observations benefit from sophisticated coaddition techniques, 
yet non-linear methods compromise ideal performance by distorting point spread function 
profiles, preserving spatial resolution is crucial for uncovering cosmic mysteries. 
We investigated non-linear coaddition algorithms, specifically median and clipped-mean, 
and found they fail to maintain a consistent point spread function for all stars. 
We developed an innovative approach, weighted clipped-mean with an optimal solution formula, 
preserving key characteristics - linearity and robustness to outliers, allowing PSF maintenance. 
We tested this new method on a dataset from the DECam, comparing coadded images with optimal 
and arbitrary weight implementations, revealing a striking improvement in maintaining PSF 
shapes, preserving small-scale details, and delivering high-quality final images. 
This breakthrough technique is now available online for the community to use.

The superposition property in multiple-input single-output (MISO) channels allows for various signal processing techniques like interference alignment and cancellation to be bypassed, although it presents challenges in achieving secure communication due to the inherent presence of confidential and public information in the superposed message. This problem is particularly prevalent in applications like federated learning and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), where the superposition property is inherent, rendering it crucial to develop secure coding schemes that can effectively address these use cases without resorting to complicated eavesdropping analyses. This paper presents a comprehensive summary of existing secure coding schemes that prioritize efficient implementation over extensive security at the transmitter end, highlighting key performance trade-offs in comparison to optimal benchmarks established using dynamic programming and neural network-based approaches. Furthermore, a comparative framework is introduced to evaluate the performance of these schemes according to their design complexity, security effectiveness, and implementation feasibility. This comprehensive report is expected to facilitate and inspire further research in this field. Experimental results demonstrating the efficacy of recently proposed schemes are also presented, along with suggestions for potential future research directions. The analysis reveals that schemes employing channel state information at the transmitter and receiver (TSI-C) generally outperform those using receiver-only channel information (RCI-C). Additionally, there is a trade-off between design complexity and security effectiveness, with simpler schemes providing adequate security for practical purposes. This study's findings are anticipated to serve as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners seeking to develop and implement secure coding schemes tailored to specific applications. The analysis's conclusions are equally applicable to NOMA and MISO broadcast channels in general. The analysis's findings also indicate that secure key allocation across users presents an attractive alternative to other secure coding schemes. This paper introduces a novel class of level-set estimators known as LSPE, which leverages spectral information to analyze time-varying signals. Building upon recent advancements in spectrogram-based estimation, LSPE reframes level-set problems to optimize expected performance. Our approach encompasses signal detection and estimation, which can be viewed as limiting cases where the focus narrows to specific parts of the spectrogram. Notably, LSPE includes notable methods like subsignal localization, which emerged from recent advances in spectrogram analysis. We derive conditions for consistency, establish performance bounds, and provide recovery guarantees for finite data samples. Furthermore, LSPE is instantiated with relevant problems like subsignal localization, which is tested using simulated data; the results demonstrate its efficacy in practice. The methodology is also extended to work with discrete spectrograms, which paves the way for applications in time-varying signal analysis using Fourier transforms. Ultimately, the proposed LSPE framework offers a unified approach to tackling a range of estimation and detection challenges. Our code is available for download at https://github.com/asharwade LSPE.

This paper introduces a novel Python module, DesmosSim, which enables the modeling and simulation of physical systems utilizing symbolic expressions within graphical interfaces. The module has the capability to accurately solve complex problems involving particle motion, where numerical methods tend to struggle. A significant advantage of DesmosSim lies in its ability to leverage symbolic computation, allowing it to handle high levels of motion complexity. Furthermore, DesmosSim provides a user-friendly interface for defining physical systems and observing simulated motion over time. DesmosSim's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application in solving three challenging problems often encountered in physics, where it outperforms numerical methods and traditional programming tools. The module's source code and a guide for usage can be accessed at https://github.com/DesmosSim/DesmosSim. A video showcasing its capabilities is available at https://youtu.be/6QqQxXwYx9U. Finally, DesmosSim offers an innovative approach to symbolic simulation, empowering users to explore complex physics problems through an intuitive graphical interface. As a result, it has the potential to revolutionize the way physics is taught and learned. Due to its ease of use and the fact that no programming expertise is required, DesmosSim can be utilized as a pedagogical tool to facilitate student learning and understanding of complex physics concepts. Similarly, it can also serve as a valuable resource for teachers and researchers in physics seeking to model intricate physical systems. Moreover, DesmosSim's capabilities extend beyond physics, making it a versatile tool for modeling and simulating a wide range of engineering and physics applications. Some potential areas where DesmosSim can be applied include kinematics, dynamics, projectile motion, pendulum motion, circular motion, motion on a plane, and oscillatory motion. By utilizing DesmosSim, users can define and solve complex motion problems involving multiple particles moving along complex trajectories, as well as explore what-if scenarios to gain insights into the behavior of physical systems. Consequently, DesmosSim offers a wealth of opportunities for exploring and understanding complex physics concepts through symbolic simulation. One potential limitation of DesmosSim is its reliance on a graphical interface, which may not be ideal for complex simulations requiring high performance. The information engine concept, which harnesses information gained through measurement to drive heat flow and work production, has been particularly intriguing in the quantum realm. However, the widespread application of this idea is hindered by a common measurement challenge: the inevitable collapse of the wave function. Since fundamental quantum principles are hard to evade, developing novel measurement methods remains essential. This study investigates the potential of continuous quantum measurement in enhancing information engine performance by leveraging non-uniform states and employing two distinct methods - quantum correlation tracking and directed measurements - to enhance its operational efficiency. These approaches not only mitigate wave function collapse but also facilitate the development of an information engine that can efficiently produce maximum work in both zero- and positive temperature environments. Ultimately, the use of continuous quantum measurement has been shown to be a viable solution for developing effective information engines. This study investigates the jamming behavior of a two-dimensional stack of disks with varying weights, confined within a square box. The jamming transition for disks of the same weight occurs only when the box becomes sufficiently small, as stated by the Jurin law. In contrast, disks of different weights jam even in the largest considered box size. However, the jamming process is delayed for lighter disks placed at the bottom of the box. To visualize the structure of jammed configurations, we represent the disk stack as a directed acyclic graph, where the weight of each disk represents its jamming threshold. These experimental results provide a foundation for future research on jamming phenomena in complex systems. All data and code used in this study are freely accessible online. \end{abstract}

In multi-orbital systems, the emergence of intricate correlations is frequently facilitated by the presence of flat bands within their respective band structures. This research focuses specifically on a particular type of lattice known as the hypergraphite structure and demonstrates, both theoretically and experimentally, that flat band-induced correlation effects can occur in this geometry, particularly when it accommodates a three-orbital configuration within its atomic patterns. To achieve this, we utilized a combination of numerical simulations, specifically tight-binding modeling and the two-dimensional Hubbard model analysis, as well as experimental verification through magnetometry and specific heat measurements utilizing EuS layers integrated onto a hypergraphite template. Our findings reveal the development of flat bands in the hypergraphite's electronic structure and, as a consequence, the emergence of long-range antiferromagnetic ordering at very low temperatures, accompanied by distinct heat capacity peaks indicative of strong correlations. This study thus establishes the hypergraphite as a suitable host for hosting flat band-induced correlation effects. Additionally, we explored an array of potential variations to the hypergraphite's atomic structure, revealing numerous possibilities that could also host similar correlation effects in their electronic structures, thus expanding the scope of this research and potentially opening doors to new generations of correlated materials. Furthermore, we examined the feasibility of creating hypergraphite films using molecular beam epitaxy and found that EuS hypergraphite films exhibit characteristics that align with theoretical predictions, thus validating the feasibility of fabricating hypergraphite-based materials through this method. Ultimately, this research has paved the way for the development of new correlated materials inspired by the hypergraphite structure. Additionally, we explored the feasibility of creating hypergraphite films using molecular beam epitaxy and found that EuS hypergraphite films exhibit characteristics that align with theoretical predictions, thus validating the feasibility of fabricating hypergraphite-based materials through this method. Ultimately, this research has paved the way for the development of new correlated materials inspired by the hypergraphite structure. The effectiveness of visual click-through rate (VCTR) prediction models depends heavily on their ability to extract relevant features from the structure and content of online advertisements. This research delves into the structural composition and semantic characteristics of visual features in multi-component ad layouts, identifying the relationship between these features and click behavior. A novel, hierarchical attention-based deep learning model, HAM, is proposed to incorporate this understanding and improve the accuracy of VCTR predictions. By analyzing the hierarchical composition of ads, HAM assigns varying importance weights to different visual components according to their semantic significance. Experimental results demonstrate that HAM outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, including CNN-based models, indicating that modeling the hierarchical structure of visual features can enhance VCTR prediction capabilities. Furthermore, HAM achieves better generalization across platforms, comparing ad groups on Bing and Google, indicating its potential for real-world application in online advertising services. This study's findings provide insights into the structural features of online advertisements, shedding light on the potential of utilizing hierarchical visual information in machine learning models. Our framework addresses the privacy vulnerabilities of conditionally dependent data in Location-based Service platforms by considering the inherent relationships between locations and developing a framework that measures privacy loss for these connections. This involves combining differential privacy and the Rényi divergence, resulting in the DP-RD metric, which formulates an upper bound on privacy loss for concurrent queries affecting dependent data. Furthermore, we demonstrate the efficacy of our framework in maintaining privacy of geographic coordinates by applying it to datasets of individuals' locations and showing its superiority over traditional methods.
