The quality of the masked speech synthesis system is evaluated by comparing it to a detailed speech representation obtained using an autoencoding technique based on speech factorization. This comparison is carried out on a large, diverse speech dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that the masked speech synthesis system yields significantly superior performance in terms of natural speech quality and expressiveness. Specifically, the masked speech synthesis system outperforms a leading approach in the field by a substantial margin, achieving a significant boost of 18.1% in terms of expressiveness and 5.3% in terms of speech quality, as measured using the MOS scale. Furthermore, the proposed system exhibits enhanced capabilities in generating speech with specific characteristics, such as a lower pitch, by comparing the input speech factors to a pre-trained speech factorization model during inference. Additionally, the system's efficiency is evaluated in terms of the computational resources required to synthesize speech, which is found to be comparable to that of the baseline method. However, the proposed system exhibits improved performance at all levels of computational cost, as measured on a range of hardware configurations, including high-end GPUs. Ultimately, the masked speech synthesis system offers superior quality, a wider range of expressiveness, and enhanced flexibility, all while being computationally efficient. This research lays the groundwork for developing more sophisticated speech synthesis systems that leverage advanced neural techniques. The proposed model and data can be accessed through a public repository at https://github.com/ymcui/MaskedSpeech. Additionally, the code for the SpeechFormer model can be found at https://github.com/ymcui/SpeechFormer. Lastly, the speech synthesis example can be accessed at https://ymcui.github.io/MaskedSpeech/index.html.

Research into sparse regression analysis is widespread, with a focus on choosing the optimal subset of variables. Techniques that implement the l0 penalty for efficient variable selection are generally non-differentiable and challenging to optimize. To address this issue, methods utilizing the l1 penalty, although easier to optimize, often select multiple variables and fail to provide clear insights. Our research introduces an innovative approach that builds on the l1 penalized model, preserving its differentiability while ensuring exclusive variable selection. This method is based on the l1 penalized model's posterior distribution, derived from a non-informative prior, and incorporates the forward-backward algorithm for efficient computation. By treating the model as a probabilistic graphical model, our approach enables the selection of individual variables by exploiting the posterior distribution's sparsity. Furthermore, simulations and real-data studies confirm the superior performance of our method in achieving accurate variable selection while maintaining posterior uncertainty, when compared to state-of-the-art l0 and l1 penalized models. Our approach is implemented in the R package called FAB, which is available on CRAN. Our method is unique in that it is the first of its kind to utilize the l1 penalized model for variable selection, as evidenced by our extensive literature review. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to various types of data, including time series and count data, by modifying the model accordingly. Our method is also applicable when the response variable follows a non-Gaussian distribution, as long as the model's likelihood and posterior distribution can be efficiently computed. Our approach is computational efficient due to its reliance on the forward-backward algorithm, which scales linearly with the number of variables. Deep Neural Network adversaries have successfully created manipulative examples that deviate slightly from genuine inputs, but a new type of threat exists in the form of Man-in-the-Middle attacks that intercept data en route to a DNN. Unlike traditional adversarial examples, which originate from the data itself, Man-in-the-Middle attacks intervene between the data and the DNN. We introduce a novel framework that tackles this specific type of attack, employing both white-box and robust adversarial attacks that reach the DNN post-data manipulation. Furthermore, we introduce empirical methods for assessing the impact of Man-in-the-Middle attacks, along with a data manipulation strategy grounded in adversarial testing. The performance of our approach is demonstrated through experiments on standard image datasets, with further details and source code available online at \href{https://github.com/alexalexandrov/mitm}{this URL}. Climate change is a pressing global issue supported by overwhelming scientific evidence, yet conspiracy theories surrounding it continue to circulate widely on social media platforms. This study delves into the prevalence of climate change-related conspiracy theories shared on Twitter, examining their proliferation, impact, and sources. Analyzing over 122 million Twitter posts, our findings reveal the significant presence of ROF (Rise of the Fifth Kingdom), a group responsible for disseminating a substantial amount of this conspiracy-related content. Additionally, we identify distinct groups associated with conspiracy theories targeting specific climate change phenomena, such as global warming denial, false narratives about the science, and anti-sustainability movements. This research provides a comprehensive understanding of the spread of conspiracy theories in social media environments and highlights the importance of identifying the underlying groups driving this spread. By documenting the evolution of these conspiracy theories, we can potentially inform targeted mitigation strategies, ultimately protecting public discourse and upholding factual information. Recent direct dark matter searches have yielded negative results, with no observed discrepancy from predictions in numerous areas. Although this alone doesn't rule out dark matter, when combined with other factors such as its abundance and consistency with cosmic observations, they collectively suggest that dark matter likely complies with standard model expectations. If dark matter is non-relativistic even after horizon crossing, a common assumption, it's plausible that it was created by a new physics sector that also resolves outstanding issues in particle physics, a goal known as completion. We present an example of such a completion involving the inverse seesaw for neutrino flavour, requiring only one additional particle beyond the standard model for stability, generating dark matter, and adequately explaining neutrino properties. Furthermore, we examine the general feasibility of this approach across various parameter spaces, demonstrating that even conservative assumptions about dark matter properties can result in detectable signatures either in direct detection or in dwarf galaxy observations, or in the search for neutrino signatures resulting from dark matter decay. Notably, in our example, the neutrino flavour sector is characterised by a near-degeneracy among neutrino masses, a distinct feature supported by the neutrino oscillation data. The associated dark matter signature in direct detection experiments is expected to be discovered either by the upcoming ton-scale facilities such as CRESST, LUX-ZEPLIN, or XENONnT, or by the current generation experiments like XENON1T, with the predicted cross-section in the $10^{-16}$ eV$^2$ range. Similarly, the dark matter-induced recoil signal in the dwarf galaxy Segue 1 is anticipated to be discovered either by the upcoming generation experiments such as CTD or by the current generation experiments like EUREKA, with the predicted number of events in both cases exceeding 3$\sigma$ even when assuming conservative parameters. Lastly, the dark matter decay into neutrinos is expected to be discovered either by the upcoming generation experiments such as CTD or by the current generation experiments like EUREKA, with the predicted number of events exceeding 3$\sigma$ even when assuming the most conservative parameters. The associated neutrino flavour effects in neutrinoless double beta-decay and in long baseline neutrino experiments are minimal, with no expected impact on the established model predictions. This paper builds on the framework of exangulated categories by introducing Serre duality in this context, alongside equivalent conditions for its existence. We then identify criteria for Serre duality's presence in specific types of exangulated categories, including derived categories of local maximal subcategories of exangulated categories with a Trivial Hom-Trail property. Additionally, we establish relationships between the duality in exangulated categories and that in corresponding derived categories. Furthermore, examples are provided to illustrate the cases where Serre duality does not apply in exangulated categories. One notable example shows that the Hom-Trail property is strictly weaker than the condition for non-vanishing of Ext-dimension in exangulated categories. Lastly, the paper introduces the concept of perfect duality in exanglated categories, along with its characteristics and the condition for its presence which is rooted in the Hom-Trail property. It is also demonstrated that perfect duality can be obtained from Serre duality under specific conditions. Moreover, the duality in the case of the derived category of a Hereditary category is analyzed. Specifically, it is shown that the duality is perfect if and only if the category has a Hom-Trail property, whereas for certain conditions on the category, the duality can be extended to obtain a Hom-Trail property. Some additional results concerning the derived categories of hereditary categories are presented, including the characterization of the duality in terms of the first syzygy functor and the characteristics of the kernel of this functor. Additionally, it is shown that the duality can be represented through a triangle equivalence involving the first syzygy functor and the characteristics of the kernel of this functor. The characteristics of the kernel functor are found to be the key in determining the presence or absence of the duality in the derived categories of hereditary categories. The study also explores the presence or absence of the duality in the case of the derived categories of hereditary algebra over a field. Specifically, it is shown that the presence or absence of the duality can be determined by the properties of the algebra, including its characteristics which dictate the presence or absence of the duality in the derived categories for certain conditions on the algebra. The study further shows that the duality can be represented through a triangle equivalence involving the first syzygy functor and the characteristics of the kernel of this functor for the case of hereditary algebra over a field with a certain condition on the algebra. This paper compares the varying outcomes earned by different higher education fields of study in Norway and Denmark. Both countries implement similar funding models, but a key difference lies in how tuition fees are handled, with Norway charging nothing and Denmark requiring students to cover some expenses. As a result, the Danish model incorporates an implicit fee capped at a government-determined maximum amount. We discover significant disparities in the earnings payoffs in both countries and find that in Norway, certain fields of study yield relatively low earnings compared to others. In contrast, nearly all fields of study in Denmark generate substantial earnings surpassing the imposed fees. Interestingly, certain fields of study in both countries fail to break even according to the country's respective funding models. Ultimately, our research suggests that the Norwegian model's lack of incentives may contribute to its underwhelming outcomes in comparison to the more responsive Danish model. Additionally, our findings shed light on the potential drawbacks of both country's funding systems, highlighting the trade-offs inherent to any funding design. Ultimately, both models fall short of effectively balancing the need to ensure students make informed choices with limited information, on one hand, and managing the potential for over-investment in certain fields, on the other. Consequently, both countries may benefit from introducing more targeted and efficient funding mechanisms. Such mechanisms could be based on actual earnings, taking into account both the field of study and individual students' abilities. Introducing an element of competition through tuition fees or other funding mechanisms that tie payments to post-secondary education outcomes may also promote more informed student choices and, in turn, lead to a more optimal allocation of students across different fields. A pilot program incorporating these funding mechanics has shown promising results in other contexts, suggesting its potential for addressing the identified issues in the Norwegian and Danish funding systems. A detailed description of this mechanism is outlined in an accompanying working paper. Both studies share a common goal of ensuring an optimal allocation of students to various fields of study. Nonetheless, they differ in their approach, with the primary paper focusing on comparing the two countries' funding systems and the working paper proposing an innovative mechanism for achieving this goal. A key difference lies in the level of generality, with the primary paper presenting more general findings and the working paper featuring a more universal mechanism. As a result, both studies may appeal to different groups of readers. A third study is currently in progress, aiming to expand on the findings of both papers by incorporating individual student abilities into the earnings predictions. This new study has the potential to yield even more accurate outcomes models. A detailed outline of this research is presented

We conducted a study of how a binary's accretion process is affected when surrounded by a disc formed through a smaller merger within a larger three-body system. Using high-resolution simulations, we found that a disc indeed develops within these systems, despite the smaller binary's mass being only 0.1% of the primary's mass. Unlike typical three-body problems, where the smaller binary's disc is evaporated quickly, our results show it survives intact. Focusing on void growth, our study examines the long-term effects of matter distribution on the universe's overall structure. We discover that the long-term behavior of voids is determined by a dimensionless parameter representing the ratio of gravitational force to pressure, rather than the vacuum's negative pressure as previously thought. This finding implies that the universe's homogeneous regions will eventually resemble a de Sitter space, with the same characteristics as the interior of Schwarzschild black holes. These predictions provide valuable insights into the long-term behavior of the universe, offering a unique opportunity for future observational studies of its ultimate fate. We examine the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model, a widely used image segmentation technique, (but) find it to be heavily influenced by noise and artifacts present in the image, which significantly limits its applicability in real-world image segmentation tasks. In order to overcome this limitation, we adapt the model to segment both the noise and the structure in the image separately. We achieve this by splitting the model into two parts: first, we find the piecewise constant regions that minimize the structure cost, then use these regions as constraints to recover the true structure cost. A second optimization takes into account both the noise and the structure costs. Through extensive experiments, we find that this adapted model outperforms other segmentation models on both artificial and real image datasets. Additionally, we successfully applied the model to segment the retinal layer in a mouse eye fundus image, which is a notoriously difficult image to segment. The model and its code are available online for public use. The main challenge of the model lies in the computationally expensive second optimization step, which takes hours to complete for large images. By applying the accelerated algorithm, we were able to reduce the processing time to just a few minutes, while maintaining comparable segmentation results. The model and its code are available online for public use at https://github.com/zhengzihh/accelerated_msmc. In the future, we plan to further improve the model's efficiency and apply it to a wider range of image segmentation tasks. Ultimately, we hope to use the model to automatically detect retinal abnormalities in mouse eye fundus images, which could aid in the diagnosis of retinal diseases. The conventional view of a black hole's interaction with surrounding matter suggests a bright electromagnetic output. Nonetheless, observations of the Milky Way's black hole, Sgr A*, and the giant elliptical galaxy, M87*, reveal extremely low levels of electromagnetic radiation. To resolve this discrepancy, alternative theories propose that a thick layer of accretion disc material obstructs our view of the black hole. Recent computer simulations investigating this phenomenon have focused on steady-state conditions. To address the dynamic nature of the accretion disc, this study employs a new simulation approach using artificial intelligence, specifically neural networks, to model high-energy processes in the disc. By incorporating neural networks into the analysis, this research finds that the spectrum of the electromagnetic radiation emitted by the black hole is indeed blocked by a dense layer, formed when a portion of the disc's material becomes trapped between the disc's inner layers and the event horizon. Notably, this phenomenon is more pronounced in the case of more massive black holes, such as M87*. Furthermore, the study discovers that the trapped area can lead to the development of a mini-halo, formed when disc material becomes embedded in the black hole's gravitational field. This mini-halo can persist for an extended period, influencing the black hole's interaction with surrounding matter and potentially producing observable effects, such as variations in the electromagnetic radiation emitted. These findings suggest that the low luminosity observed in supermassive black holes, such as Sgr A* and M87*, can be attributed to a dense layer trapping our view of the electromagnetic radiation emitted by the black hole. Moreover, the study's approach using neural networks for simulating complex physical phenomena can be applied to modeling various other astrophysical systems. Finally, the study's discovery of a mini-halo and its potential to affect the black hole's interaction with surrounding matter offers new avenues for further research in the field of astrophysics. The application of Natural Language Processing in text extraction from ID cards has gained significant interest due to the rapid growth in mobile device usage. This study proposes a comprehensive system for extracting ID card information, incorporating an advanced dataset collection method and a sophisticated deep learning framework. To enhance accuracy, we employed data augmentation techniques on ID card images and collected a substantial dataset comprising 102,000 ID card images with varied backgrounds and lighting conditions. To overcome background interference during extraction, we developed a deep learning framework integrating attention mechanisms and ensemble methods based on a fully connected network. Experimental outcomes demonstrate the exceptional performance of our proposed system, surpassing existing state-of-the-art techniques with an accuracy rate of 97.23\%. This superior performance can be largely attributed to the integration of ensemble methods, yielding an overall improvement of 1.13\% compared to using a single model. This pioneering research showcases the potential of deep learning in large-scale ID card text extraction through data augmentation, highlighting its immense value for NLP applications. We utilize Generative Adversarial Networks to enhance low-resolution astronomical images captured by space telescopes with limited bandwidth. The method involves training on a dataset of high-resolution images with added noise to mimic real-world observational conditions. The adversarial network is then employed to restore the noisy images to their original sharp form. Experimental results demonstrate the significant improvement in detail achieved through our method, particularly visible in the increased number of Meganz stars detected in images of the Large Magellanic Cloud before and after enhancement. With a fast reconstruction speed due to its piecewise constant nature, this method is now readily accessible for use in space telescope data analysis. This paper introduces a novel, decentralized learning approach that fosters a collaborative environment for multiple robots to work together with multiple human participants. The framework is based on Federated Learning, where data remains local and only model updates are shared, to avoid compromising entire systems due to potential data leaks. We apply this concept to robots interacting with humans in multi-robot settings, leveraging a combination of local stochastic gradient descent and model aggregation to achieve efficient learning. The effectiveness of this framework is demonstrated through its successful training of a shared motion planner on multiple robots working together with various human operators, and the comparison of its performance with traditional centralized learning methods. The results show that the proposed decentralized system produces motion plans of similar quality but with reduced communication overhead, making it particularly suitable for complex applications involving large numbers of robots and multiple human participants. This paper examines the connection between link prediction in knowledge graphs and relation extraction. We note that link prediction benefits from relation information and tends to perform better on connections involving one or two established relationships. Furthermore, there's a notable overlap in the techniques used for link prediction and relation extraction in terms of modeling and minimization techniques. These similarities suggest that relation extraction can be viewed as a specialized form of link prediction. We propose a novel approach that leverages a shared model to perform both tasks simultaneously. We test this approach on various benchmark datasets and find that it yields comparable results to existing methods. Notably, it delivers significant improvements on datasets involving single-relation targets, suggesting that there's room for further enhancements in current relation extraction methods. High-dimensional data is often efficiently handled by neural network models, but they also come with a high computational cost, hindering their use on resource-constrained devices and affecting generalization to new, unseen data. We investigate the representation learning capabilities of neural networks and discover that a local, rather than global, functional approach can lead to improved generalization for low-dimensional signals. This is achieved by introducing a Gaussian process layer that models the relationship between nearby data points, enabling efficient learning of compact representations. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method on various synthetic and real-world datasets, showing superior performance and significantly reduced computational requirements compared to conventional neural network models. Notably, our local functional approach also facilitates better generalization to new data points, both within the same class and across different classes. The source code is available at https://github.com/google-research/local-neural-networks.

This paper introduces a novel model called VAPG for describing VM-based attacks and defenses in cloud computing, particularly in terms of their impact on network traffic. The existing research on virtual machine-based attacks is limited, and there is a significant gap in understanding potential threats and defenses within this domain. Through VAPG, we have identified various attack strategies that can be employed using VMs, as well as different defense mechanisms to prevent these attacks. Our framework has been applied to study packet injection attacks in several research projects. The ultimate goal of this thesis is to contribute to the development of a comprehensive strategy for identifying VM-based attacks and defending against them. The proposed framework is versatile and can be utilized for investigating other types of attacks in the future. Our research has shown that VAPG can effectively identify malicious traffic caused by packet injection attacks and can accurately detect such attacks up to 97% of the time. Furthermore, our framework can identify the origin and destination of the attacked VMs in nearly all cases (with an accuracy rate of over 95%) and can differentiate between legitimate and malicious traffic with high precision. The main contributions of this research are the development of a novel VAPG model, the creation of a VM-based attack identification system through machine learning, and the successful application of the VAPG framework to detect packet injection attacks. The results of this research have been presented in several scientific papers based on the following topics: full network traffic analysis, traffic filtering, traffic classification using machine learning, and the integration of VAPG with a service discovery mechanism. The outcome of this research has been implemented as an open-source tool called VAPG, which is available on GitHub for public use. The VAPG tool has been utilized to conduct the experiments and gather the results discussed in this thesis. Our investigation focuses on the adaptability of large language models, specifically whether they can easily learn new languages with limited data available. We explored transferring knowledge from a multilingual model trained on 50 languages to 6 diverse languages with limited data, and our key findings are as follows: (1) while scaling model sizes effectively improves adaptability, it does so at a significantly higher cost than achieving the same result alone through increasing dataset size; (2) a universal model can learn specific patterns of each language more efficiently when given a general framework; (3) while there's a common pattern of similar words in similar languages, the uniqueness of new languages is still well-captured by their own data even when using a universal model; (4) there's a trade-off to be balanced between the complexity of models, the diversity of languages, and the availability of data; (5) there's a threshold beyond which further increasing model complexity doesn't yield substantial improvements in adaptability. Based on these findings, we recommend developing models with capabilities tailored to the specific requirements of the target languages rather than investing in overly complex models. Additionally, we suggest that efforts to create more comprehensive multilingual datasets can lead to improved adaptability, and we hope that our study will guide future research in this area. The proliferation of social media has enabled widespread dissemination of opinions, with a significant portion appearing in informal narratives rather than structured arguments. Despite their prevalence, the stories shared online often lack consideration in informed discussions, potentially due to difficulties in parsing their complex structures. This study proposes a new analysis framework that integrates machine learning and human interpretation to uncover the underlying architectures of these social media narratives, facilitating their inclusion in informed debates. Using this approach, we successfully reconstructed the narratives of two contentious issues, healthcare and immigration, in two major English social media platforms, Twitter and Reddit. Our evaluation indicates that the narratives we uncovered exhibit distinct argumentation patterns, bearing significant logical and semantic relationships, which were absent in flat opinion expressions. This research sheds light on the critical role social media narratives play in shaping public understanding, and could be exploited to devise targeted persuasion campaigns. Furthermore, it offers a novel solution for exploring social media's wealth of information, and contributes to the broader objectives of computational linguistics in two key ways: by enriching our knowledge of the social media domain through thorough corpus construction, and by developing innovative analysis techniques tailored to its unique characteristics. Additionally, our work paves the way for using NLP tools to investigate other complex social phenomena, such as conspiracy theories and fake news dissemination. Our research involved creating a highly accurate map of CMB lensing across the entire sky, and used it to measure the movement of galaxies and the underlying mass within those areas. Deep learning models excel in various applications (e.g., self-driving cars, medical diagnostics) but fall short due to vulnerabilities to deceitful inputs (e.g., adversarial attacks). Our research introduces a framework ensuring robustness in deep learning models by harnessing the strengths of both neural networks and constraint programming. We develop a novel approach for effectively training these robust models, which involves an iterative process of optimization and verification. Within this process, we employ a novel neural network capable of providing an upper bound on the model's loss under adverse conditions, while a separate constraint programming module identifies the worst-case input triggering the maximum loss. This information is then passed back to a modified neural network, which refines its parameters to minimize the predicted loss for the identified adversarial input. This cycle repeats until a balance is reached between loss and robustness. By combining this framework with regularization techniques, we achieve superior performance compared to the state-of-the-art methods, all while guaranteeing robustness against the most permissive perturbations. The proposed framework is implemented in constraint programming platform MiniSat, with source code available at https://github.com/LOST-EPFL/CP-Based-Robust-NN. Empirical evaluations on standard datasets reveal that our approach outperforms other methods, with computational performance comparable to or better than the alternative methods when feasible. Notably, we achieve the best results on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets with a test accuracy of 83.5% and 50.7%, respectively, while maintaining an impressive robustness against adversarial inputs with a test accuracy of 100% and 88.2% on the same datasets. These results represent a significant improvement over the current best test accuracy on adversarial examples, which stands at 85.2% on MNIST and 57.8% on CIFAR-10 achieved by prior work. Furthermore, we successfully validated the robustness of our model on a real-world image by applying adversarial perturbations, which otherwise would have triggered a wrong prediction. This achievement marks a significant milestone in ensuring the robustness of deep learning models using constraint programming. Finally, we successfully applied our framework to verify the robustness of a real-world image classification model, thereby showcasing its practicality and paving the way for its deployment in critical applications in the future. The underlying structure of social networks holds significant insight into the spread of rumors. This study investigates how spatial proximity and earlier transmission events (precursor features) impact the rapid decline and reduced peak of rumor diffusion. We discovered that areas adjacent to earlier rumor outbreaks experience increased participation rates and greater peak rumor intensity, whereas regions farther away experience a sharper decline. A mathematical model was developed to explain these findings and validate the accuracy of the observed phenomena through various validation methods. Additionally, this model enables analysis of the optimal strategies for limiting a rumor's spread within a local area. When comparing this approach to a more comprehensive spread mitigation method, which aims to halt the rumor entirely, we found that focusing on contained spread can lead to a higher cumulative participant count, especially in large network configurations. This difference in approach is more pronounced in randomized network settings than in highly clustered ones. Overall, this research provides valuable insights into the distinct dynamics of local area rumor spread and encourages further exploration into the varied social phenomena observed across different geographic and social environments. This study examines how effective different dimensionality reduction techniques are at preserving essential information in hyperspectral image data, thereby enabling better pixel classification. We compared several methods, including PCA, CCA, CCA-RL, and NCA, and found that PCA and CCA consistently provide the best signal reconstruction while also achieving high classification accuracy across various datasets. Notably, these methods surpass the performance of deeper neural network-based dimensionality reduction approaches. The proposed framework offers insights into constructing straightforward dimensionality reduction modules that are compatible with complex feature learning systems. Additionally, we developed a simple and efficient approach called Taxonomic Feature Enhancement (TAFE) that selectively removes redundant bands from hyperspectral images, resulting in improved reconstruction and classification capabilities. The proposed TAFE method significantly contributes to a better understanding of hyperspectral image processing and can be applied to improve existing deep neural network-based approaches. Deep neural networks require a substantial amount of data to train, resulting in a significant storage burden that also poses compression challenges. Various compression methods are available, such as quantization, model pruning, and compact model designs. Each method induces a distinct compression pattern that affects how data is transmitted to the accelerator. In order to optimize full communication, we need to consider how the compression pattern interacts with bit allocation between the host and accelerator. This joint optimization problem is the focus of our proposed framework, which yields a compression pattern independent of the specific network architecture. Our approach was thoroughly tested using real-world models and demonstrated superior performance to existing state-of-the-art techniques. Specifically, we achieved an average improvement of 11% and 20% in latency for mobile and server-based applications, respectively, while also reducing data transmission time by 4.35 times. Our findings show that a systematic approach to pattern design can lead to faster and more efficient data transmission to accelerators. Protein structure prediction has seen significant advancements in recent years, thanks largely to the de novo approach. However, the structures obtained are often distant from their experimental counterparts, necessitating further refinement. A novel method, ProCS, employs a unique approach to improve protein structure accuracy by transitioning between conformational space. ProCS uses a multi-scale potential to guide structure refinement, starting with broad conformational movements and narrowing down to precise adjustments. This approach involves dividing the protein into segments and optimizing the arrangement between them. ProCS's effectiveness has been validated through comprehensive testing on high-resolution structures and challenging structures with limited data. Compared to other top refinement tools, ProCS consistently outperforms in the former category while achieving comparable results with fewer parameters than other state-of-the-art methods. In the latter case, ProCS demonstrates significant improvements over existing methods. The ProCS algorithm, along with additional information and 35 refined protein structures, is freely accessible at https://github.com/ResearchGroupZhang/ProCS. Interactive visualization tools are available at https://zhanggroup.org/procs.

In the context of deep learning, the choice of loss function is often overlooked despite its potential impact on performance. This study delves into the properties of a previously underappreciated loss function, KL Divergence, and explores its effectiveness in various applications. However, our research reveals that training models using KL Divergence can result in poor performance, unless certain modifications are made. This finding highlights the importance of carefully selecting loss functions for specific tasks. Furthermore, KL Divergence has the unique property of being a non-symmetric function, allowing it to exhibit monotonicity properties that are desirable in certain applications. In addition to loss minimization, we identify two primary use cases for KL Divergence: constraint satisfaction and function optimization, and demonstrate the effectiveness of KL Divergence in these scenarios through theoretical justifications and experimental validation. Finally, our work includes an empirical analysis of KL Divergence in the context of overcomplete coding tasks, and surprisingly finds that it can achieve comparable results to state-of-the-art techniques. Overall, our research aims to promote the use of KL Divergence as a powerful tool for deep learning applications. All code has been openly released on GitHub at the repository link.

This paper delves into the properties of a theoretical model, comparing its adherence to fundamental principles with that of a more straightforward model based on standard parquet theory. Through detailed analysis, it becomes clear that the more complex model fails to meet certain essential criteria, specifically conservation and crossing symmetry, yet surprisingly, its overall structure remains similar to that of the simpler model. Furthermore, a more extreme version of this theoretical framework, derived using techniques of renormalization group flow, is also examined and is found to completely abandon traditional notions of amplitude composition while still maintaining certain essential properties. Crucially, this extreme model is shown to accurately describe the behavior of genuinely renormalizable theories, such as SYK and lambda-lambda, thus providing a crucial connection between its derivation and these established theories. Ultimately, this extreme model is proposed as a viable candidate for a more fundamental theory of quantum field dynamics, one that is both self-consistent and compliant with fundamental principles. Importantly, this extreme model is distinct from another theoretical framework, known as holographic duality, and is shown to potentially be applicable even at finite coupling, thus offering a significant opportunity for further exploration and investigation. Finally, this extreme model is proposed to be an ideal tool for the systematic study of quantum field dynamics across a broad spectrum of different dynamics, including both weakly coupled and strongly coupled scenarios. Some potential applications and implications of this extreme model are also explored and discussed. These include its potential to resolve long-standing conflicts, such as the problem of factorization breaking and the status of the S-matrix, and to provide a crucial connection between the principles of renormalization group flow and the structure of quantum field dynamics. emergency incidents. Currently, software tools gather input from callers through

approach called Unconstrained Risk Information Collection that lets them talk
freely while being monitored by these systems. This system first identifies the
incident type, then switches to a suitable conversation style, and finally uses
artificial intelligence to organize the collected data. We've developed an
experimental setup with over 500 real-life voice clips to test its performance,

Over time, deep neural networks have excelled in numerous applications, yet require an abundance of labeled data, which is costly and time-consuming to obtain. To mitigate this issue, active learning techniques were devised to efficiently select the most informative samples for classification purposes. However, traditional methods relying on uncertainty or diversity metrics inevitably overlook one or both of these requirements due to their limitations. In response, we propose a semi-supervised, entropy-based active learning algorithm that simultaneously maximizes both uncertainty and diversity in the selected samples, while also ensuring convergence of the models representing the underlying data distributions of the selected and unselected data points. We further validate our approach by comparing it to established methods on a range of classification tasks and observe consistent performance improvements. The proposed method, along with its corresponding code, can be accessed on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/asharif1991/SSAEL. Additionally, the used datasets are available at https://www.csie.ntu.edu.tw/~wfeng/datasets.html.

This research examines the variation in sound quality, or timbre, found in popular music recorded between 1955 and 2005 across various genres, focusing specifically on how it changes over time. Using a tool that can pinpoint distinct sound qualities in music, we analyzed the characteristics of 2,000 songs and discovered a decade-by-decade trend of similarity in sound profiles that mirrors the pace of technological change in the music industry. Interestingly, this pattern holds true across different genres, despite their internal dynamics. Additionally, we found that new artists are more likely to introduce novel sound qualities to the musical landscape, and the shift in sound qualities over time can be predicted by looking at technological advancements and the resulting stylistic evolutions in the past. This study marks the first comprehensive investigation into the temporal transformation of sound qualities in a broad range of musical recordings. Our findings suggest that the progression of sound qualities in music follows a predictable path, characterized by gradual change and the occasional sudden shift, similar to technological innovation. This research has implications for understanding how the sound of music changes over time and can inform the development of algorithms to predict future sound profiles. Moreover, it may provide insights to music producers, composers, and artists seeking to create innovative sounds. This order was then expanded by Bachmat into a complete framework for measuring the strength of mathematical axioms using a notion of degree. A crucial component of this framework is how containment relationships are defined between inference rules, which themselves are defined through a notion of reverse implication. This containment concept relies on the use of minimal proof objects to define the boundary between being contained within and containing more loosely. In contrast, Prawitz's work focused on the individual properties of the inference rules themselves without exploring their interconnections. As an alternative, our work develops a method for determining the degree of a given axiom solely by considering its individual component inference rules, thus eliminating the need to refer to containing or contained relationships. Instead, we define these relationships through a notion of reverse implication, which in turn relies on the properties of minimal proof objects. This approach aligns with Prawitz's original focus and also shows that the framework of proof-theoretic semantics as developed by Bachmat is in fact a special instance of our own method. Additionally, our work demonstrates that the same method can be adapted to analyze not just the axioms of a theory but also any individual inference rule or proof object within that theory. Furthermore, our work reveals that the standard method for analyzing the complexity of formal theories - which is based on analyzing the individual components of proof objects - is actually equivalent to analyzing the properties of these objects using the framework of proof-theoretic semantics. Finally, our work explores the relationship between the concepts of containment and reverse implication by showing that in certain situations these concepts are interchangeable, although in general they represent distinct and independent ideas. As such, our work offers a more nuanced understanding of the role of containment relationships in the framework of proof-theoretic semantics, while also identifying potential areas for development in the field. Moreover, batching yields comparable results to an optimized sequential approach, saving a significant amount of time in comparison to state-of-the-art sequential methods. As a result, batching has the potential to greatly enhance the practical application of reward learning in industries where efficiency is crucial. The tau lepton serves as an ideal particle for investigating hadronic interactions in lattice field theory due to its relatively light mass. Accurately determining the tau's mass is crucial for this research. This work presents a detailed measurement of the tau's mass using data from decays into kaons and neutrinos, carried out within the context of lattice field theory. Our analysis relies on the latest version of the Lattice QCD simulation software and the Maxima computer algebra system to analyze data from the RBC and UKQCD collaboration's ensemble, consisting of 2+1 flavors of quarks with a 1.74 TeV free quark mass, on the lattice. Our results involve a comparison of the tau's mass when bound to hadrons versus when it is at its free state, as well as an evaluation of the errors associated with this measurement. Our final result is a tau mass prediction of 1.7469(57) GeV, which aligns with experimental measurements within a margin of error that is roughly 3.25%. This study also introduces a novel method for determining the tau's mass that is based on the exponential decay of correlations between the bound and free states, which yields an upper limit on the errors associated with this measurement. Furthermore, our study examines the potential for future advancements in lattice field theory to achieve a precision of 1.6% on the tau's mass prediction, which could potentially bring it into line with experimental measurements. Finally, our study explores the potential for applying the same methods to obtain predictions for the masses of other bound leptons, such as muons and charmed taus. This study's methods and results are expected to contribute to future advancements in lattice field theory, particularly in the context of hadronic tau decays. Additionally, our study's results are expected to be presented at an international conference on particle physics in the near future. This article presents a novel method for finding first integrals for a broad category of higher-order Euler-Lagrange ordinary differential equations. It applies this approach to the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, a second-order equation, and discovers a first integral in addition to the conserved current previously known. The proposed method is also extended to conservative systems of Euler-Lagrange ODEs and used to find a first integral for the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator in higher dimensions. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that these results can be represented as polynomial combinations of variable changes, which facilitates computation. Finally, the article confirms that these first integrals are indeed independent of one another. Additionally, it is shown that the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator is a first integrable system, and a general approach is outlined to make it integrable through variable transformations. Lastly, the article explores the potential application of these findings to the original Pais-Uhlenbeck field equations. Recent research has focused on linking 2D sketches to 3D objects, yet most studies considered this as a mapping task. However, sketches fundamentally represent incomplete representations of objects, thus it's more natural to view this as a retrieval task. Given this perspective, we re-examined the existing methods and found that incorporating global features improves overall performance. Furthermore, we discovered that for abstract shapes like those found in everyday objects, global features are more effective than local details in retrieval tasks. Building on this insight, we developed Sketch2CAD, a new framework that leverages global features through a hierarchical approach combining with local details via self-supervised alignment. By employing this strategy, we achieved superior retrieval accuracy on the widely-used ShapeNet dataset, surpassing state-of-the-art performance by a substantial margin. Additionally, we achieved a remarkable 71% success rate in retrieving 3D shapes from 3D sketches on average, a notable improvement over previous studies. Notably, our approach also demonstrated remarkable cross-domain generalization capabilities and achieved a remarkable 63% success rate when retrieving 3D shapes from 2D sketches. This research introduces a novel concept in reinforcement learning, combining intrinsic motivation with extrinsic rewards. Our goal is to expedite training by leveraging this intrinsic-extrinsic structure. We investigate a specific scenario where an intrinsic reward structure provokes a spontaneous forward model, yet an extrinsic reward structure demands precise model precision. Our study shows that this combination can result in more efficient training, particularly when both types of rewards are incorporated into a single optimization process. We develop a corresponding algorithm, Self-Regulated Policy Learning (SPL), and empirically demonstrate its effectiveness by surpassing state-of-the-art performance in three challenging game environments. Notably, SPL achieves this improvement while relying on minimal computational resources. Our findings suggest that integrating intrinsic and extrinsic rewards in a unified framework can significantly boost training efficiency. Additionally, our work sheds light on the potential of intrinsic rewards in driving agents towards optimal solutions. Our source code is publicly available for replication purposes. In the realm of autonomous navigation, a crucial task is to create a map that enables a mobile agent to reach its desired destination. Most current approaches build upon a classic agent-world representation and assume perfect mapping is achievable, but this assumption is flawed as mapping is inherently error-prone. In this research, we introduce a novel model called MemoNav that tackles the challenge of robust spatial memory by learning from multiple sources, including both local and global information. Unlike traditional navigation methods, MemoNav incorporates a memory module to store environmental details and adapt its mapping strategy accordingly. We evaluated MemoNav in a simulated environment and discovered that it outperforms existing navigation methods by efficiently adapting map complexity in response to memory constraints. Specifically, MemoNav either creates detailed maps for familiar areas or generates sparse maps for unfamiliar regions, resulting in significantly higher success rates compared to other methods across a range of memory settings. Moreover, we found that MemoNav exhibits a higher degree of exploration within unfamiliar areas compared to other strategies, indicating its improved performance is not solely due to chance. In contrast, its adaptive mapping behavior is a deliberate tactic for navigating new environments effectively. In conclusion, our research demonstrates that MemoNav's a novel approach to navigation can yield positive results, and we propose it as a potential solution for a similar challenge in the domain of autonomous driving. The full details of this research can be found in our paper at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01124. An implementation of MemoNav is available at https://github.com/aleclee20/MemoNav. In the future, we aim to evaluate MemoNav's performance in a real-world autonomous driving setting. Contrary to existing sum-utility maximization methods that necessitate global information exchange, this best response framework enables local decisions without the need for communication among cells. The long-standing enigma surrounding the Hoyle state in $^{12}\textrm{C}$ continues to be explored, with a recent study focusing on the presence of non-sequential decay patterns. By examining the energy levels of $^{12}\textrm{C}$ following the $\alpha$-particle resonance at 7.65 MeV, researchers uncovered evidence suggesting a substantial portion, approximately 70\%, of the Hoyle state decays through a non-sequential process. This new finding is in addition to the established sequential decay pattern. When combined, the two theories effectively explain the observed energy spectrum. The non-sequential decay pattern is hypothesized to result from a rapid transition of the three $\alpha$-particle components directly into the ground state of $^{12}\textrm{C}$. This study offers a fresh perspective on the Hoyle state, highlighting its complex internal dynamics and the interplay between sequential and non-sequential processes within its structure. The observed phenomenon may also be applicable to other complex atomic systems. The research is now available in the latest issue of the journal Physics Letters B. For a class of channels with causal state information, we establish a fundamental connection between the characteristics of the state sequence and the capabilities of the channel, demonstrating that the memory capacity is directly tied to the entropy of the state sequence. Specifically, we show that if the entropy of the state sequence grows at a rate proportional to the number of symbols transmitted per unit time, the channel possesses a capacity of at least proportional to that same quantity, effectively rendering it infinite in a communications context. This outcome is mitigated, however, when the entropy of the state sequence is bounded by a constant, in which case the channel's capacity is finite and proportional to that constant. We also derive an efficient coding scheme that achieves this capacity, which is itself proportional to the constant bounding the state sequence's entropy. This result is significant as it implies that the performance of a channel with extensive memory can be severely limited, whereas a channel with relatively stable characteristics may be capable of efficient data transmission. To illustrate these findings, we examine two specific examples in detail. This discussion begins by establishing why complex numbers are necessary components in Quantum Mechanics, and then proceeds to derive basic principles of quantum theory from the assumption that Quantum Mechanics is formulated solely within the context of complex numbers. In this context, the fundamental assumptions made include the topological characteristics of complex space and the definition of complex differentiation. Subsequent developments lead to Schrödinger's equation, the interpretation of wave functions as representations of quantum states, and the availability of observables represented as Hermitian matrices. However, the conventional norm of quantum states is found to be incompatible with the standard characteristics of complex vector spaces. An alternative norm is proposed that is consistent with the properties of complex vector spaces, and this solution draws parallels with the choice of Lebesgue measure on real or complex spaces. Finally, the discussion concludes by examining the implications of the Schrödinger equation within the context of complex Hilbert spaces. Various attempts to extend Quantum Mechanics to involve higher-dimensional number systems have been proposed, and it is demonstrated here that such attempts are unnecessary, and the use of complex numbers is sufficient to derive the fundamental principles of the theory. Nevertheless, the possibility remains that future developments in Quantum Mechanics may necessitate the utilization of higher-dimensional number systems, and this would be analogous to how complex numbers themselves were initially introduced to represent plane vectors. Furthermore, the discussion touches upon the potential for Quantum Mechanics to be formulated within the context of differential forms, and this is seen as a desirable outcome, as it would result in a right-handed calculus being more intuitive and aesthetically pleasing. Ultimately, the exploration of right-handed quantum mechanics remains an area of ongoing research, and it is anticipated that further investigations will shed more light on its potential and limitations. A condensed version of the discussion has been presented in arXiv:2111.12117. Additionally, a series of lectures on the subject has been posted on YouTube at youtube.com/watch?v=aiwoHgfjyNo. Relevant supporting material is available at the website of the International Center for Theoretical Sciences at ictscat.org under the tag 'right-handed-quantum-mechanics'. Furthermore, a forthcoming book 'Right-handed Quantum Mechanics' will provide a more in-depth examination of the subject. This research examines the effect of limiting the geodesic distance in a graph, particularly its metric dimension. We find that truncating the geodesic distance at a certain point creates a new metric dimension, which is fully characterized in terms of the original graph's parameters when the truncation point is reached. However, this problem remains unsolved for all other possible cutoff points. Notably, constraining the geodesic distance in a tree graph creates a new metric dimension that is half the size of the original, which we prove through a straightforward algorithm. Additionally, we derive formulas for the minimum metric dimension of various graph classes resulting from this restriction. Furthermore, we investigate how this concept is related to other distance-based metrics in graphs. Finally, we explore potential applications of this investigation. To further understand the problem's complexity, we calculate exact values or provide upper bounds for the new metric dimension for specific graph types, such as circulant graphs, complete bipartite graphs, and certain combinations of these, illustrating that in some cases the new metric dimension is equal to the original, while in others it is one, two, or three. These findings are presented in a series of tables. Moreover, we examine the relationship between the minimum geodesic distance in a graph and its topological dimension, demonstrating that these two values can differ in certain graph types. Lastly, we investigate the behavior of the minimum geodesic distance in a graph's vertices as it approaches zero. Ultimately, our research provides a comprehensive understanding of the effect of limiting the geodesic distance in a graph, offering new insights into this concept. A comprehensive model was developed based on the experimental data to provide insights into the O3-UV reaction kinetics. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that an O3-UV contact time of around 10 seconds is sufficient to remove all sulfur dioxide in the flue gas. Finally, a comparison of the O3-UV process with other advanced air pollution control technologies reveals that it offers a unique combination of high efficiency, relatively low operating costs, and a relatively small footprint. Pruning methods that enable earlier termination of unnecessary computations have been highly effective in enhancing search performance. However, these methods are typically suited for static datasets and are not well-adapted to handle real-time time series data streams, where they can lead to prolonged processing times due to the inability to take the current time point into account when evaluating similarity. Furthermore, their failure to exploit the ordering information in the time series stream results in reduced search efficiency. The LMT-Index leverages a combination of lower bounding, monotone decrease, and early abandonment strategies to achieve substantial gains in search efficiency, outperforming existing approaches by up to 7x in our empirical testing across diverse datasets. In particular, the LMT-Index has shown remarkable effectiveness in processing data streams from various domains such as speech recognition, medical diagnosis, and weather forecasting. Notably, the LMT-Index has been found to be particularly beneficial when combined with a popular approximate nearest neighbor search technique, resulting in a search efficiency up to 4.5x higher than the alternative. This study investigates the impact of feedback styles on the performance of novice programmers, employing a large-scale, online setting where students' source code is evaluated against a set of predefined requirements. Four distinct feedback styles are explored, each varying in the level of access to the instructor's perspective: basic feedback focusing on code syntax, basic feedback including suggestions for improved code, reference solutions with and without explanatory comments. To assess the effectiveness of these styles, three metrics are used: code coverage, adherence to requirements, and programming skill as measured by grades. Conducting the study twice with different populations yielded consistent results, showing that the style offering insight into the instructor's perspective produces higher code coverage and improved grades, while the basic feedback styles perform similarly but fail to exceed the quality of not providing feedback at all. Notably, the medium-style feedback, suggesting ways to enhance the code, did not surpass the performance of the other two feedback styles. Based on these findings, providing clear explanations in addition to revealing the instructor's perspective may be beneficial for guiding novice programmers. This research contributes to the understanding of how to effectively use source code feedback, has practical implications for teaching and learning programming, and opens the door to further exploration of its potential. Additionally, the study's results can be utilized to inform the development of automated code review tools that more effectively guide novice programmers. Finally, the research highlights the value of examining the qualitative aspects of learning behaviors in addition to quantitative metrics such as code coverage. This knowledge can be applied to other educational settings where similar trade-offs exist between automated and human instruction. The study's code and data are publicly available for replication and extension. \end{abstract}

We introduce a novel metric to measure how much a graph is being smoothed out by a given GCN layer and utilize this progress towards development of a more efficient, over-smoothing-resistant algorithm. This research offers a rigorous examination of four widely employed estimators for determining the number of common stochastic trends, all of which are based on various modifications of the augmented Dickey-Fuller test. Our investigation demonstrates that these estimators produce reliable results, remaining accurate even in the presence of significant deviations from normality and a wide range of sample sizes. To account for non-normality, we utilize both theoretical results and simulations, which indicate that the performance of the estimators can be enhanced by adjusting their critical values. Notably, the findings reveal that the behavior of the estimators can be improved by incorporating a heavy-tailed adjustment, resulting in more robust outcomes. Furthermore, the research offers practical guidance on selecting suitable methods to identify common stochastic trends in the presence of atypical data. To facilitate implementation, accompanying software has been developed for easy use by applied economists. Conversely, when assuming normality, the estimated number of common stochastic trends is often lower. Galaxy clusters act as gravitational lenses that distort background objects, a phenomenon commonly observed in astronomy. Recent research has focused on detecting the faint effects of small objects, such as galaxies or stars, on galaxy clusters. We employed a new, efficient technique to analyze data from the Hubble Space Telescope's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys, allowing us to detect the influence of small objects on the lensing clusters MS 0737.0+6152 and RXC J0014+1609. Our results show that this technique can be used to detect the effects of objects much lighter than previously thought, without requiring detailed information about the cluster's mass distribution. We found that in MS 0737.0+6152, the presence of low-mass objects does not significantly affect the lensing distortions, whereas in RXC J0014+1609, the effects of these objects are noticeable. These findings suggest that the mass distribution of galaxy clusters can sometimes be incorrectly inferred due to the presence of low-mass objects. This discovery may have important implications for the interpretation of lensing data in the future. We also found that the mass distribution of low-mass objects in MS 0737.0+6152 and RXC J0014+1609 differs from that of galaxy clusters in general, with low-mass objects being more concentrated than expected. Finally, we found that the lensing effects of the low-mass objects in MS 0737.0+6152 and RXC J0014+1609 can be accurately reproduced using a simple model, indicating that the effects of these objects are generally consistent with each other and with the properties of the cluster as a whole. This suggests that the effects of low-mass objects can be effectively accounted for by assuming a smooth mass distribution in galaxy clusters, as is commonly done. However, we also emphasize that our findings suggest that low-mass objects can have a significant impact on the lensing effects of galaxy clusters in certain situations, particularly if the mass distribution of these objects is concentrated and extends close to the center of the cluster. Ultimately, our results highlight the importance of accurately characterizing the effects of low-mass objects in galaxy clusters in order to draw reliable conclusions about the mass distribution of these systems.}

A key finding is that content providers benefit when internet service providers collaborate, as this leads to increased investment in shared infrastructure, ultimately resulting in improved access and higher demand for their content. In contrast, cooperation has a limiting effect when infrastructure sharing is not an option, as content providers may suffer from reduced availability and slower access to the internet. A real-world case study involving content providers and internet service providers in Japan highlighted the pivotal role of cooperation in addressing the content providers' key concerns. Furthermore, it allows for the precise definition of weakly naturally trivial transformations, resulting in a unified understanding of the concepts of equivalence and weak equivalence in categories. We investigate the fit of exponential and polynomial $\alpha$-attractor models to the cosmological data combination Planck 2018, incorporating lensing, CMB, and galaxy clustering data, as well as a Hubble dataset. These models exhibit a diverse range of behaviors in their Hubble rates, which is analyzed in relation to the model's stability. While polynomial models display a more stable Hubble rate, they often show a disagreement with the combined cosmic data, with exponential $\alpha$-attractor models providing a better fit in this context. However, a comparison with the $\Lambda$CDM model reveals that exponential $\alpha$-attractor models are generally marginally disfavored, while polynomial models show a marginally better fit than the $\Lambda$CDM model in this case. Furthermore, we examine the likelihood ratios of these models, demonstrating that polynomial $\alpha$-attractor models exhibit a preference for lower $\alpha$ values and vice versa. Consequently, we suggest that future research should focus on the simplest exponential $\alpha$-attractor model to achieve the most accurate fit to the observed data. Lastly, we investigate the model's predictions for the matter density parameter and find that the $\alpha$-attractor models typically yield a higher value compared to the $\Lambda$CDM model, with the polynomial models exhibiting a stronger trend in this regard. Nonetheless, both exponential and polynomial $\alpha$-attractor models are capable of predicting a value of the matter density parameter that aligns with the results obtained from a future cosmological mission, such as the proposed Luca satellite. Ultimately, we conclude that the $\alpha$-attractor models offer a compelling framework for understanding the late-time universe due to their simplicity, flexibility, and ability to fit the observed data reasonably well. Moreover, we emphasize the significance of analyzing the late-time universe dynamics in relation to the model's stability to avoid misinterpretations of the data. Consequently, we advocate for the continued exploration of the $\alpha$-attractor models in the context of cosmology.

By developing a two-asset dynamic portfolio model with hidden asset and portfolio weights, the analysis shows that the first four cross-sectional return moments in the portfolio match the corresponding asset moments. Furthermore, the study estimates a dynamic portfolio model using daily UK stock market data from 1994 to 2021, discovering that the first four moments of the portfolio's annualized returns are 0.0009%, 0.0149%, 0.0809%, and 0.2309%, respectively. Compared to the first four moments of the FTSE100 index over the same period, the differences were found to be 0.0007%, 0.0030%, 0.0600%, and 0.0900%. Notably, the analysis reveals that the model outperforms static portfolio strategies in terms of both the gross and net returns on investment. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the model's performance is comparable to a widely used dynamic portfolio strategy designed to manage hidden asset risk. We introduce a novel deep learning approach that uses synthetic noisy data generated by Cardiac Arrhythmia (Arrhythmia) disease classification models to enhance cardiac abnormality detection in real-world applications. Traditional methods rely on explicit noise addition to existing data, but our method yields high-quality synthetic data without requiring any existing samples. We demonstrate that training a classifier on this synthetic noise can effectively improve existing data when real data is available, but our approach excels when data is scarce. We further show that our method successfully detects cardiac abnormalities in various environmental noises and common real-world interference, surpassing a model that utilized only existing data with no augmentation. Ultimately, our approach has the potential to greatly expand the applicability of deep learning in cardiac arrhythmia detection. We developed an approach to calculate electric dipole transition amplitudes for hadrons based on their internal structure. This method uses projected contributions from the initial hadron, its core, and peripheral regions to estimate transition probabilities. We applied this framework to $B\to X\nu$ decays and examined dipole form factor properties. Our analysis further involved investigating the $D\to K\pi$ form factors and identifying inconsistencies in existing lattice Monte Carlo simulations. These form factor studies were conducted using various light quark masses and lattice spacings in the almost continuum and physical quark regime, respectively. Our results were then utilized to evaluate the magnitude of electroweak penguin operators in the $B\to K\pi$ transitions. This research provided novel insights into the effects of electroweak penguins on $B\to K\pi$ transitions. Additionally, we explored the $D^+\to K^-\pi^+$ form factor $f_+(Q^2=0)$ within the nearly continuum and physical quark regimes and also examined the form factor in the transition $D_s\to K^+e^- \bar{\nu}_e$. Our findings from these form factor calculations are in line with recent experimental measurements. Finally, we investigated the $D\to \ell^+\ell^-$ decay rates and angular distributions, incorporating theoretical uncertainties. Our work is now available in the public domain as a shared code. We also compared our formalism to existing approaches, including light cone sum rules and QCD factorization, to assess consistency. This research paper investigates the twists of a torus when acted upon by a finite group, and how this action's equivariant cohomology helps to describe these twists by establishing connections with Munoz's work on the subject. Additionally, we expand upon the results by deriving more detailed information about the twists' properties, such as their generation and relations, using the structure of the group action, and the properties of the torus, including its boundary and any additional features it may have. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of a 'twist set' as a way to describe the distinct twists in an action, and we explore the properties of this set, including its structure and the relationships it bears to the action's support, splits, and extended actions, as well as the scenarios in which these sets are finite or isomorphic to the group ring of the integers. A non-credible second-price auction has sellers failing to fully capitalize on their revenue potential, as proven through previous research, and sellers who disregard the auction's terms do not necessarily act in their best interest, as this study finds. To explain this phenomenon, this study examines how sellers' cognitive biases and behavioral traits contribute to their decision-making in non-credible second-price auctions. In an experiment involving online interactions, this study discovers that sellers who engage in unfair bidding behavior, disregarding the auction's rules, often do so to express a desire for revenge against buyers, rather than a desire for increased revenue. Furthermore, sellers who engage in both unfair bidding and revenue maximization efforts are more likely to exhibit cognitive biases, such as mind-reading abilities, than those who do not engage in unfair bidding. This research suggests a novel cognitive explanation for the known phenomenon of sellers failing to fully capitalize on their revenue potential in non-credible second-price auctions. Additionally, this study's findings have significant implications for the design of online auctions, as sellers' cognitive biases and emotional expressions in these events should be taken into consideration. Finally, this study contributes to the broader understanding of the interplay between cognitive biases, emotional expressions, and decision-making in online events. Notably, this leads to an explicit presentation of the local cohomology rings of these varieties. Additionally, this formalism allows us to compute the minimal resolution of the quotient space obtained by removing the maximal ideal from the local ring of a Hessenberg variety. Furthermore, this presentation also gives rise to an explicit formula for the K\"ahler form on the tangent bundle of the Hessenberg variety, as initially proposed by Hillebrand and Sommers. The occurrence of flavor anomalies in both kaon and $B$ meson systems appears
to be linked by a common factor, with this connection suggesting the presence
of lepton-flavor universality violation. A simplified model representing a
universe devoid of additional leptons, with the exception of a single extra
fermion, is examined in this investigation. Within this framework, the anomaly
is resolved; however, this model is found to be incompatible with the constraints
imposed by charged kaon decays due to an excessively low kaon decay constant. 
An alternative model is then proposed where the anomaly is resolved without
introducing any new parameters. In this new model, the extra fermion has a mass in
the vicinity of 100 GeV, with its mixing with standard matter controlled by the
weak angle $\sin^2\theta_W$, thereby yielding the desired outcomes for both
kaon and $B$ meson systems. Furthermore, this model is found to be in harmony
with the constraints derived from direct dark matter searches, solar neutrino
observations, and the Higgs boson production and decay measurements. 
Finally, the potential for future experimental studies to discern this new
fermion is explored, with the investigation indicating that it can be produced at
the LHC via its decay into a photon and a quark, with predicted production cross
sections ranging between 0.1 and 100 fb, contingent upon the new fermion's mass. 
Consequently, discovering this new fermion may be feasible in the near future. 
Ultimately, the occurrence of the new fermion offers a promising avenue for the
resolution of the long-standing flavor anomalies in both kaon and $B$ meson

We introduce the QASPER dataset, an extensive collection of question-answer pairs in simple Spanish, designed to enhance the accuracy of machine translation through human-like interactions. By building on the foundation of the CoQA dataset in English, the QASPER dataset was created using an automatic translation method and subsequently refined through human evaluation in Spain. We utilize the QASPER dataset to test the performance of machine translation and question answering abilities in Spanish. Our research reveals that failure leads to a rapid growth of instability, whereas success prevents it from happening. However, a successful explosion can still prevent the formation of a massive, rapidly expanding star if the neutron-rich matter behind the shock is not dense enough. We also found that the development of the shock wave plays a crucial role in regulating the growth of the instability, particularly through the expansion that follows a delayed explosion. Ultimately, a more comprehensive understanding of the complex processes involved is necessary to accurately predict the behavior of supernovae. Based on this understanding, various scenarios are being explored, such as the role of non-radial oscillations and the impact of magnetic fields and turbulence within the collapsing core. regions with higher Hall conductance, more energy is transferred, enabling
