This paper presents an innovative approach to managing DNA data storage's most basic component - the primer pair - to optimize the efficient utilization of DNA data storage's fundamental building block, the storage partition. Our research reveals that existing DNA data retrieval methods are hindered by a significant storage efficiency limitation due to the high rate of misidentification events triggered by each primer pair. To overcome this issue, we have developed an advanced DNA data retrieval algorithm that can adapt to varying primer designs without compromising its overall performance. By integrating this new primer design strategy, we have achieved a remarkable improvement in storage efficiency and have enabled the simultaneous reading of multiple partitions, even with poorly designed primers, thus boosting overall system performance. Additionally, we have conducted comprehensive testing to validate our novel primer design methodology and demonstrated its practical applicability in a fully functional DNA data storage system. Experimental results show that our proposed method can boost storage density by 4.5 times and boost read throughput by 20 times compared to the best existing approaches. Our work lays the groundwork for the development of high-performance DNA data storage systems through strategic primer design. Topological states in momentum space, exemplified by nodal lines and points, share a common trait of hosting exotic boundary modes. Unlike surface states found in nodal points or Nambu-Goldstone modes, these boundary modes are isolated and appear within momentum space "deserts". A distinct feature of nodal lines is that they can be wrapped by topological surface boundary modes, as seen in Weyl points or on the surface of topological materials. This unique characteristic makes them connected to a new class of "hyper-Surface duality" in momentum space, where the nodal lines serve as a key element. Finally, we provide a list of materials that exhibit topological nodal lines, offering a valuable resource for researchers to study these phenomena experimentally. The goal of this research is to examine how the stability of algorithm performance is affected by the interaction of hyperparameters when using supervised learning methods. Through an in-depth analysis of the theoretical aspects, we identify a local maximum of the stability function, characterized by an optimal hyperparameter combination that minimizes perturbation propagation. We also demonstrate the practical applications of this research by investigating the effects of hyperparameters on the stability of a neural network classifier. The findings reveal that the hyperparameters' performance stability can be accurately predicted using the correlation matrix, and by optimizing the hyperparameters, we can significantly enhance the stability and overall accuracy of the classifier. Specifically, under the conditions tested, we observed an average improvement of 8.8% in accuracy and a 44% decrease in prediction errors along with increased stability, as measured by the difference between classification and prediction errors. A key factor limiting the broader adoption of reinforcement learning (RL) is its inability to adapt to sudden changes in complex, dynamic environments. To address this limitation, our research focuses on developing an advanced evaluation method for RL algorithms that can operate in increasingly challenging situations. We introduce a curriculum with gradual, controlled modifications to environment complexity, enabling RL algorithms to be assessed across a spectrum of difficulty levels. By continuously boosting the curriculum level as agents learn, our approach ensures that agents are consistently challenged and evaluated only after they've fully grasped the current challenges. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through comprehensive testing on a suite of iconic robotic tasks, which we enhance with a new set of complex variations featuring disparate structures to represent varying levels of curriculum complexity. Our results show that our evaluation method successfully identifies the optimal algorithm for each environment and highlight the significance of curriculum design in RL training and assessment. Additionally, the developed suite of complex robotic tasks is made available for further research and future evaluation at https://rllab.github.io/curriculed/. The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/rllab/curriculed. A video showcasing our research can be found at https://youtu.be/8Q8Q8Q8Q8Q.

This research examines a set of integers $A$, which contains $N$ elements, and explores its properties regarding occurrence in arithmetic sequences. Given a fixed number $k$ and an arbitrarily small positive number $\theta$, the investigation demonstrates that if the product $|x_p|^{d+1}$ is greater than $k$, where $x_p = \frac{x+1}{p}$ iteratively for $d+1$ times, then the conjugates of $x$ are outside the sequence. The novel aspect here is that previous results required the product to be greater than a function of $k$, involving $\log k$, whereas the current finding is more precise. Furthermore, we show that if the product can take on values smaller than $k$, while still fulfilling the given condition, then the conjugates of $x$ should be included in the sequence. The COVID-19 pandemic has caused significant strain on healthcare systems worldwide, with the highest burden seen in intensive care units. To effectively manage available medical resources, it is crucial to accurately forecast the number of patients requiring ICU admission in the near future. In contrast to traditional methods relying on historical data for prediction, this study proposes an innovative framework that leverages the analysis of visual art to forecast ICU admissions. Utilizing the creative potential of artistic features, which capture unique aspects of social behavior, the framework aims to improve prediction precision. To validate its efficacy, the framework has been tested on real-world COVID-19 data. Building upon prior research, the framework incorporates new stylistic and thematic features derived from GAN-based artwork. These features encompass diverse attributes, such as artistic style, color palette, and subject matter related to ICU admission criteria, including respiratory rate, saturation level, and temperature. By incorporating these features into a temporal-aware self-attention model, the framework achieves enhanced prediction performance compared to existing methods. Notably, the incorporation of artistic features improves prediction accuracy by 5.6% and 2.2% factors on two different data sets. Our research focuses on whether utterance-level representation learning can be
advanced through multi-task training approaches. To answer this question, we employed
the UAMI dataset, which we modified to incorporate out-of-context components.
Our findings indicate that when only context is utilized for pre-training, the
representation of utterances lacks significance. Conversely, utilizing just
utterance information yields substantial contributions. Furthermore, we discovered
two key multi-task techniques: UAMI-BERT can be enhanced by cross-lingual tasks or
the differentiation of similar sentences, whereas the UAMI-MLM can benefit
exclusively from the cross-lingual task. Lastly, we confirmed that the UAMI-BERT
and UAMI-MLM can be effectively combined to achieve the optimal performance. Our
findings were verified through extensive experiments and thorough analysis. Our
code and dataset modifications are publicly available for replication purposes.

A new approach has uncovered that residual quantum properties in a measurement outcome can be extracted using weak measurement, leading to multiple fidelities in quantum engineering. Furthermore, research has demonstrated that this concept is applicable not just to quantum systems but also to any device or physical system - whether it be classical or quantum. Our study examines this idea in the context of random phase-averaged coherent fields, a topic of interest due to their potential to model undetermined classical light. We have developed a method to extract residual quantum properties from these fields by applying a specific weak measurement procedure. The findings show that partial or complete quantum features can be extracted if the measurement procedure is adjusted appropriately. We have also calculated the maximum achievable fidelity and found that partial quantum properties can enhance the field's brightness beyond the classical limit. While full quantum extraction leads to traditional laser behavior with zero added brightness enhancement, intermediate fidelities balance the conflict between extraction efficiency and post-measurement brightness. The novel idea of applying weak measurement to analyze and manipulate non-quantum systems may offer insights into modeling complex physical phenomena where the quantum nature is unclear. It could potentially provide a novel approach to mathematical modeling, potentially opening doors to new computational tools. The research presented is experimentally feasible using modern technology and could potentially lead to innovative applications in physics and computer science. The findings of this study are expected to be applied in future investigations into the extraction of residual quantum properties in other systems as well. The concept of weak measurement has far-reaching implications that extend beyond the realm of quantum physics and may have a profound impact on the field as a whole. The research presented is original and contributes to the ongoing discussion regarding the role of measurement in physics. In the field of relationship psychology, relationships evolve through a series of interactions influenced by various external factors. Researchers have recently developed methods to model these processes using graph recurrent neural networks. However, these graphs are typically static, whereas real-life relationships are dynamic by nature. To reflect this change, we introduce a novel framework known as Relationship Evolution Network (RENet). It integrates a gated recurrent unit (GRU) based mechanism at each node to update relationship states accordingly. Furthermore, a relationship transfer mechanism is implemented through an attention-based approach to temporarily transfer knowledge between nodes to establish a temporary network. To optimize this temporary network, we employ a node importance mechanism that selects the most relevant nodes for knowledge transfer. Through extensive empirical validation on multiple datasets, we demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed Relationship Evolution Network compared to existing graph-based models. Notably, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the tasks of predicting relationship stages and classification. To facilitate further research, we also present a publicly accessible repository containing our source code and the experiment results. https://github.com/Chen-Ethan/RENet. During an in-depth analysis of complex graphs, a detailed examination of each node may not be necessary; some nodes provide minimal or no new insights compared to others. This realization has led us to develop a method for efficiently training neural network models by selectively focusing on the most informative nodes in each training iteration. This strategy allows the model to learn from relevant nodes more efficiently, and by doing so, it can be trained much faster. We've tested our approach on various types of graphs, and the results show that it significantly improves training speed without compromising accuracy; in fact, the model performs just as well as similarly complex ones trained conventionally. Interestingly, when applied to nodes in an already learned graph, this strategy can be used for efficient transfer learning and efficient approximation; in our experiments, we've seen significant improvements in both cases. We've also developed an innovative method to determine which nodes are most informative, which provides valuable new insights for graph analysis. Overall, this new approach offers a groundbreaking way to efficiently handle complex graphs, and its applications can impact various fields such as biochemistry, social network analysis, and material science. We've developed a user-friendly, open-source system that makes it easy for researchers to adopt this new technique and explore its potential further. This system can be accessed at https://github.com/NeuroScapeLabs/ASGNP. Additionally, the code for reproducing the experimental results is available at https://github.com/NeuroScapeLabs/ASGNP-Repros. We've also included a detailed explanation of the experiments and how to customize the system for your own research needs at https://neuroscaipelabs.github.io/ASGNP. Quantum deep learning holds significant potential to propel advancements in both deep learning and quantum computing. Despite this promise, the field is hampered by a lack of comprehensive training data and efficient processing capabilities, as current research often relies on theoretical foundations from both fields, but is hindered by practical limitations. To advance this field, more attention needs to be devoted to developing standard toolkits that can effectively integrate deep learning and quantum computing. This is similar to the experience of overcoming initial hurdles in developing neural networks. This paper aims to stimulate research in quantum deep learning by a) reviewing the current state of research in the field from both a theoretical and practical perspective, and highlighting the dual challenges it poses, and b) identifying key areas for further research and outlining a potential roadmap for future work. The author's objective is not to provide an exhaustive review but, rather, to contribute to the field by pointing out critical gaps and obstacles. This study is significant because it is the first to tackle quantum deep learning from a broad perspective that considers both fundamental and practical aspects. As such, it is hoped that this research will inspire new developments in this field. We have developed a step-by-step proof strategy for achieving a PTAS in minimizing general-valued CSPs with crisp constraints. Research findings by Akiba, Mahoney, and Chen (STOC'20) provided an initial PTAS for the specific case of real-valued CSPs with arithmetic and max-plus propositions. Our work builds upon their concepts, demonstrating a PTAS for the broader general-valued CSP class with crisp constraints. In the process, we have introduced more versatile versions of the sum-of-squares procedures originally proposed by Akiba et al. These new procedures incorporate rounding techniques that allow for the direct application of iterative rounding methods, yielding significantly clearer PTAS calculations. Furthermore, we have devised a novel method of decomposing large CSP instances into more manageable sub-problems, thereby facilitating the PTAS achievement. Lastly, we have explored connections to semidefinite programming and the Augustin calculus in order to formally justify the effectiveness of our PTAS algorithms. Specifically, we have established that certain semidefinite programming relaxations for CSPs can be effectively rounded using the concepts from the Augustin calculus, thereby justifying the existence of PTAS algorithms in these cases. These findings hold significant value as they enable the precise formulation of PTAS algorithms for a wide range of CSP classes, thereby facilitating the formal proof of PTAS existence through more intuitive and clear algorithmic constructions. Ultimately, our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the relationships between SDP relaxations, the Augustin calculus, and PTAS algorithm design, thereby illuminating new avenues for future research in this field. Additionally, our work has implications for the more general class of valued CSPs that include fractional and crisp constraints, as well as the specific case of real-valued CSPs with arithmetic and max-plus propositions, as demonstrated by Akiba et al. in STOC'20. Semantic segmentation in color image production heavily relies on details from hyperspectral images, but direct conversion is complicated by the differences in resolution and dimensions. We conducted a study of KIC 9267654, a rapidly oscillating Ap star discovered using Kepler data, to gain insights into its interior structure. This research utilized a comprehensive approach, combining photometric observations, spectral analysis, and theoretical modeling to understand the star's unusual characteristics. Our findings revealed a unique rotation velocity distribution across the star's surface, best explained by a mode with a spatial structure resembling a $J_2$ pattern, similar to other ROE stars. To account for this phenomenon, we considered various theoretical models, incorporating differential rotation, shellular rotation, and tidal interactions. Ultimately, we concluded that a conservative model involving tidal interactions induced by a nearby 0.5 day companion is the most plausible explanation for the star's unusual features, including its rapid oscillations, surface abundance patterns, and peculiar rotation velocity patterns. This discovery highlights the potential for transiting planets in binary systems to leave detectable signatures in the star's light curves. Our research also suggests that similar effects could be at play in other ROE stars, particularly those exhibiting similar rotation velocity patterns, potentially offering new avenues for investigating binary and planetary systems. This study has implications for understanding the evolutionary history of rapidly oscillating stars and their connections to wider binary populations. Ultimately, further observations and analysis are necessary to confirm or refute our theoretical findings. Based on our results, follow-up studies of other ROE stars are recommended to investigate possible binary and planetary influences on their behavior. This research has significant theoretical and observational implications for understanding the origins and evolutionary paths of rapidly oscillating stars and their connections to binary and planetary systems, particularly through the analysis of their light curves using space-based missions like Kepler and TESS. This paper introduces a randomized algorithm for solving a fundamental polynomial equation over integers in the Randomized Arithmetic Matrix Addition (RAMA) model. This model combines a random input access matrix with arithmetic matrix addition, allowing for efficient handling of polynomial integer calculations. Our solution builds upon a surprising integer factorization technique, leveraging this factorization to develop a randomized algebraic number field solution. This RAMA algorithm runs in $OND^{\omega+1}$ time, where $N$ represents the magnitude of the given integers, $D$ represents the degree of the given polynomial, and $\omega$ represents a constant between 2 and 3 that represents the exponent for matrix multiplication efficiency. This result improves the efficiency of polynomial equation solving within the RAMA model by a factor of at least logarithmic in $D$. Additionally, this work describes a parallel RAMA algorithm for solving polynomial equations, achieving an $OND^{\omega}$ time complexity and offering further evidence of the model's computational efficiency. These findings are further substantiated by a newly discovered factorization technique of random integer lattices, which demonstrates that this problem can be solved in $2^{D+1}N^{\omega+1}$ time. This factorization is complemented by a newly constructed random integer lattice that is structurally distinct from previously described lattices, revealing that it can be efficiently constructed within the RAMA model. This distinction, along with previous work on random integer lattices, allows for the development of a randomized algorithm for solving polynomial equations through lattice-based methods, which runs in $D^2N^{\omega+1}$ time and offers an alternative solution to our factorization-based approach. Notably, this polynomial equation solving algorithm is the first of its kind to be efficient in the RAMA model while also being potentially feasible in a purely deterministic setting. These results are further substantiated by a newly discovered factorization technique of random integer lattices, which demonstrates that this problem can be solved in $2^{D+1}N^{\omega+1}$ time. This factorization is complemented by a newly constructed random integer lattice that is structurally distinct from previously described lattices, revealing that it can be efficiently constructed within the RAMA model. This distinction, along with previous work on random integer lattices, allows for the development of a randomized algorithm for solving polynomial equations through lattice-based methods, which runs in $D^2N^{\omega+1}$ time and offers an alternative solution to our factorization-based approach.

Self-supervised learning has gained significant attention for enhancing recommendation systems, particularly session-based recommendation (SRB) over the past few years. A notable exception is the application of session-based contrastive learning, which typically relies on existing data to train models, ignoring the potential enhancement of data augmentation through user interactions. We introduce an innovative approach that seamlessly integrates self-supervised learning with augmented interactions to boost recommendation performance. Our method is the first to leverage user preferences in a self-supervised manner for augmenting data, thus outperforming state-of-the-art baseline methods with substantial gains of 13% and 9% in terms of click-through rate and conversion rate, respectively, without requiring any labeled data. Our source code and experiment results can be found at https://github.com/ChenXu7129/AuCLST.

Researchers have proposed various methods of introducing inductive biases into recurrent neural networks (RNNs) in order to enhance their performance, particularly in object categorization tasks.  In this study, we examine how auxiliary variables introduced during training are retained within the recurrent process and assess their impact on final task outcomes.  We discovered that the auxiliary variables developed within the recurrent neural networks were reminiscent of the auxiliary variables used during training, exhibiting a correlation of 0.95 on average.  Additionally, our experiments revealed that these internal variables contribute substantially to task success, with performance declining by as much as 75% when disabled.  A closer examination of our findings suggests that the recurrent process is primarily composed of memory management operations, with object representations accumulating in memory rather than being updated through recurrent applications.  These discoveries are further supported by the creation of a simplified model, in which an external memory component successfully replaced the recurrent neural network in a broad range of object categorization tasks.  This model outperformed the recurrent neural network on which it was based, as well as competing state-of-the-art models, by a margin of 10%.  In particular, it demonstrated superior performance on the challenging ImageNet dataset, achieving a classification accuracy 2.5% higher than the recurrent neural network and 0.5% higher than the state-of-the-art deep neural network.  A comprehensive set of ablation studies was conducted in order to validate the robustness and generalizability of this model.  The results of these studies confirm that the model is capable of adapting successfully to a wide range of task types, including both classification and localisation tasks, as well as video event detection and action recognition tasks.  In addition, we observed that the model exhibits task-specific characteristics, such as eye movements, which are reminiscent of the auxiliary variables developed during training.  These findings are further supported by the creation of a simple interface, in which a human observer accurately predicts the class of an image based on the eye movements of the recurrent neural network.  In particular, it achieves a classification accuracy 10% higher than the recurrent neural network, as well as performance comparable to that of a trained human, when eye movements are used as input. In non-Hermitian systems, the skin effect can be significantly influenced by particle interactions. To investigate this, we consider an extended version of the Hatano-Nelson model, consisting of a chain with interacting sites connected to a quasi-one-dimensional environment. By utilizing complex eigenvalue trajectories and numerical simulations, we examine the skin effect and phase transitions within this model. Notably, increased correlations weaken the skin effect, and we find that increased interactions can stabilize the skin effect under specific conditions. Our results indicate that the skin effect can coexist with localized phases, and we identify a phase diagram with distinct phases comprising skin, delocalized, and localized states. Furthermore, we propose a physical explanation for these phenomena. Our study provides a crucial connection between the skin effect and correlation-induced phase transitions in non-Hermitian systems. Additionally, we explore the skin effect's response to changes in environmental dimensionality. For example, when the environmental dimensionality is increased from two to three, the skin effect can persist, and we observe a third-order phase transition between the skin and delocalized phases in this scenario. Our research offers new insights into the skin effect in complex systems. A widely used technique, change detection through unsupervised temporal analysis, is compared to a supervised method using data from a commercial satellite imagery provider. While considering that the unsupervised method doesn't need manually labeled data, it is examined whether it outperforms the supervised method in terms of accuracy. To achieve this comparison, randomly split datasets were used to train and assess both methods. Results indicate that the supervised method excels when validation sets are concerned, yet surprisingly, the unsupervised method fares better with novel data. Furthermore, an investigation into the reasons behind this disparity included an analysis of the supervised method's reliance on rare, anomalous data points. Consequently, a modified supervised method was developed to address this issue, as well as an approach to seamlessly integrate the unsupervised method with the ability to manually correct its output using expert knowledge. Ultimately, the combined efficient and accurate data processing pipeline showed potential for improved performance in change detection analysis. Additionally, the study provided valuable insights into the characteristics of anomalous data and the behavior of supervised methods, which can be applied to a broader range of temporal analysis applications beyond change detection. Lastly, the research highlighted the practical challenges of relying on expert knowledge for validating change detection results, particularly when dealing with large areas and infrequent visual inspections. Researchers have successfully directed and controlled the magnetic exchange interaction in solid silicon by introducing a small number of dopant atoms. By using advanced numerical techniques to simulate crystal properties, the influence of various dopant positions on the magnetic properties of the surrounding silicon molecules has been extensively examined. The results show that the effective magnetic exchange interaction can be significantly altered by positioning dopants at specific locations on a silicon crystal grid. Furthermore, analysis reveals that the most effective magnetic exchange occurs between silicon molecules located at a distance of approximately three lattice units from the dopant. The study's findings provide a framework for optimizing the placement of dopants in solid silicon to either hinder or enhance magnetic properties. This research has the potential to open new avenues in the study of magnetic solid silicon. Additionally, the methods employed in this research can be applied to the study of other materials with complex crystal structures. with various techniques and tools being continuously developed and improved. In this context, 
a comprehensive open-source library known as LibOPT has been created to facilitate the testing 
and validation of optimization methods against a standardized set of benchmarking functions. 
This benchmarking library, also part of the LibOPT framework, comprises a diverse set of 109 benchmarking 
functions organized into categories based on their search spaces. Each function is accessible via its name 
or index within these categories, allowing for straightforward evaluation. In addition to the standard benchmarking 
functions, specialized sets have been developed for efficient global optimization and problem-solving.

This research calculates the transitivity degree for specific algebraic varieties, including those beyond the scope of toric manifolds, as demonstrated in an earlier study. Specifically, we derive transitivity values for Quotient bundles of projective bundles and for Fano bundles, providing a complete answer in cases where the underlying variety is a Fano bundle over a high-dimensional projective space, despite the associated middle Ext algebra being complex. Additionally, we identify the transitive toric manifolds as those corresponding to sections of toric vector bundles with at most one non-trivial splitting module. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between line bundles on a transitive variety and characters of the Weyl group for positive roots, as well as determine the transitivity degree for certain products of projective spaces and Schubert varieties within partial flag manifolds. Finally, we compute the transitivity degree for certain invariant subvarieties resulting from the action of a torus on a product of two projective spaces, as well as a specific bundle on a flag manifold derived from the symmetric group's action. These findings are presented in a table for reference. Lastly, we pose several open questions for further investigation.

This paper introduces MARBERT, a highly sophisticated model that combats misogyny.
Built upon the robust BERT architecture, MARBERT is the first to integrate
misogynistic language directly into its training, allowing it to achieve exceptional
performance in detecting misogyny compared to other state-of-the-art models.
Our comprehensive evaluations reveal that MARBERT outperforms other models across
various metrics, including a substantial 5.6% improvement in detecting misogynistic
text on the SemEval 2019 task L3 dataset. Furthermore, MARBERT exhibits a
remarkable capacity for generating coherent, misogynistic text. Our research
demonstrates that incorporating explicit misogyny into the model's training is
crucial for the model's effectiveness in identifying misogynistic content. In
conclusion, MARBERT stands out as a superior model for detecting misogynistic
content, showcasing impressive potential in various applications. The model and
source code are freely accessible at https://marbert.github.io/.

policy induction.  Ultimately, our findings demonstrate that this simple 
likelihood constraint can significantly enhance the robustness of the learned

A novel quasi-interpolation formula is developed, building on an innovative radial basis function (RBF) that combines linear and Gaussian functions with differing dimensions. This interpolation method can seamlessly accommodate grids of irregular shapes and sizes within a D-dimensional space, providing an accurate approximation of functions that may be missing data. The proposed formula can be derived from either a stochastic or deterministic approach and is derived in detail for a 1D and 2D space. The constructed interpolation methods maintain their convexity and monotonicity properties. The article also presents a convex optimization problem that determines the weights for optimal approximation of target functions. The proposed interpolation method is then applied to three real-world problems: solving a Laplace equation, performing image denoising, and completing missing data in a matrix. The results show that this RBF-based approach outperforms other interpolation methods in producing smooth, accurate reconstructions that preserve monotonicity. Natural language provides a framework for describing problems and predicting outcomes in numerous applications. Consequently, developing machine learning models that produce state representations with a logical connection to the underlying linguistic structure is highly desirable. This research investigates whether a trained neural system can produce tokenized expressions that reflect the distributional properties of their surrounding context, as previously established through analysis of human-created lexical-semantic frameworks. Our experiments reveal that a sustained period of training is necessary for a neural network to capture the inherent semantic characteristics within its internal representations. Furthermore, we developed a novel, unsupervised quantization technique that draws upon this extended training period, allowing us to extract meaningful, linguistically connected bitvectors that accurately restore the original continuous representations. Interestingly, the resulting bitvectors exhibit characteristics similar to those of human-produced word senses. This study further explores the concept of linguistic case in conditional transition models for the game of Text-Based Grid World, revealing that a neural network equipped with a linguistic case feature achieves the highest level of performance and demonstrates a notable increase in efficiency when compared to a model relying solely on a policy-based reinforcement learning approach. Our findings and supporting code are accessible at https://github.com/alegnue/adl. Additionally, all experiments were conducted using the huggingface transformer library (https://github.com/huggingface/transformers). Personalized item recommendation aims to suggest items that individuals are likely to engage with, by learning from their past interactions. The process typically involves ranking items based on the user's familiarity with them, in order of relevance. A limited number of recent items usually receive detailed processing, while older items are quickly evaluated with less consideration. This can be seen as a partial attention to the user's past interactions. We draw inspiration from this pattern, as well as the successes of neural networks in addressing complex recommendation challenges, to develop a more comprehensive approach. We propose a method that 1) leverages networks to focus on both the user's historical interactions and the recommended items, 2) utilizes an innovative mixture of learned and fixed item similarity matrices to capture both short-term and long-term trends in the data, in an unsupervised manner, 3) incorporates the user's overall engagement level as a base score, in addition to network-based recommendations. We test our approach on real-world datasets from two diverse sources, which consistently demonstrate its superior performance compared to established baseline methods. Notably, this approach has shown significant improvement on a particular dataset. We have made our source code available.

Active particles powered by molecular motors are a key area of study due to their potential to model complex biological systems and develop innovative technological applications. A particular type of particle, consisting of two linked units, has been underutilized despite offering insights into cellular processes and nanoscale machinery. To address this gap, we design a method for creating a dimeric motor protein on a surface using DNA-based building blocks, utilizing a steering wheel analogy to describe its motion in response to force and velocity. This construct, influenced by thermal forces and surface constraints, exhibits a range of motion patterns that can be adjusted to mimic different dimer configurations, powered by molecular motors in various shapes. This work lays the groundwork for using DNA-based building blocks to model active dimer motion and explore novel technological applications. Moreover, our study demonstrates the first instance of accurately measuring the torque applied to a DNA construct under steady conditions, a significant achievement in the field. This research has the potential to revolutionize the development of innovative machines at the nanoscale.

We introduce Co-Imitation Learning, a novel approach to learning collaborative policies without requiring expert guidance or prior knowledge of fellow agents. Building on prior work, we extend the concept of Imitation Learning, which typically involves mimicking expert actions, though often struggles to account for the absence of these demonstrations. Co-Imitation Learning bridges this gap by incorporating collaborative agent behavior, leveraging past shared experiences to learn a shared goal. By doing so, our method enables multiple agents to independently develop effective collaborative strategies in its absence, achieved through the integration of two key components: a shared goal learner that utilizes mutual guidance, and a collaborative agent learner that incorporates the goal while also considering past interactions. Our approach outperforms existing methods in collaborative tasks, according to both empirical evaluations and complex real-world benchmarks. Identifying the source of network interference is a crucial task in various applications, but resolving its origin in practical settings can be challenging due to numerous potential culprits. To do so effectively, it is essential to gather information about the specific units within the network that are most likely contributing to the interference, as well as their level of activity. In this research, we introduce a method to pinpoint the focal units driving interference through an analytical model. Our approach is tested in a real-world environment involving wireless sensor units, and the results demonstrate its superiority over a widely employed randomized technique. The findings indicate that selecting the optimal focal units significantly enhances the detection of network interference. To accelerate computations, we also propose a speedy approximation method. Ultimately, the outcomes of this research demonstrate that highly targeted and efficient investigations of network interference are achievable. X-ray diffraction confirmed that the material remains in its same structure across various temperatures down to 0.5 K, but failed to detect any magnetic field effects. In contrast, muon spin relaxation measurements indicate significant influence of magnetic fields at low temperatures, indicating a transition towards a spin liquid state below 0.6 K. The observed field effects are attributed to the emergence of a spin liquid state characterized by the destruction of long-range order and the presence of quasi-long range order, accompanied by the formation of 'frustrated' bonds. Notably, this almost-ideal spin liquid exhibits exceptionally short-range order up to 0.6 K, with a correlation length exceeding the distance between adjacent ions by 3-fold. The application of magnetic fields disrupts this long-range order, replacing it with a more disordered state characterized by the rapid decay of correlations with increasing field strength. The observed behavior is consistent with the predictions for the behavior of quantum dimer models under magnetic fields. The study demonstrates that [Cu(pz)$_2$(2-HOpy)$_2$](PF$_6$$_2$) serves as an exemplary model for understanding the interplay between quantum fluctuations and magnetic field effects. Furthermore, this study highlights the unique capabilities of muon spin relaxation and susceptibility measurements in elucidating the intricate magnetic properties of complex materials. The discovery of a spin liquid transition within [Cu(pz)$_2$(2-HOpy)$_2$](PF$_6$$_2$) provides significant insights into the underlying physics of quantum dimer models and the nature of valence bond glassy states, potentially paving the way for the development of new materials exhibiting similar spin liquid properties. This model incorporates axions of mass $m_{a}\simeq10^{-3}\,\mathrm{eV}$ derived from the $\eta$-invariant modulus field and additional axions stemming from the geometric and dinuclear motions of the Sun and neutron stars, respectively. The model further features complex axions of mass $m_{S}\simeq10^{-9}\,\mathrm{eV}$ and $m_{T}\simeq10^{-7}\,\mathrm{eV}$, arising from the complexified Goldstone modes of the $SU(2)_L$ gauge theory and its dark counterpart $U(2)_D$, respectively, both of which are a consequence of the strong and electroweak gauge dynamics. Specifically, we suggest examining the prospects for detecting the axion-like fields in atomic force experiments and searching for the axion itself in forthcoming astrophysical and terrestrial investigations. A significant breakthrough in classical quantum circuit simulation occurred when Huang and Yuen discovered a way to classical simulate circuits composed of Clifford and T gates more efficiently, specifically reaching an exponential improvement in certain scenarios. Building upon this discovery, our research enhances classical simulation of these circuits further by achieving a significant boost in output probability approximations. We demonstrate that exponential improvements can be achieved not only in specific scenarios but also in general cases, resulting in a more efficient classical simulation of quantum circuits. Additionally, we make a significant connection between the recently developed simulation protocols and a fundamental problem in quantum computing, the Approximate Quantum Polynomial-Time Algorithm problem, and show that our findings imply a related quantum computing complexity lower bound. This study presents an initial binary catalog derived from the LAMOST time-domain survey's initial data release and related optical follow-up data from the SDSS, AST3, and other sources.  Utilizing light curve inference models, we obtained a comprehensive understanding of the observed photometry and further developed a physical model for the binary systems, incorporating data from multiple sources.  In total, we examined 1,017 binary candidates, 906 of which were coupled with an estimated binary nature based on their light curves.  Additionally, we included 111 systems exhibiting clear eclipses, bringing the total number of binary stars in the catalog to 1,017.  By applying a detailed analysis, we found that our binary catalog aligns with established star population patterns in the LAMOST survey's field of view.  We also discovered that our binary sample is composed of 54.2% detached systems, 29.4% semi-detached systems, and 16.4% close binary stars exhibiting close proximity.  Furthermore, we found that the detached binary stars are more common in the green valley and the close binary stars predominantly reside in the young blue region.  Lastly, we found that the detached binary stars generally exhibit smaller radii and higher masses than their single star counterparts, a phenomenon that warrants further investigation in future studies.  We anticipate that our binary catalog will serve as a valuable resource for further research into various celestial phenomena.  In the future, we plan to incorporate forthcoming LAMOST data releases and related follow-up data into the catalog to further expand our understanding of binary stars.  In addition, we aim to incorporate data from other space-based missions such as Gaia and TESS to further enrich our catalog.  In the long run, we envision our catalog to be an indispensable tool for studying binary stars across the entire sky. In recent years, a trend towards edge analytics and real-time data processing has emerged, driven partly by the proliferation of mobile devices and the surging interest in the Internet of Things (IoTs). However, as devices become more miniature, so do their power sources, necessitating the use of energy-efficient hardware, including true random number generators (TRNGs). We design a novel TRNG utilizing tunneling randomness through a nanowire tunneling array, resulting in exceptionally high throughput and remarkably low power consumption. Our innovative TuRaN TRNG incorporates an advanced filtering technique based on Gaussian mixture models to surpass the performance of leading post-processing methods. We further integrate TuRaN with a high-performance cryptosystem, exemplified by the AES-128 encryption algorithm, in a unified integrated circuit, yielding a substantial 2 orders of magnitude improvement in energy efficiency and a 4 orders of magnitude improvement in area efficiency compared to the state-of-the-art in TRNG design. Our work sets the stage for the development of next-generation TRNGs and showcases the potential for randomness to be harnessed from tunneling phenomena in large-scale industrial applications. These connections are particularly evident in interlacing graphs such as trees or in scenarios involving a single path with varying edge weights. However, our findings are not limited to these specific cases and can be applied more broadly to graphs with particular properties. At its core, this research is motivated by a desire to understand the spectral measures of random walks on general graphs through the analysis of Green functions, a concept well-studied in the context of trees. A key insight is that the expected value of a squared Dirac mass function with varying amplitudes equals the negative of the graph's Laplacian. In investigating hybrid stars composed of quarks and nucleons, researchers have employed three-flavor MIT bags for quarks and nucleons within a Dirac-Sea framework. By combining these bags with different equations of state for neutron stars, various hybrid star models have been developed. Specifically, two approaches - the "constant bag model" and the "variable bag model" - are utilized to understand the behavior of matter. The constant bag model treats the quark phase as consisting solely of three-flavor MIT bags, whereas the variable bag model incorporates a background density-dependent mean field. Notably, this variable bag model is distinct from the standard nuclear matter equation of state used in neutron star research. By utilizing a density-dependent bag constant, the variable bag model offers a comprehensive representation of quark matter. Theoretical masses of hybrid stars are calculated based on this framework and are subsequently compared with existing estimates. Furthermore, the study examines the influence of bag constant and density-dependent behavior on quark matter, as well as how these factors impact the maximum hybrid star mass. Ultimately, the research reveals that the variable bag model yields hybrid star masses that are generally lower than those obtained using the constant bag model. Interestingly, when the variable bag constant is calibrated to mirror the incompressibility modulus of neutron star matter, the resulting hybrid star masses exhibit a notable resemblance to those obtained using the constant bag model at the same incompressibility level. Additionally, the study touches upon potential avenues for experimental verification of the hybrid star model via gravitational wave observations produced by binary neutron star mergers. The research concludes by highlighting the significance of the hybrid star phase in understanding the behavior of compact stars and the underlying principles of dense matter. Ultimately, the findings underscore the importance of continued exploration into the complex and multifaceted nature of dense matter.

La$_{2-x}$Sr$_x$CuO$_4$ (LSCO) is a well-studied material that exhibits metal-to-insulator behavior when its temperature or hole doping levels change. Our research has discovered that this material can also undergo a thickness-dependent metal-to-insulator transition within a specific range of temperatures and doping levels. This phenomenon was achieved by creating ultra-thin crystals using a technique called molecular beam epitaxy. Our measurements revealed that extremely thin films of LSCO ($\sim$1 nm) become insulating even when they are near the metal-insulator transition point, at low levels of doping. Furthermore, we observed that as the thickness of these films increases, their electronic properties change, eventually matching those of thicker samples, where they exhibit metallic behavior. Our findings suggest that ultra-thin crystals can be used to study the fundamental electronic properties of LSCO in a previously unexplored regime. Our research also highlights the potential for further investigation into other materials with similar thickness-dependent properties. Ultimately, this knowledge could lead to innovative technologies based on superconductivity and other unique electronic phenomena. This study examines the evolution of the Cryptocurrency Trading Network from January 2020 to December 2021. Our time-dependent analysis focuses on key characteristics: node degree distribution, clustering coefficients, fracture lines, community structures, and transaction volumes. This period saw the network partition into multiple components, influenced by the community structures and node linking patterns. We found that the Cryptocurrency Trading Network's organization is driven by a small group of popular cryptocurrencies, surrounding a core of dominant Bitcoin. Similar to other financial systems, the network exhibits a hierarchical power-law distribution, with a large proportion of low-activity nodes. Notably, the increasing complexity is mirrored in the rising transaction volumes, as measured by the total daily transactions and money exchanged. Our findings provide valuable insights into the dynamics of the Cryptocurrency Trading Network, highlighting the significance of Bitcoin and the influence of transaction volumes on network organization and complexity. This research may serve as a foundation for forecasting the future development of the Cryptocurrency Trading Network. Based on historical trends, we anticipate the network to continue exhibiting a power-law distribution and an expanding fracture line structure, with the potential for further complexity in the coming years. Conversely, a possible shift towards decentralization could result in a more balanced and homogeneous network. Regularization techniques are commonly used in deep learning model training to control overfitting and promote generalization, with certain methods also directly influencing the complexity of the models. This paper explores how training heuristics affect the complexity of deep learning models through a different perspective - by analyzing the complexity of the function classes these models originate from. It specifically examines how parameter normalization regularization affects the complexity of deep learning models, with a focus on convolutional neural networks, and finds that this type of regularization has a unique property in that it decreases the complexity of the models it is trained on, contrary to other common regularization techniques. This property is confirmed through theoretical analysis and is also observed in experiments, with results showing that training models with parameter norm regularization leads to simpler function classes, resulting in improved performance on out-of-distribution data and semi-supervised classification tasks. The benefits of parameter norm regularization are also found to extend to model pruning, with experiments showing that models regularized using this method and then pruned achieve better results than those of unpurged models and comparable results to state-of-the-art methods for deep model compression. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of these findings for understanding the behavior of deep learning models and highlights potential applications of parameter norm regularization in deep learning. With this work, the paper establishes a new perspective for evaluating the effectiveness of regularization techniques, and the results presented can be used as a foundation for future research in this area. In this context, we examine the effectiveness of data augmentation techniques as a means of scaling up training models for automated essay grading. Our approach builds upon the transformation embryo method and adapts it to create an automated pipeline that creates an enormous quantity of virtual data sets from a small set of actual essays. We then use these generated data sets along with standard transformer models to develop a grading model, which outperforms a baseline model trained solely on real essays in cross-domain and self-domain evaluation scenarios. Notably, our augmentation technique shows superior performance even when the model is subsequently applied to grading essays outside its training source. For models based on marginal relationships that involve discrete random variables, we have found that exact inference becomes computationally intensive. In response, researchers have turned to approximate methods. This study focuses on the problem of evaluating the accuracy of these approximations. Two approaches are employed for this assessment: one based on a precise analysis and another using simulation. Through this investigation, we are able to derive tight bounds on the accuracy of approximations and also uncover a previously unnoticed connection between naive Bayes classifier performance and the precision of approximations. These findings are anticipated to provide insight and guidance in selecting models and approximations for real-world problems. In support of these conclusions, we include examples from the domains of network biology and social network analysis. In the former, we examine the relationship between the performance of naive Bayes classifiers and the structure of protein interaction networks, revealing a correlation between high classification accuracy and precise approximation of conditional probabilities. In the latter, we investigate the impact of introducing artificial edges into a network and their consequences on model estimation and approximation accuracy. These experiments are conducted using synthetic and actual social network data. Additionally, we apply our proposed methods to the analysis of air pollution datasets to illustrate the practical value of our research. The distribution of opportunities within a society often favors certain groups, yet the long-term implications of this favoritism on future generations' socioeconomic standing are frequently overlooked. In this research, we develop a mathematical framework for studying the effects of unequal access to opportunities on family lineages' overall well-being, with a focus on the interaction of nature-induced and merit-based factors. Utilizing this model, we examine a range of unequal opportunity scenarios and show that, regardless of the specific conditions, some family groups will inevitably experience a significant decline in their socioeconomic status. Our model is then applied to two real-world contexts – the distribution of primary and secondary education in rural Kenya and the availability of early investing opportunities in a small economy. Additionally, we create a tool that enables users to predict the probable decline in socioeconomic status in various real-world scenarios. The potential and limitations of our model are discussed, along with possible extensions that could further clarify the decisions surrounding opportunity allocation. Our research suggests that equal access to opportunities is necessary to ensure that future generations are not disproportionately negatively affected. Moreover, our model highlights the value of accurate forecasting in making informed decisions regarding opportunity allocation, particularly when opportunities are scarce and highly correlated with individual success. Edge computing offers an alternative by de-centralizing compute power, however, managing the energy consumption of individual edge facilities remains a challenge. In this paper, we introduce a dynamic energy management system for edge computing facilities that utilizes a prediction model based on time series analysis of energy consumption. Our system optimizes energy consumption by identifying patterns in past usage and applying two efficient strategies: a reduction strategy and a suspension strategy. These strategies enable the prediction model to trigger optimal energy-saving actions. Experimental results demonstrate that our system effectively reduces energy consumption and surpasses a baseline model in savings. Notably, our suspension strategy outperforms the reduction strategy in most scenarios, indicating its greater effectiveness. Furthermore, our system exhibits excellent performance even in the absence of a perfect prediction model, making it a reliable choice for managing energy consumption in edge computing facilities. Overall, our approach can aid in the development of various energy management systems for edge computing facilities. In terms of future work, integrating our system with other technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and cloud computing could be beneficial. Additionally, exploring alternative optimization methods, such as neural networks, may also be a promising direction for further investigation. Multi-limbed robots face significant motion planning challenges due to their complex dynamics and numerous possible configurations. Current methods often apply single optimization techniques or combine different approaches with limited success, as these fail to account for the relationship between configuration and dynamics. We present a novel framework that breaks down the optimization into distinct stages tailored to various factors such as configuration, velocity, and acceleration, allowing for more precise handling of these variables. Furthermore, we introduce a new stage focused on generating feasible joint configurations that is grounded in human balancing principles. The effectiveness of our approach was demonstrated through improved planning performance for a 7-DOF octopus robot and a 12-DOF humanoid robot, as evidenced by reduced planning times and higher success rates. These gains were particularly pronounced when dealing with complex tasks involving rapid movements and late task corrections. This study investigates the behavior of a cup of coffee when rotated using an inertial plane. By employing both analytical and numerical approaches, we examined how dynamics are affected by altering the pivot point's position. The majority of our findings show that shifting the pivot leads to motion patterns differing significantly from a simple spin. We also explored the possibility of creating stable, long-lasting symmetrical patterns, similar to those observed when spinning a coin. These investigations were carried out using a more comprehensive model that accounted for the cup's movement across an inertial plane, taking into consideration factors like liquid viscosity and emptying rates. By analyzing the resulting equations, we were able to identify key factors influencing the formation of stable patterns and ultimately determine the conditions under which a cup of coffee can be consistently spun without emptying. Our research uncovered an intriguing threshold effect, where a subtle adjustment in pivot placement could often lead to pouring of the liquid. Additionally, we observed that certain dynamic patterns could trigger a rapid succession of movements, potentially resulting in the liquid's sudden change in motion, thus explaining the phenomenon of a cup of coffee "chugging." These discoveries shed new light on the intricate behavior of a cup of coffee during rotation and revealed previously unexplored dynamic motion patterns. Furthermore, our research demonstrated that even a simple system like a cup of coffee can display a wide range of complex motion patterns in response to rotation. These findings are expected to inspire further investigations into the dynamic motion of physical systems. Our study also led to the creation of a movie illustrating the cup-of-coffee dynamics for different pivot positions, which can be accessed at https://sciting.github.io/CupOfCoffee/index.html. This paper builds upon existing research into Data-parallel Distributed Stochastic Gradient Descent (DR-DSGD) by examining its convergence properties in the context of large-scale decentralized learning applications. By assuming a balanced communication environment where each device sends and receives information of the same size, the analysis reveals that DR-DSGD achieves a convergence rate of O~$((\sqrt{K} + K/n) \log T)$, where $K$, $n$, and $T$ represent the function's smoothness parameter, the number of devices, and the total number of iterations respectively. Notably, the relationship between convergence rate and parameters is remarkably accurate, with the result showing little dependence on the number of devices, iterations, or environment dynamics. To further enhance performance, two regularization methods are proposed which can enhance the communication efficiency by reducing the size of data packets. Experimentation using these techniques confirms their effectiveness in achieving better convergence rates and improved communication efficiency compared to existing methods. Our findings provide a comprehensive framework for the analysis and optimization of DR-DSGD, yielding significant gains in communication efficiency and convergence speed. The techniques developed can be applied in various large-scale decentralized learning applications, as evidenced by our experiments on image classification and language modeling across multiple platforms. The code is publicly accessible on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zhengyuyang2020/DR-DSGD. Destabilizing effect variables in safety-critical systems can significantly
impair performance and create hazards, yet their current safety standards fail to
account for these factors. This paper introduces a concept for measuring the impact
of these variables and proposes a mechanism to mitigate their effects, thereby
ensuring a higher level of safety even in the presence of destabilizing influences.
The proposed mechanism relies on an optimization technique with a safety constraint,
which can be efficiently implemented using a dynamic measuring device that captures
the behavior of the system over a limited time frame. The safety of this
destabilizing influence compensation system has been validated through formal proof. 
Additionally, we demonstrate the applicability of this concept in air traffic control.

The approach is primarily constructed by drawing from the language of machine learning, yet its underlying principle is fundamentally grounded in the core of 3D space groups. We demonstrate that using the $L$-function of a level-$p$ modular form, as defined by Ginzburg-Rubinstein-Soudry, the number of $p$-core $p'$-partitions can be calculated by applying a formula derived from the Riemann hypothesis. Under this hypothesis, the formula yields an explicit expression in terms of $p$, and when combined with the results of Merca for $p=5$, it provides a general formula applicable for prime numbers greater than 5. If the Riemann hypothesis is false, we present an alternative method to compute the partition counts by employing the Descent algorithm of Ginzburg-Rubinstein-Soudry, and the findings are exemplified for the cases of $p=5$ and $p=7$. The study also includes a program written in GAP to verify and extend the general formula it proposes for the partition counts of $p$-core $p'$-partitions. By applying this general formula, the study calculates the largest $p$-core $p'$-partitions for the prime numbers 11, 13, and 17, and presents a conjecture regarding the structure of these partitions for any prime number $p$. Furthermore, the study includes a database of the partition counts for $p$-core $p'$-partitions with $p$ ranging from 5 to 37, as well as the generating functions for these partition counts, calculated using the modular forms $L(p,\chi_{4},\psi_{p})$ and $L(p,\chi_{8},\psi_{p})$. This study enhances the robustness of point cloud models by incorporating geometric concepts to certify their performance across various real-world conditions. propose a new method for quantifying the impact of foreground removal, as
well as a statistical approach to assess its effects in a more objective manner.

analysis to provide unbiased estimates of its parameters. To illustrate this
point, we demonstrate its application in the context of Planck data and $wCDM$
model, presenting the results in tandem with those derived from the two
removal techniques discussed earlier. Importantly, we find that our approach
yields results that are more consistent with the fiducial model, while also
providing tighter constraints. To facilitate further research, we have made
the code and data underlying these analyses accessible.

The proposed method stands out from conventional solutions, as it explicitly addresses the inherent indeterminacy in conformal factors. By leveraging the conformal freedom, we've reformulated the Hamiltonian constraint as an ordinary differential equation whose solution encompasses both the physical degrees of freedom and the conformal factor. Although this solution is non-trivial and highly subject to energetic considerations, it offers a degree of regularity that allows it to be incorporated within a proposed extension of the standard Dirac method for solving the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints. The key feature of this proposal is the incorporation of the conformal structure as a fixed background against which the physical degrees of freedom are defined, thereby yielding a product structure similar to that of Dirac SEOs. The proposed method is illustratively exemplified using a simplified model based on the Einstein soliton. Although this model is highly simplified, it facilitates the exploration of the method's applicability to more intricate situations. Furthermore, it's observed that the intrinsic characteristics of the Einstein soliton facilitate a reduction to a linear system of ordinary differential equations whose solutions can be computed in closed form. This simplification enables a thorough examination of the effectiveness of the proposed method and paves the way for further research into its potential utility. The key difference between the proposed method and the multi-scale scheme lies in their treatment of the Hamiltonian constraint. While the multi-scale scheme approximates the Hamiltonian constraint by linearizing it around an initial guess, the proposed method leverages conformal freedom to explicitly address the inherent indeterminacy in conformal factors. We introduce Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), a simple and efficient semi-supervised learning technique that increases the reliance on accurate label information while dealing with a large amount of unlabelled data and limited labelled data. PILE employs a pairwise model to create logistic models, one for each class against all others, using only the labelled data. It iteratively updates these models by selectively incorporating unlabelled data based on the current logistic models' predictions, effectively increasing the weight of confident unlabelled data. As a result, PILE enhances the separation between classes and improves the overall performance. Our experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate that PILE outperforms or matches the performance of popular unsupervised and semi-supervised learning methods, including ensemble techniques, models utilizing probability distributions, and those relying on nearest neighbors, in both low and high data settings. The source code can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/tyliu20/PILE. Additionally, we have included performance metrics on other methods for completeness.

In this study, we present a novel finite element method for the vector transport equation. We test the approach by applying it to a relevant magnetohydrodynamics model in a realistic domain and observe significant speedup when solving 100 time steps. Additionally, the method produces precise and converging solutions in both smooth and discontinuous cases. This research focuses on resolving the issue of inaccessible entropy. Given a probability distribution, $f$, as input, the problem aims to compute its Shannon entropy, Condent entropy, or Kullback-Leibler divergence relative to a reference distribution, $g$. Since these quantities aren't readily available when represented symbolically, a new class of computationally efficient algorithms is proposed to tackle this challenge. Our approach involves two novel contributions: First, a method to approximate the conditional distribution, $f$, based on a sample of its underlying random variable is introduced. Second, high-precision entropy calculations are developed for both Shannon and Condent entropies. Our results demonstrate that these algorithms can efficiently handle complex distributions with minimal error. Additionally, the study explores the applicability of these tools in two practical scenarios: (1) solving the minimum relative entropy multiple-sphere covering problem and (2) computing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between two probability distributions represented symbolically. Our algorithm successfully tackles challenging instances that previously required grid-based approaches. Importantly, our results show that by utilizing our approximate conditional distribution, the accuracy of entropy calculations can be maintained at a high precision ($10^{-8}$) without the need for precise distribution evaluation. Our work thus offers a versatile toolkit for efficiently computing entropies in a wide range of scenarios. Moreover, this research highlights the potential of this toolkit in addressing various problems in coding theory and cryptography. As an example, it successfully solves a long-standing problem in quadratic forms and Thomae's problem in combinatorial cryptography. Our approach also offers promising prospects for future research in this area. Finally, our study suggests that our algorithm may find applications in probabilistic models involving continuous variables, such as continuous hidden Markov models. To validate this hypothesis, a related problem is proposed for future investigation.}

We define two essential types of measures, one characterizing the system's state and another representing the flow of units between stations. Focusing on the long-term behavior, two key aspects are investigated: first, the inherent properties of the workflow that influence its evolution, and second, the potential equilibrium conditions. To address the first concern, we establish a crucial property linking these measures with the invariant sets of the workflow's transition dynamics. To tackle the second concern, we demonstrate the existence of equilibrium measures under two distinct conditions: one based on randomness and boundedness of the workflow and another based on a more general condition applicable to any workflow. Notably, when the second condition is met, a unique equilibrium measure can be determined through a straightforward calculation. To facilitate this analysis, we introduce a novel spectral approach, which enables us to identify the unique ergodicity of the workflow's transition dynamics under any randomness, including both time-homogeneous and time-nonhomogeneous scenarios. Furthermore, this spectral method allows us to derive a formula for calculating the unique equilibrium measure in these cases. In recent years, hybrid quantum methods have gained traction as a way to take advantage of the computational advantages of quantum computers while minimizing their limitations, which are mainly related to imperfect qubit reliability. This trend has inspired the creation of HQA, a framework that combines classical and quantum techniques. Within the HQA framework, a significant class of computationally complex problems are solved, including the partitioning issue in power networks, which is also a challenging issue in terms of computation. To evaluate the performance of HQA, it was compared with the most advanced classical algorithms under realistic conditions that mimic the characteristics of current near-arithmetic qubit devices. The results show that HQA outperforms its classical counterparts in terms of accuracy, runtime, and scalability. The analysis indicates that hybrid approaches offer a viable solution to tackle complex computational challenges, even in the absence of a quantum advantage in terms of error correction, as long as there is a significant difference in the computational complexity of the problem. Therefore, this hybrid strategy has the potential to deliver substantial performance improvements on a wide range of complex problems, as long as they exhibit a significant increase in computational complexity. Recent studies of the Milky Way's center have generated considerable interest due to both/and evidence for a central bar and spiral patterns. To resolve this ambiguity, we employed a novel, realistic model of the central bar dynamics, uncoupled from nearby stellar discs. Through data-driven analysis of observed line-of-sight velocity distributions, we identified a preference for a central bar model at 300 pc with a minor-to-major axis ratio of 0.047. This preference is consistent with observations of the Sgr C cloud's anomalous velocity and velocity dispersion. Furthermore, we detected signs of a central bar surface density pattern in line with data, although a clear distinction from central spiral patterns remains challenging via velocity distribution analysis alone. To conclusively distinguish between different structural models, we suggest combining line-of-sight velocity distributions with other observational indicators, such as near-infrared photometry and astrometry. Ultimately, a comprehensive multi-component analysis is required to fully elucidate the Milky Way's central structure.

In this study, we examine the connection between multimodal and multi-objective optimization, demonstrating that the latter can naturally lead to scenarios where the former attains its outcomes. We designate this occurrence "multi-objective cross-over" (MOX). Through theoretical analysis and experimental verification in a simulated environment and using real-world benchmark problems, along with their corresponding visual representations, it is shown that incorporating diversity or similarity metrics in the multi-objective optimization of the TSP can successfully yield exact solutions to a related version of the MM-TSP. This finding highlights a significant practical implication, as it may cause local optima to become global optima, thereby potentially hindering the convergence of the multi-objective optimization process to its original form. This phenomenon is confirmed through empirical results. Additionally, a related concept known as "multi-objective emergence" (MOE) is introduced to describe situations where the multi-objective optimization process spontaneously generates solutions that are optimal in both fitness and diversity. Finally, the potential risks and benefits of proactively targeting such multi-objective cross-overs in future research are discussed. This work is expected to inspire further investigation into the underlying mechanisms of these phenomena in order to enhance optimization efficiency and potentially uncover new discovery pathways. We've found that certain clouds of unitaries have a well-defined center when equipped with a unique metric that measures stabilizer size. This cloud is comprised of unitaries that stabilize a fixed metric space under the group action of translation. When the stabilizer is not trivial, this new metric joins the original metric to create a complete distance function, resulting in a center that can be determined uniquely. This reformulation has several benefits, allowing us to prove unique existence in related theorems, such as Sturm's comparison theorem and Harnack's inequality. This cloud can be applied to study the difference operator on a metric graph, a mathematical concept that arises in the study of condensed phases in nonlocal theories, particularly in the distributionally nonlocal phase of quantum gravity and the nonlocal phase of the Gaussian cluster state. By analyzing this difference operator, we've found new insights into its spectral and asymptotic behavior, revealing a key connection to a well-known theorem in graph theory that counts the clouds' eigenvalues. This graph-theoretic approach enables the calculation of lower bounds for the differences between nonadjacent points on any graph, resulting in a new proof of a previously known inequality. This inequality itself has a previously unknown extension, expressed as $|x-y|\geq 1-H(x|y)-H(y|x)$, where $x$ and $y$ are points on a metric graph. This new inequality bears resemblance to a theorem in quantum information theory and can be applied to investigate the entanglement of a Bell state on a metric graph. Furthermore, we've discovered that this Bell entanglement is minimized only when the state is maximally entangled, and this research has far-reaching implications for the study of condensed phases in nonlocal theories. This paper presents the design of a compact, wideband antenna for use in aerospace applications, intended for operation across a frequency range of 8 to 10 GHz. The proposed antenna, constructed using a substrateless structure, comprises two identical elements paired for dipole operation. The compact size of the antenna, measuring 12 by 12 by 2.95 mm, allows it to meet the requirements for half power beamwidth and gain within a specified frequency range. The developed antenna achieved satisfactory results, including a gain of 6.2 dBi and beamwidths of 11 and 9 degrees within its desired frequency range, also exhibiting resistance to variations in air dielectric constant caused by weather conditions. The proposed antenna is now in use for global positioning satellite applications on the Canadian Space Agency's M3MSat mission.
