A key challenge in achieving fault-tolerant quantum computing lies in decoding errors from quantum codes. The process of doing so efficiently is a difficult problem, even more so when using traditional methods. We've discovered an innovative approach using a reinforcement learning technique to develop effective error correction strategies. Our quantum error correction method was successfully tested and demonstrated better performance than a standard minimal weight path decoding method. The results show a significant improvement in decoding efficiency, specifically a reduction of at least one in the number of steps required to fully recover an error or an increase of at most half in the weight of the remaining errors. The structure of our decoding algorithm is straightforward and easily implementable in a quantum environment. We've also developed a variant of the algorithm suitable for use in a classical environment. The performance of this version surpasses that of the minimal weight path method by at most twice in the weight of the remaining errors. The core of our approach revolves around introducing an information metric that facilitates the direct conversion of error syndromes into the weights of decoding paths. This novel metric has far-reaching applications, as it enables the direct conversion of error syndromies into the weights of decoding paths. The reinforcement learning agent learns a policy to select the most suitable path based on the information gained from previous steps. We've validated our approach through simulations involving the quantum surface codes and extended it to include a variant suitable for use in a classical environment. The results show that our method excels in terms of efficiency, requiring at most half as many steps as traditional methods to achieve similar outcomes. The code used in this research is freely available at https://github.com/strawberryfieldai/qecc_rl for anyone to replicate our findings. Additionally, our approach has been incorporated into the open-source software package QIP as qecc_rl package, accessible at https://github.com/strawberryfieldai/qipc. We've developed and tested a new measurement technique based on the qubit-based quantum jump method that achieves high levels of precision in reading the state of a quantum system. Specifically, this approach accurately determines the position of a quantum particle with unprecedented precision, surpassing the fundamental limits set by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. Traditionally, this level of precision would require extensive classical data processing of quantum information, but our method outperforms this standard approach, yielding more accurate results from the very beginning of the measurement process. Furthermore, our technique remains efficient even when dealing with complex quantum systems involving multiple interconnected particles. To validate our findings, we successfully demonstrated its effectiveness in a realistic quantum experiment simulating Schrödinger cat states and precisely measuring the state of a quantum particle even after it has interacted with its environment. This breakthrough method offers promising possibilities for accurately measuring quantum systems that are prone to interaction with their surroundings. Additionally, our research highlights the potential for the quantum jump method to be applied in a variety of practical applications, enhancing the precision of quantum measurements in real-world scenarios. Digital-analog quantum computing methods can leverage coherent quantum states to efficiently model complex quantum systems on a large scale, surpassing the limitations of conventional quantum computing. By applying this principle in an optical quantum network, we can simulate the behavior of the Fermi-Hubbard model using quantum states with arbitrary photon numbers. The results show that the interaction between photons in the network corresponds to the repulsive Fermi-Hubbard interaction, and the accessible Hilbert space scale independently of the system size, enabling simulations of complex many-body behaviors. The demonstrated quantum simulation technique paves the way for exploring complex quantum systems on a large scale using digital-analog quantum computing methods. Moreover, since quantum states with arbitrary photon numbers can be generated experimentally, our approach presents a feasible solution for tackling complex many-body problems. The potential of our method is further exemplified through its application in studying phase separation and complex structures within the Fermi-Hubbard model. Deep learning models often excel at processing intricate data sequences but struggle with modeling long-term dependencies within these sequences.  Longer training sequences can help with this issue, but this approach is impractical due to increased training time. An alternative is compressing complex sequences into a compact set of features that are then used to build accurate classifiers. However, developing a useful feature compression algorithm is a difficult task as it's challenging to predict the classifier performance from sequences. We've created an algorithm inspired by the pruning of neural network weights that can effectively reduce the size of training sequences, resulting in significantly shorter sequences and faster training times. Once trained, the compact sequences can be used to achieve high classification performance on long data sequences. This study introduces an advanced genetic algorithm, weighted mutation genetic algorithm, to enhance the light-gathering capabilities of narrow sensors within complex, scattered environments, significantly improving their resolution and contrast. Compared to the traditional genetic algorithm, it achieves better results, leading to a 25 percent reduction in signal increase required to attain the same level of improvement. Additionally, the study accelerates WMGA's mutation process using a variational autoencoder, enabling it to achieve high-quality results within a significantly shorter iteration period. Experimental findings validate the effectiveness of this approach in achieving high-resolution images from scattered sensors, and the improved mutation mechanism and learning-based optimization techniques collectively boost performance by 22 percent. Furthermore, integrating WMGA and end-to-end deep learning enables the creation of a learned mutation module that can adapt to various environments, producing high-quality results for unknown types of scattering situations without needing to modify the code. Images de-noised by this method reveal clearer details, and numerical data indicates a 35 percent reduction in iteration count to attain equivalent results. This technique achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods but excels them all in all tested scenarios, showcasing its superior capabilities. Speaking of deep learning, self-supervised learning has become increasingly prominent in recent times. Notably, the contrastive learning approach has been widely adopted in various applications due to its effectiveness. This body of research is vast, but we highlight some notable examples for the sake of brevity. For instance, the DeepCluster method applies the contrastive loss in a pre-trained network to generate fixed cluster labels for subsequent self-supervised training. On the other hand, there are approaches like Graspling and SimCLR that employ contrastive loss on images directly or integrated with traditional supervised methods. Notably, these methods often rely on high-quality labeled data, which can be costly to obtain. This study proposes an alternative approach by integrating contrastive loss with a generative adversarial network, leveraging self-supervised data augmentation to improve performance using unlabeled data. Experimental findings validate the effectiveness of this approach, achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art supervised methods on CIFAR10 and ImageNet, while also achieving competitive performance on other benchmarks such as Places365 and STL10. This study investigates how to utilize limited computational resources effectively when conducting policy learning. We focus on enhancing the efficiency of testing samples by merging multiple policy evaluations. Our analysis reveals that using multiple testing samples leads to more precise value function estimates, which in turn facilitates better policy improvement. We therefore introduce the efficient value function estimate, a test-efficient value function estimate characterized by minimal test requirements. This estimate outperforms existing alternatives and is paired with an adaptable sampling method that determines the ideal number of testing samples based on available computational resources. Our approach is combined with a novel variant of the well-known natural policy gradient method that uses the efficient value function estimate, resulting in a test-efficient natural policy gradient method that achieves better performance without requiring additional computational resources. Our findings are supported by numerical evaluations, which show the method's effectiveness in various challenging policy learning scenarios. We introduce a new model for short-rate dynamics that combines both stochastic and deterministic elements, allowing it to address the challenges presented by negative interest rates. This model has the advantage of bypassing the limitations of the standard Kalman filter approach, while still maintaining analytical solutions for key metrics, such as expected future interest rates and differences between short and long rates. In addition, our model features a flexible stochastic volatility component that captures the common phenomenon of increasing volatility in response to rising interest rates. We develop a novel filtering method that leverages both stochastic and deterministic aspects, allowing for efficient estimation of the model parameters. The performance of our model is demonstrated through superior empirical results compared to alternative models in two key areas: 1) matching observed market data for interest rate derivatives, and 2) generating plausible dynamics for interest rates, volatility, and their respective skewings. Notably, our model successfully reproduces the observed negative skewness in interest rate dynamics, a feat that proves challenging for other models. Finally, we apply our model to analyze the implied volatility of at-the-money interest rate derivatives over time, revealing a significant positive correlation that is absent in other models, and further highlighting the importance of accurately modeling both negative interest rates and associated volatility risk. Overall, our model offers an attractive solution for pricing interest rate derivatives, especially in environments with widespread negative interest rates. This research introduces a range of cluster-robust estimators that significantly outperform their conventional counterparts, even in small sample scenarios. We initially report the formulae for derived estimators and explain their implementation in typical econometrics contexts, such as regression analysis. We also discuss key factors to consider when applying these new estimators, including model requirements and the impact of cluster size variability. We further examine the performance of these estimators in Monte Carlo simulations and assess their robustness properties. Notably, we identify that all proposed estimators exhibit superior performance in scenarios with small cluster sizes, often matching or surpassing the conventional estimators' performance in larger cluster settings. We also conduct a practical assessment of these estimators through replication studies of established academic and real-world research, as well as a new analysis of the 1985 Chicago housing market data. Our results indicate that the newly developed estimators are a practical and effective tool for addressing heteroscedasticity of unknown form in small to medium-sized samples. We make these estimators available through the Stata software package 'clusterrobust' at this website: https://mattblackwellstats.github.io/clusterrobust/index.html. A corresponding R package 'clusterrobust' can be accessed at this repository: https://github.com/mattblackwellstats/clusterrobust. Both packages can be installed using the standard procedures for R and Stata software installation. Additionally, documentation for these packages can be found in the respective repositories and through the cited help files. We anticipate that these estimators and associated software will be beneficial for researchers working with cluster-corrected standard errors in a range of fields. We welcome suggestions for further improvements at mblackwell.economics@gmail.com. This study enhances the computational efficiency of complex interactions between fluid flows and multiple objects by adapting and refining the multi-time-step algorithm (MTSA). Direct numerical simulations of a turbulent flow surrounded by multiple objects were run with and without optimization techniques to compare their performance. Results show that the optimized MTSA reduced computational time by 50% without affecting accuracy, achieving a significant speedup improvement over traditional methods. Additionally, MTSA allowed for larger time-step sizes that maintained stable solutions, further increasing its efficacy. We then explored and extended MTSA to tackle problems involving complex geometry by successfully applying it to simulations of flows around complex objects and also to simulations of turbulent transport near numerous discrete sources. MTSA's efficiency improvements were notable in these cases, achieving a 30% to 40% speedup increase. MTSA's potential applications extend to a wide array of fluid dynamics simulations across various fields of study. A set of straightforward and adaptable implementation guidelines is provided to facilitate its adoption by researchers and engineers. MTSA's source code is available for download on the Git Hub platform under the public domain.

The movement of a liquid confined within a narrow channel, surrounded by two stationary walls into which it can penetrate, has been the subject of study for several years, particularly in the context of inkjet printing. As the liquid interacts with the walls, it draws in surrounding air, which in turn influences its movement dynamics. Researchers have now used advanced imaging techniques to visualize the interplay between this penetrated air and the liquid itself, revealing its penetration dynamics in greater detail. Their high-resolution measurements show that the air enters the channel more quickly than the liquid, yet ultimately follows a similar pattern of movement. As the liquid establishes a stable flow pattern, the air continues to flow in an alternating, oscillating motion, effectively creating an alternating flow system. This air penetration behavior has been found to be influenced solely by the air's viscosity relative to the liquid's viscosity, rather than other factors such as surface tension or Reynolds number. This new understanding of air-liquid interactions could also be applied to other systems in which fluids penetrate into confined spaces. Furthermore, their findings highlight the importance of considering the inherent uncertainties present in any high-resolution measurement data when interpreting the results, using a technique known as the "uncertainty quantification method". This approach effectively enables researchers to extract more accurate information from experimental data, effectively increasing its resolution. By applying this method to their data, they were able to achieve a level of detail equivalent to that obtained using much higher flow rates, ultimately facilitating a greater understanding of the underlying physics involved. This new approach could potentially be applied to other domains in which experimental data is limited. As a result, researchers may uncover new insights into complex systems that were previously inaccessible to them. Ultimately, this new understanding of air-liquid interactions, coupled with the innovative "uncertainty quantification method" approach, could open up new avenues for exploring a wide range of complex systems in various fields. This, in turn, could lead to a greater insight into the intricate dynamics involved in many real-world phenomena. By applying these insights, engineers may be able to design more effective cooling systems for electronic devices, develop new methods for manufacturing micro-channels, and design innovative new devices. This research has the potential to significantly impact a wide range of fields in which fluid dynamics plays a crucial role. This research introduces the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), an advanced probabilistic model designed for analyzing complex information networks. In contrast to conventional probabilistic techniques, HDTM is suited for information networks characterized by dense local structures and sparsely connected longer-distance relationships. Building upon a hierarchical Dirichlet-algorithmic representation of HDTM, the work develops efficient computational methods and empirically demonstrates the model's superior performance in uncovering document and network structures compared to established alternative approaches. Furthermore, the study showcases the effectiveness of HDTM in extracting meaningful patterns in real-world Twitter and Facebook datasets. Notably, HDTM successfully identified organized groups of users with shared political interests on Twitter. Similarly, the model used user profile information to reveal hidden clusters of users engaged in similar online activities on Facebook. Overall, the research highlights HDTM as a powerful tool for revealing the intricate structures of large information networks. Further details can be found in the accompanying thesis: "Probabilistic Models for Revealing Structures in Information Networks" (https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04231). HDTM has been open-sourced under the Apache 2.0 license at: https://github.com/krishanm/HDTM. Our analysis suggests that a substantial portion of intermediate-mass black hole mergers may be attributed to a different formation pathway, distinct from the standard one, especially noticeable at higher mass black hole densities and eccentricities. Notably, this model exhibits stable long-range entanglement, distinct from the entanglement found in the critical properties of an interacting topological insulator. We examine the entanglement structure of this model, and find that it can be characterized by a complex entanglement spectrum with contributions from both real and imaginary components. Additionally, we identify that the entanglement caused by the magnetoelectric coupling can be quantitatively compared to the entanglement caused by the interaction in a topological insulator through a scaling relationship. This suggests that the entanglement caused by the magnetoelectric coupling represents a critical case of the entanglement caused by interactions, and that the Witten effect provides a universal description of this limiting behavior. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the entanglement caused by the magnetoelectric coupling can be destroyed by a weak time-reversal symmetry-breaking perturbation, and that this destruction results in a topological Anderson insulator phase. We calculate the entanglement properties of this phase, and find that it exhibits a unique entanglement structure characterized by a localized entanglement distribution. Finally, we identify that the entanglement caused by the magnetoelectric coupling can be destroyed by a weak time-reversal symmetry-breaking perturbation, and that this destruction results in a topological Anderson insulator phase with a topological ground state protected by a combination of magnetic and magnetoelectric coupling effects. This model represents a novel realization of a topological Anderson insulator caused by magnetoelectric coupling, and provides a new example of a protected topological ground state resulting from the interplay of magnetic and magnetoelectric coupling phenomena. In contrast, if the delays within such systems are eliminated, their dimensionality suddenly increases, exemplifying a significant structural change. Utilizing the concept of effective dimensionality, we successfully predict complex dynamical behaviors, including the creation of periodic patterns and chaotic phenomena, under varying diffusion conditions in delay nonlinearities. Our findings are further validated through the observation of a transition from chaotic to turbulent behavior, illustrating the implications of our research. Additionally, we explore the potential of using delay nonlinearities with varied diffusion to create complex, high-dimensional dynamics, while also highlighting the significant structural changes that occur when such delays are minimized. Ultimately, our study provides a novel approach to understanding complex systems characterized by multiple delay sources and varying diffusion conditions. While operational semantics focuses on generating random outcomes, denotational semantics strives to capture precise probability values. To bridge this gap, we develop a probabilistic type and checking system tailored to the F$_\omega$ language, ensuring that well-typed programs can be accurately represented by context-independent probability distributions. Our methodology, sought to be novel, differs from existing high-order probabilistic program semantics, which often adopt relational interpretations, instead considering a more conservative approach, only defining a limited subset of program operators. As a positive outcome, our work yields a semantically grounded method for statically analysing probability measures in a conservative manner. Furthermore, we investigate the essential conditions under which our framework can be extended to support more complex program operators. Recent advancements in design mining have shown significant potential in linking product design with business objectives, yet conclusion stability and cross-project relevance remain significant challenges. To address these limitations, this research introduces a two-stage approach that enhances design mining: (1) a new objective function that balances conclusion validity with stability, achieved through regularization and the integration of multiple cross-project datasets; and (2) a method for improving conclusion relevance across projects by re-training filters using data from multiple projects. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of this approach, yielding improved conclusion stability and increased relevance across projects. Furthermore, this research achieves this progress while maintaining the accuracy of internal validity through the integration of statistical methods. Empirical findings are documented in a publicly accessible dataset and code repository. Based on industry feedback, this research explores practical applications of design mining within product development. Ultimately, this study proposes a new framework for design mining that prioritizes conclusion stability and cross-project relevance while maintaining internal validity. The proposed framework is positioned for potential integration into leading design mining tools. A potential extension of this research is explored in the accompanying discussion section. The proposed evaluation framework can serve as a standard guide for future research within the domain. Road conditions significantly impact people's daily lives, influencing their commute times and overall well-being. In countries with limited access to high-tech infrastructure, a smartphone-based solution can play a vital role in monitoring road conditions. By collecting and processing data via a smartphone app, we can accurately identify cracks on road surfaces. The developed framework incorporates image preprocessing techniques, a long short-term memory (LSTM) model, and a thresholding method to enhance the precision of damage detection. Notably, our approach only relies on a lateral camera view, eliminating the need for front-facing cameras, making it easily accessible and widely available. Experimental results demonstrate the exceptional performance of our proposed algorithm, surpassing alternative methods in both precision and recall. The comprehensive study further highlights the significance of various image enhancement strategies, ultimately contributing to improved road condition monitoring. A user-friendly smartphone app was designed and implemented to facilitate seamless data collection, and the source code is freely available for reference and adaptation. Imitation learning relies on agents mimicking expert behaviors within similar environment settings. Disparities between agent and expert environments can significantly impede learning progress. To address this challenge, we introduce an automated framework for pinpointing and rectifying these discrepancies. The proposed method leverages computational resources to create detailed 3D reconstructions of environments, facilitating accurate alignment or detection of differences. In our experiments, this framework successfully identifies and resolves discrepancies that hinder learning from pre-recorded trajectories in at-home robotic cooking scenarios. Additionally, this framework's detection capabilities have been applied to various environment comparison tasks. The proposed work is now available at https://github.com/alexeydg/env_diff_imitation. This research introduces a method to identify repetitive relationships among association rules by leveraging the principles of logical implication. Each association rule is considered a hypothesis, and the collective knowledge of all previously derived rules serves as the backdrop against which to assess its entailment. By analyzing the entailed rules, one can pinpoint the extent of redundancy within the rule set, with results presented in a concise format that highlights the maximum scope of such redundancy. Furthermore, our approach enables the direct identification of the most compressive subset of rules, thereby enhancing classification efficiency and eliminating unnecessary hypotheses. To facilitate high-performance processing, our methodology incorporates optimized strategies for rule pre-processing and logic simplification, thereby effectively mitigating potential computational hurdles. Our approach is comprehensive, covering all instances of redundancy, and is versatile, applicable to various data contexts, as exemplified by our experiments using market basket, protein detection, and language translation datasets. Additionally, we showcase the utility of our approach in a live demonstration. Our methodology is encapsulated in an open-source Python library, freely accessible at https://github.com/AmrYasser/ReRed. – – – The current version of this research is confined to association rule mining; its extension to other types of mined knowledge is envisioned for the future. – – – The authors would like to extend their appreciation to the reviewers for their insightful comments, which significantly contributed to the enhancement of this research. This paper employs generating functions to investigate properties of $q$-Ansioul-Hermite polynomials. A generating function for these polynomials is derived and used to establish key properties, including identities, equations and special product formulas. Notably, the same approach can be applied to obtain analogous results for other types of special polynomials. The study of $q$-Ansioul-Hermite polynomials is carried out without reference to a specific parameter value, which is in contrast to the more common treatment found in the literature. Derivatives of the $q$-Ansioul-Hermite polynomials are also examined in this context. The findings presented in this paper include a generalization of a familiar result for classical Hermite polynomials, namely that they are equivalent to a specific type of Jacobi polynomial, with the $q$-Ansioul-Hermite polynomials exhibiting a similar property for the $q$-Jacobi polynomials. The results presented in this paper can be expressed in terms of an expression for $\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f_{n}(q) z^{n}$ where $f_{n}(q)$ represents the $n$th degree $q$-Ansioul-Hermite polynomial. The approach employed in this study is analogous to that used for other types of special polynomials and is consistent with standard notation. The properties investigated include identities, equations and product formulas. In order to optimize radio map estimation, we need to efficiently collect measurements, thereby reducing unnecessary overhead. This research investigates how to optimize measurement collection based on a map uncertainty metric, and identifies a simple model that accurately represents uncertainty and facilitates optimal solution calculation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this optimal solution can be achieved by solving a modified version of the original problem, and validate our approach through simulations, outperforming existing methods. Additionally, we leverage the structure of our optimal model to enhance localization performance, and improve existing radio map estimation methods, thereby enhancing their accuracy. Simulation results reveal a substantial enhancement in localization precision and a significant reduction in measurement collection overhead. Specifically, we observe improved mapping quality and reduced overhead of 95% and 75%, respectively, while achieving superior localization performance. Notably, these gains are achieved while ensuring that the overhead of radio map estimation does not impede regular operation. Consequently, this work accelerates localization while maintaining optimal radio map quality. Finally, we highlight the broader applicability of our research to other measurement collection tasks. Firstly, we note that these techniques can be applied to scenarios involving multiple devices. Secondly, we observe that similar challenges arise in dynamically configuring measurement collection processes. Lastly, we propose future research directions in adapting these techniques for tasks beyond radio map estimation, such as channel mapping and event detection. Lastly, we outline potential avenues of research in addressing the non-metric aspects of these tasks within the aforementioned domains. Anomalies in data sequences can significantly hinder the efficiency of systems and lead to errors, thus detection is a crucial task. The majority of current methods rely on manually identified irregularities, which are supplied as labeled data for the model to learn from. Nevertheless, this process is impractical due to the resource intensity and difficulty in pinpointing all anomalies. This research delves into unsupervised anomaly detection in sequence data, focusing on discovering irregularities without relying on labeled data. We employ Recurrent Neural Networks combined with auto-encoding and feature extraction techniques to identify anomalies in SE bug reports. The approach was tested and found effective in recognizing previously unknown anomalies, outperforming existing methods confirmed by expert evaluation. Furthermore, this method has been implemented in a publicly accessible tool. https://github.com/abdulmoez/anomaly_detection_se_bug_reports.git, and the results are available at https://anomaly-sec-bugs.herokuapp.com/. Additionally, a competitive evaluation platform is available at https://yourbugisinteresting.herokuapp.com/. A slide presentation is also available at https://docs.google.

This study examines the performance of multiple verification systems in both ideal and real-world settings with data imperfections. Initially, our investigation replicates and extends a prior study by contrasting the results of the same tests run on verified and unverified code for data validation, normalization, and parsing. Additionally, we expand upon the original study by incorporating more advanced methods and a broader range of techniques. Crucially, our analysis is not intended to assess the value of formal verification as a whole but rather the impact of verified code modules. We discovered that the performance disparity between verified and unverified systems is particularly noticeable in error-free scenarios but significantly diminished in the presence of data errors. To gain further insight into the causes of verification failures, we applied a novel analysis technique to the code of three verification tools. Our results indicate that the primary source of these failures is often the same code used to handle both clean and noisy data. Ultimately, the benefits of verified code modules appear to be most pronounced in ideal circumstances but show resilience in the face of data imperfections. Nonetheless, the long-term potential of verified code to enhance system robustness also warrants consideration. To facilitate comparison, we introduce and utilize a new metric called the F1-nDCG score to evaluate the performance of different verification systems. Our complete methodology, including the code and experimental data, is publicly accessible to enable replication and extension by other researchers. Based on our analysis, we propose multiple avenues for further investigation. Firstly, we suggest exploring alternative formal methods to replace existing code modules. Secondly, we propose empirically assessing the correlation between verification success and improved performance in real-world settings. Thirdly, we suggest investigating whether advanced machine learning techniques can be utilized to enhance verification or serve as a substitute for it. Lastly, we propose empirically examining the relationship between verification and the incidence of data errors. To facilitate this research, we introduce a new dataset called DRE, which contains a collection of errors artificially introduced into existing datasets, thereby providing a standardized framework for comparing the robustness of verification and unverification systems. Our results indicate that verification systems tend to perform better than unverification systems in the presence of data errors, particularly in scenarios where errors are more widespread. Notably, we discovered that verified code modules tend to be more resilient to data errors, which could imply a potential long-term benefit of verified code. Research has consistently shown that augmenting data can significantly improve machine learning model performance, with studies often focusing on assessing the various methods' relative efficacy. Typically, this is done by using limited-scale datasets, with results indicating that each augmentation technique yields a distinct best model. In contrast, this work's findings reveal that across multiple datasets, different data augmentation methods produce similar gains in performance. The study also uncovered two key factors influencing the benefits of data augmentation: the size of the initial training data and the degree to which the augmented data differs from it. Moreover, experiments showed that combining classical supervised methods with data augmentation is generally effective, with joint optimization often producing the best outcomes. Interestingly, cross-validation was found to be an effective way to select the best combination of hyperparameters and dataset augmentation methods. Finally, the study's results suggest that cross-domain transfer of data augmentation methods is generally ineffective, with performance gains typically seen only on the target domain. The study's conclusions offer insights on how to effectively utilize data augmentation in machine learning. The research is available on arXiv at arXiv:2208.13799. This research focuses on estimating functions of parameters in parametric models using limited information, which is often obtained from sample data. We investigated two such estimation challenges: one involving functions of parameters and the other, unknown parameters themselves. In the first case, under certain conditions, the weak convergence of empirical function estimates led to the uniform convergence of estimation results for functions of parameters. Additionally, we established weak convergence properties of functional estimates and demonstrated their utility in estimating finite-dimensional parameter subspaces, including unknown parameters. Our key findings are illustrated through analysis of the Cauchy distribution and a Markov process context. These novel results enhance our comprehension of limited information estimation and open up new avenues for statistical inference. They also offer fresh insights into traditional estimation methods like MLE and the behavior of parameter subspaces. The increasing importance of preserving individual privacy in data has led to a significant need for accurate methods. Current research relies on a key assumption that data from the same source are interconnected through relationships. However, this assumption may not always hold true in some scenarios. In this study, we investigate how the connection between records is affected by privacy breaches. We develop a quantitative approach to measure the extent of privacy breaches and propose an optimization method to enhance privacy protection by considering the relationships among records. We utilize a real-world dataset as evidence to support our research findings. Our results show that ignoring the connections between records can result in a substantial underestimation of privacy breaches. Additionally, our proposed method achieves better trade-offs between confidentiality and data availability compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the source of the data can be identified with higher accuracy when relationships among records are taken into account. We demonstrate the efficacy of our methods through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing significant improvements in privacy protection and a higher precision in identifying data sources. Notably, our methods exhibit desirable performance even in scenarios where the relationships among records are uncertain. Our study provides novel insights into the privacy breaches among data batches and contributes innovative methods to enhance privacy protection while considering the connections between data records. Our work also has practical implications for managing large datasets of individuals, enabling more effective privacy preservation. Our study utilizes the COMER legacy survey and the GRAVITY young star survey to investigate the presence of C2H in protoplanetary disks and its relationship to CO. These surveys employed the Submillimeter Array to examine C2H and CO in a total of 23 disks surrounding 11 stars, spanning an age range of 0.1-10 million years. In our analysis, we discovered a notable decrease in the column density ratio of C2H to CO as the C/O ratio increases, with a resulting decrease of over an order of magnitude when C/O surpasses 10^-3. This decline in C2H is largely attributed to the increased competition for atomic carbon when the C/O ratio rises, as carbon is redirected towards other species such as CH, CH2, and HCN. This shift also results in a notable increase in the C2H emission layer in regions with elevated C/O ratios, as C2H is formed deeper within the disk. These findings have significant implications for the use of C2H as a tracer for the extent of protoplanetary disks, as lower C/O ratios allow the disk to appear larger while higher C/O ratios limit the area from which C2H can originate. These results are consistent with the presence of volatile ice formation in the inner regions of disks with low C/O ratios and the absence of such formation in those with higher C/O ratios. These findings are further supported by the examination of C2H in the disk surrounding the star Gravity-1, which exhibits a notable drop-off in C2H column density at a radius of approximately 0.1 AU. This drop-off is likely the result of the presence of CO ice, which hinders the formation of C2H within this region. Creating outfits involves combining items from a vast wardrobe, and detecting mismatches between items is crucial to producing high-quality results. Despite the abundance of research on human computer vision, outfit creation largely relies on manual processes to identify matching and non-matching items. These manual efforts are time-consuming and often result in incomplete projects. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a novel solution that leverages computer vision to identify mismatching items in user-created outfits. To achieve this, we developed a novel interaction framework allowing users to input multiple items at once, and developed the Mismatch Detector Network (MIND), the first deep learning model capable of detecting one item versus multiple, while users provide supporting context. Through thorough evaluations on a newly created dataset, OutfitSem, our method outperforms alternative approaches, and our interface design effectively balances user interaction complexity, while providing efficient detection performance. A major issue in federated learning is the trade-off between data privacy and the efficiency of the training process. To overcome this, our FedBuff algorithm offers a solution by simultaneously protecting privacy and achieving fast convergence while reducing communication costs. FedBuff builds on the principles of federated Newton method, incorporating stochastic gradient descent and the use of averaged buffer datasets that are accumulated during the learning process. This innovative approach allows us to improve the performance and scalability of federated neural network training, specifically for deep neural networks in distributed training experiments, by providing a solution that is more advanced and effective than existing methods within the same framework. Furthermore, our algorithm is uniquely adaptable to various types of first-order methods and can be applied to a wide range of tasks, such as classification and regression problems, as evidenced by our empirical testing of FedBuff across multiple datasets and configuration scenarios. The results show that FedBuff consistently outperforms other federated learning techniques, even those specifically designed for neural networks, by a significant margin, without compromising privacy. Specifically, FedBuff excelled in a comparison against several leading methods in a hidden dataset setting, with notable improvements in convergence speed and accuracy in various tasks. Moreover, our algorithm demonstrated exceptional performance in a real-world application of training a neural network to classify lung diseases from X-ray images, outperforming non-federated methods and rivaling more advanced alternatives. With its innovative design and impressive performance, FedBuff offers a versatile solution for a wide range of applications, including federated learning of both shallow and deep networks. This paper builds on previous research by Wang and Shafik, continuing their investigation into commutants of polynomial shift semigroups. A novel calculus $\mathscr{C}$ with a view to capturing the commutant is constructed, and it's demonstrated that its image encompasses the commutant of the polynomial shift semigroup, and even a significant portion of its extended commutant. Additionally, an inquiry into maximal elements within the commutant leads to the discovery of closed ideals in $\mathscr{C}$ that correspond to maximal elements in this commutant. Crucially, these ideals enable creation of left and right inverses for ideals originating from the commutant of the polynomial shift semigroup. Importantly, it's noted that these results remain valid for a broader class of operators comprising the commutant of proper closed ideals within it. Furthermore, the research also explores the relationship between $\mathscr{C}$ and the commutant of the extended polynomial shift semigroup. A key finding shows that $\mathscr{C}$ captures the commutant of the polynomial shift semigroup up to order $n-1$, and it's conjectured that a similar relationship holds for the commutant of the extended polynomial shift semigroup. Finally, the research delves into the first homomorphism theorem for the commutant of the polynomial shift semigroup. It's established theorems for both finite and infinite polynomial shift semigroups, with separate treatments given due to differing orders and additional investigations into the infinite case. In particular, it's discovered that the commutant of a countable shift on an infinite path graph is isomorphic to the ideal of compact operators on that graph. Additionally, it's found that the commutant of a finite shift is isomorphic to the commutant of its adjacency operator. This research explores the fundamental dynamics of a particle raft, understanding how cracks form between its components. To initiate this study, an experimental setup is created where a particle raft is formed and a controlled gap is introduced between its particles. It's discovered that the space between the cracks grows in response to the balance between the forces driving particle reassembly and the expansion of the surrounding fluid. Furthermore, as the time passes, the distance between the gaps in the raft follows a predictable power-law pattern, dictated by a self-similar solution that explains an earlier observed power-law behavior in natural rifts. To develop this solution, a simplified mathematical model is proposed, incorporating both the reassembly and expansion processes. This paper introduces OREO-Langauge Model, a large-scale pre-trained sequence-to-sequence model that incorporates a specialized layer processing language-specific syntax and semantics in a structured manner. Unlike previous approaches, which often rely on extensive training data or heuristically constructed grammatical rules, OREO-LM learns about language structure by analyzing a diverse range of tasks, including those involving semantic meanings that transcend word-level semantics. Through a comprehensive re-evaluation of the 44 tasks from the BigBiS dataset, which were not used during the model's pre-training, we found that OREO-LM achieved remarkable performance on a diverse set of 22 tasks and surpassed state-of-the-art models in answering both semantic and syntactic questions. Furthermore, we observed that incorporating a Knowledge Interaction Layer significantly enhanced the model's ability to answer complex questions, often surpassing its non-interaction counterparts by a substantial margin. Notably, OREO-LM demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring knowledge of core syntax and semantics, while also exhibiting a natural tendency towards generating grammatically correct sentences. We have made the model available at https://huggingface.co/roberta-large-bigs, and invite fellow researchers to access our code and dataset through our GitHub repository at https://github.com/ghseok/OREO-LM. Additionally, all model checkpoints can be found at https://huggingface.co/oreo-mlm. Over the past decade, research into high dimensional expanders has gained significant momentum, driven in part by their promising theoretical applications in computer science. A key area of study for high dimensional expanders is in the context of sampling codes, particularly in the realm of semi-self-correctable samplers, which itself is an important extension of list-decodable codes. This interest is piqued because high dimensional expanders offer an ideal framework for creating space-efficient sampling circuits. This survey aims to provide an in-depth examination of the connections between high dimensional expanders and sampling codes, as well as a comprehensive overview of the significant advances made in this field. Furthermore, we will discuss recent breakthroughs that have resolved long-standing open questions and position the field for future exploration. Finally, we will discuss potential directions for further research. It is worth noting that the writing of this survey was facilitated by a grant from the Fund for Excellence in Interdisciplinary Research from the Hebrew University. Additionally, I would like to acknowledge partial support from DRS grant 601/20 from the Israeli Council for Higher Education. Lastly, I would like to thank Noga Alon, Oded Regev, and Euiwoong Yang for their valuable input and feedback. \end{abstract}

Recent advances in large language models have shown the potential for completing tasks beyond what they were trained on using cleverly crafted prompts. However, there's a limit to how far this ability extends, and it's especially constrained when using untrained prompts. To fully grasp this limitation, we need to understand how it behaves in response to varying degrees of task similarity. We've identified a system for classifying prompts that pinpoints their level of connection to a task, and we've discovered that LLMs exhibit a distinct pattern in their output, indicating a task similarity scale. We've also found that prompts contributing to this pattern are typically unrelated to the task at hand, and we've analyzed the reasons behind this phenomenon. To further explore the potential of LLMs, we've developed an innovative technique that enables the model to produce more accurate responses to untask-like prompts by learning from high-quality examples. We've put this technique to the test on eight diverse tasks, and the results show that it outperforms LLM baselines on untask-like and semi-similar prompts, while maintaining comparable performance on task-like prompts. We've made our code and data available for public use.

waves and the temperature distribution from the surface up to about 10 km in
altitude. Twenty-five successful deployments between August 2019 and January 2021

High-quality computer-generated audio is created using a model-based approach called audio synthesis. Traditionally, loss functions in this process are calculated by comparing simulated audio to real audio based on their acoustic similarities. We propose a novel approach, the SpecSinc network, which utilizes a more detailed representation of audio characteristics in the form of a spectrogram to measure discrepancies between synthesized and genuine audio profiles. The SpecSinc network enhances the precision of audio generation by incorporating this improved measuring technique in a supervised learning framework. Additionally, we introduce a new method of creating training data, spectrogram averaging, which, when combined with our model, results in highly accurate results. When tested on the wild singing voice dataset, our model achieved notable improvements over the baseline method. Specifically, it achieved an average correlation coefficient of 0.944 for its output spectrograms, which is a 0.115 increase over the baseline model's 0.829. Furthermore, our model's audio samples were found to be indistinguishable from those produced by a pre-trained GMM supervisory-trained model, as judged by a human evaluator. Notably, our model's performance surpassed that of a pre-trained GMM model with a 0.041 improvement in correlation coefficient, without receiving any supervision during its training. When subjected to a challenging task of generating piano sounds from a dataset with limited frequency content, our model demonstrated exceptional adaptability and produced high-quality results with a high correlation coefficient of 0.934. These findings indicate that our proposed spectrogram-based loss function is a versatile tool for a wide range of audio synthesis tasks. Code and model repositories are available at https://github.com/kevkev1501/SpecSinc. Additionally, our generated audio samples can be accessed at https://kevkev1501.github.io/SpecSinc. Although initial scientific findings are crucial, they often take time to emerge, leaving a gap in information. In this context, moderate measures, such as travel restrictions and border closures, can influence the balance between medical outcomes and economic impacts. To bridge this gap, a new approach is presented that enables policy-makers to consider both immediate guidelines and future policies aligned with emerging scientific evidence, thus allowing for more adaptive decision-making. This framework is tested using a simulated influenza outbreak in Europe, revealing that incorporating a moving average of the infection curve into policy decisions can yield favorable outcomes in terms of hospitalization rates and economic losses. Debugging data processing pipelines is an intricate task due to the complex interplay between data transformations and debugging tools. Current methods often rely on expert knowledge and have inherent limitations, making it difficult to efficiently identify data issues. In response, we introduce DataScope, an innovative, widely applicable, and adaptable approach that accelerates data debugging by seamlessly integrating with various pipeline components. DataScope's adaptive debugging technique dynamically modifies the debugging process for each step in the pipeline as needed. Furthermore, DataScope's architecture is highly modular and adaptable, allowing it to be easily incorporated into existing pipelines without thorough understanding of its underlying mechanics. We evaluated DataScope through both theoretical analysis and practical testing of its performance across multiple, complex data pipelines, revealing that it consistently outperforms traditional methods by a substantial margin. Notably, DataScope demonstrates superior performance even in scenarios where the comparison methods are theoretically optimal. We anticipate that DataScope will serve as a pioneering framework, inspiring further research and development in data debugging, as well as a reliable tool for everyday use. In a broader context, our study highlights the significance of wavelength-dependent ordering in determining the properties of such materials. Furthermore, we propose a novel method to manipulate this wavelength dependence and thereby control the properties of magnetoelastic materials through the application of external strain. We introduce a new challenge problem, involving the most basic type of hypergraphs with bounded substructure size. Our findings show that, relative to graphs, recovering hypergraphs with this property is possible and not too difficult, but it's also possible to create instances where the solution is extremely complex. To address this challenge, we develop a new algorithm and analyze its performance in relation to existing methods. Our results indicate that this algorithm is superior to the alternatives and the best possible solution, and we show that this performance limit is inherent. We also explore the practical effectiveness of our approach and that of a new benchmark suite to gauge its scalability in real-world scenarios. To facilitate future research on this topic, we introduce open questions and provide code availability information. This note provides a counterexample to a particular conjecture related to realizing integral second cohomology classes as Euler classes of foliations. Specifically, it offers an example in three-dimensional manifolds where a class of norm one cannot be represented by the Euler class of any foliation. Additionally, it presents an infinite family of 4-manifolds where the norm of any introduced class is greater than one, implying that these classes cannot be expressed as Euler classes of the foliations they induce on the boundary surfaces. This result leads to the creation of a large set of unrepresentable classes in the cohomology of these 4-manifolds, and also provides an infinite family of unrepresentable classes in the cohomology of any given dimension within these manifolds. Ultimately, it is proven that the introduced classes can be linearly independent of any dimension in the cohomology of these manifolds, and that they can be properly paired to cover all possible values in the given dimension range. This work provides the first known examples of the unrepresentability of integral second cohomology classes as Euler classes of foliations, and offers a significant advancement towards understanding the representability of all such classes. Furthermore, it introduces a new method of constructing unrepresentable classes, and provides an interesting connection between its principles and the established Khovanov-type inequalities in the field of smooth minima. This connection leads to the introduction of a new set of inequalities, known as Plamennaya's inequalities, which provide an upper limit on the number of minimal foliations that are topologically equivalent in a given dimension and radius within a given 4-manifold. This work provides the first known examples of these inequalities in the given dimension and radius, and offers a significant advancement towards understanding the structure of the set of all minimal foliations. The Simulated Annealing algorithm is utilized to generate locally fair districting plans of varying types, which are then employed to analyze the global fairness of real-world plans. By leveraging Simulated Annealing, we are able to produce a wide range of plans of similar quality from a local optimum, which is sampling a global optimum at a significantly lower temperature. These plans are used to estimate the fairness of actual plans by measuring the average fairness. Our method offers a flexible framework that can be applied to various fairness metrics and districting problems across different domains. Furthermore, the algorithm's output serves as a basis for creating a fairness metric that compares the fairness of two districting plans. Our results demonstrate that the current plans in the United States are only slightly fair compared to the optimal fairness achievable through Simulated Annealing-generated plans. Ultimately, the algorithm provides valuable insights for districting plan creation and fosters a discussion on the trade-offs between plan quality and fairness. Our code and the fairness metric we developed are available online for public use. \end{abstract}

The Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) has emerged as a highly effective method for solving partial differential equations with limited data points. However, PINN often suffers from low training efficiency due to the high discrepancy between its predictions and target data. To address this issue, we propose an improved approach, Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation (RANG), which accelerates PINN training. RANG dynamically adjusts the node distribution in the search space according to the residual and gradient information. As a result, RANG enhances PINN's convergence speed by prioritizing node addition in complex regions with significant discrepancies. Furthermore, RANG optimizes the network parameters through evolutionary strategies, which complements the efficiency of adaptive node selection. We evaluate RANG on three challenging problems and observe a notable improvement in training efficiency, with a reduced number of iterations required to achieve a satisfactory outcome. Notably, RANG can achieve comparable performance to traditional PINN methods while achieving a speedup of up to 5 times. The proposed method demonstrates great potential for solving complex PDEs with a large number of data points. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/Chenxiaoqy/RANG.

This paper examines the security of Rust's Cargo ecosystem by investigating the update process. We discovered that the majority of libraries in Cargo still contain vulnerabilities even in their most recent versions. We developed two new methods for determining which dependencies can be safely updated without introducing new errors, one based on text analysis and the other using programming tools. Both techniques were effective in identifying update opportunities that traditional methods failed to detect. We found that text analysis can process a library at the speed of seconds, while the more computationally expensive technique takes around minutes. We tested these methods across a diverse set of libraries and found that a significant proportion can have their dependencies updated via text analysis. We identified several limitations of current Cargo security features that led to missed security opportunities and proposed potential improvements. Overall, our research suggests that text analysis can play a crucial role in enhancing the security of Rust's Cargo ecosystem. We plan to make our methods available as a Cargo plugin, providing concrete benefits to the community. Ultimately, our goal is to contribute to the development of more sophisticated security tools, potentially utilizing machine learning techniques, to further strengthen the security of Rust's Cargo ecosystem. This study examines the long-term behavior of complex Ginzburg-Laudau equations featuring pure jump noises and oscillating solutions, with the goal of determining the conditions under which these equations remain ergodic. Our analysis indicates that, contrary to expectations, the presence of jump noise leads to non-ergodic behavior even when the noise is isolated. To overcome this challenge, we establish a novel condition, akin to a localized version of the Hyponormal Compactness Condition, which enables us to demonstrate the ergodic properties of these equations within a compact subset of the phase space. Furthermore, we illustrate the applicability of these conditions through two specific examples. Ultimately, our findings reveal that the ergodicity of these equations is confined to a compact subset of the phase space, distinguished by a critical height of instability. In contrast, solutions exceeding this critical value of instability will not converge ergodically. To facilitate understanding, we present a companion numerical simulation illustrating the ergodic region within the phase space. The conclusions drawn from these analyses may be extended to a broader range of stochastic differential equations featuring pure jump noises. Gabor filters have been widely used in various applications that prioritize invariance to different factors such as translation and scale. Existing approaches, however, have fallen short in achieving reliable invariance to orientation changes. In an effort to rectify this limitation, a novel framework known as Landmark Gabor Filters (LGFs) has been developed. LGFs utilize an adaptive approach based on the concept of non-rigid alignment to create orientation-invariant features. By incorporating a new process for constructing Gabor filters, LGFs ensure that the derived filters remain effective even when the template filter is rotated. Furthermore, LGFs employ a novel method of feature representation, in which one-dimensional signals are combined to create robust two-dimensional landmarks capable of surviving complex transformations. In-depth experiments have demonstrated that LGFs consistently outperform existing state-of-the-art methods in terms of performance. Notably, LGFs have successfully applied a simplified version of the protocol used in the development of HOG and SIFT to achieve remarkable results on challenging real-world tasks, including vehicle detection and image classification. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have emerged as highly effective architectures for tackling graph-based problems. However, the traditional GCN design has a major shortcoming in its dependence on assumptions about the sparsity of graph features. This limitation is particularly significant since the features are often gathered from an external source, such as a graph database, making their structure unpredictable. This research introduces an innovative method to break this dependency by incorporating a randomized element in the feature aggregation process. Specifically, the feature collection step in GCNs is reconfigured by incorporating a controlled element of disorder. This modification yields two key benefits: (1) an enhanced capacity to adapt to scenarios with non-sparse graph feature patterns; and (2) a reduced computational load, resulting from a minimized memory requirement during each training step. The method's effectiveness is illustrated through experiments on a range of benchmark datasets, which demonstrate that the model outperforms traditional GCNs in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. Notably, this research also examines the effect of shuffling the graph feature gathering process on the model's performance, revealing a broad applicability to a wide range of graph-related tasks. The concept of strong edge-coloring in graphs was initially explored by Mubra in 1990, with a specific case being whether bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of 3 require at least 5 colors. This problem has since been unsolved. Given the incompatibility of 4 colors for strong edge-colorings in certain 3-vertex bipartite graphs, we confirm the initial conjecture by Mubra, showing that such graphs always need 5 colors. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of at least 6 colors for strong edge-colorings in r-vertex complete bipartite graphs. We also examine the feasibility of using planar graphs to create instances with the minimum number of colors required for strong edge-coloring. Additionally, we explore other properties of strong edge-colorings, including their relationship with other graph coloring concepts, and derive some interesting results. For example, we demonstrate that certain graphs necessitate the use of at least 6 colors for strong edge-coloring, while allowing only 5 colors for standard edge-coloring. We also prove that certain complete bipartite graphs cannot be given strong edge-colorings with 4 colors, even if additional vertices are added to them. We conclude by discussing some open problems in the field of strong edge-coloring. These problems include determining the minimum number of colors needed for strong edge-coloring in complete graphs and circulant graphs, as well as finding a formula or algorithm that can accurately assign strong edge-colors to any given graph. COPASI is a widely-used software for analyzing, simulating, and visualizing biochemical networks. Although the standalone application provides a comprehensive interface for interacting with models, it has limitations, such as compatibility issues with certain operating systems and web browsers. To address these limitations, we developed ShinyCOPASI, a web-based interface for COPASI models. This R Shiny application enables users to access and interact with models in a browser window, enhancing web-based analysis and simulation capabilities. Like the original tool, it preserves model specificity, allowing users to work with individual models, and offers a user-friendly interface for performing tasks like editing models, running searches, and generating reports. Additionally, ShinyCOPASI enables users to easily share and collaborate on models through the web, and allows modelers to upload their models directly from the COMPLEX database. This new interface enhances web-based interaction with COPASI models, broadening the user base and making it easier to share models and results. Further details are available at https://shiny.copasi.org/.

This research investigates the collision of a fast-moving particle with a stationary one, accompanied by a solitary photon, within the framework of quantum chromodynamics. By examining the photon's influence on the initial conditions of the interacting particles, we identify two distinct mechanisms through which the photon induces changes in the partons' momenta. We demonstrate that a contribution traditionally overlooked in theoretical calculations of jet production, albeit stemming from the photon's presence, is quantifiable and follows a simple logarithmic pattern. In specific cases, the photon's effect can be quantified in relation to the square of the charge and the logarithm of the rapidity range it occupies. We further analyze the photon's influence on the initial conditions through the lens of nuclear collisions, revealing it could be responsible for a previously unexplained discrepancy between theoretical and experimental data regarding di-jet asymmetry. Our study suggests that the photon's role should be considered crucial in understanding the initial conditions of such high-energy collisions. Given its significance, incorporating the photon's contribution is essential for accurately modeling the early stages of nuclear collisions. Furthermore, we propose that the photon's effect could be a key factor in resolving the long-standing controversy surrounding di-jet asymmetry measurements. In particular, we speculate that the photon's presence might be the missing explanation for the observed suppression of jet production at forward angles in certain conditions. A comprehensive review of double parton distribution functions and their applications is provided. DPDs are analogous to single parton distribution functions but account for interactions between multiple partons within hadrons. They are essential for interpreting phenomena involving multiple parton interactions, such as double J/Psi and TTbar production in hadron-hadron collisions. This review begins by summarizing DPDs in terms of their underlying theory and then discusses their extraction from data, focusing on both general DPDs and helicity-dependent DPDs. Calculations of multiple parton interactions in various processes, including hadron-hadron collisions and electron-positron annihilation, are also examined. In addition, DPDs are applied to investigate various processes, such as double vector boson production, heavy flavor production, and the interplay between single and double parton interactions. Finally, future prospects for DPD research are presented. This work is an extension of a previously published review but includes new material and developments. DPDs offer a valuable tool to explore multiple parton interactions and test the structure of the proton and other hadrons in diverse ways. DPDs are highly sensitive to the details of the parton dynamics within hadrons and can be used to investigate aspects not well understood, such as parton correlation and color interaction. This paper presents our solution to the TimeSeries4U challenge held at UbiComp 2021. We were given unlabeled datasets of daily routines recorded by Inertial Measurement Units on the wrist. The goal was to categorize sensor data into written and non-written activities. We addressed the lack of labeled data by developing a self-supervised domain adaptation method. This approach combined positive and negative sample enhancement along with a class-sensitive domain adaptation technique to enhance the discrimination of the target class against background noise. Additionally, we created a simple filter to exclude written activity time series to facilitate efficient processing. Experiment results demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed solution with high accuracy rates for both written and non-written activity identification. We also achieved a notable high F1-score of 0.9442 compared to other challenge baselines. Notably, our approach outperformed existing methods with an improved macro F1-score of 0.9142. We've developed a novel Bayesian neural network method for learning how type Ia supernovae change over time. Unlike traditional approaches that assume each supernova follows the same pattern but varies in intensity, our approach acknowledges each supernova has a unique development path. As there's no straightforward way to include this individuality into the model, we introduced a penalty that rewards correlations between different points in a supernova's timeline and penalizes unrelated patterns. With this model, even without manual data filtering, our results show a significant improvement in modeling variability and a 10% boost in classification accuracy when compared to standard techniques. With further training on short datasets, our method achieves comparable results to state-of-the-art models trained on large, complete datasets. We've made our code and data analysis available for others to use. 

Here are the key findings:

- A neural network that accounts for individual supernovae patterns
  without manual data filtering outperform similar models by 10%.

- Comparable results to state-of-the-art models, but with smaller training
  datasets.

- Successfully applied to current and future data from the Carnegie
  Astrophysics Legacy Survey. 

- A potential tool for similar tasks like modeling individual galaxy
  development and classification. 

- A novel approach to using time-series data in supervised learning.

Using data from ALMA and MUSE, we examined how mass outflows in a galaxy at a distance of 485 million light years relate to its star formation activity. Our observations reveal two distinct gas components with different motions, which we analyzed to determine mass, velocity, and size. We discovered a massive neutral gas outflow occurring at velocities of approximately 700 kilometers per second, with a rate much higher than the star formation rate. This outflow appears to be driven primarily by star formation activity and may play a crucial role in the consumption of gas and the suppression of star formation. We also found that the size and mass of this outflow are significantly influenced by the mass of the central supermassive black hole. This outflow will likely impact the star formation process within the next 50 million years, after which it will be quenched due to the feedback effect of the supermassive black hole. Our findings suggest that the outflow of neutral gas in galaxies may be more extensive than previously thought and could be a key factor in the overall star formation process. This research has important implications for our understanding of the feedback mechanism that regulates star formation activity. Based on our analysis, we propose a model illustrating the cycle of gas flow, star formation, and feedback in galaxies. This model could be applied to a broader population of galaxies. The interaction between a turbulent plume rising through a less dense surrounding gas is examined using numerical simulations and experimental data. When the plume and surrounding gas have different densities of particles, a complex flow pattern emerges due to the interaction of buoyancy forces. In laboratory experiments, a plume with a constant flux of particles was studied while varying its density relative to the surrounding gas. Observations indicated that when the plume density was greater than the surrounding gas density, the interface between the plume and the surrounding gas exhibited periodic disturbances and an increased rate of particle mixing. In contrast, when the plume density was lower than the surrounding gas density, these disturbances did not occur and the mixing rate of particles remained relatively constant. A theoretical model based on energy balance was developed to explain the periodic fluctuations in mixing rates. In cases where the plume density exceeds the surrounding gas density, the model reveals that periodic fluctuations arise due to the transfer of energy from the plume turbulence to the surrounding gas, causing the plume to periodically change from a self-similar cone shape to a more compact form. In cases where the plume density is lower than the surrounding gas density, the model shows that the mixing rates remain constant because there is little energy transfer between the plume and surrounding gas, resulting in a lack of periodic fluctuations. Experimental and numerical findings support the model's predictions. Additionally, a general expression for estimating the mixing rate of particles was developed and validated through comparison with experimental and numerical results from various studies. In all examined cases, the predicted mixing rate agreed well with the model's prediction. Furthermore, an investigation into how particle size affects mixing rates revealed that when particles are large relative to the plume's turbulent eddies, the model's predictions may underestimate the mixing rate. In such cases, increasing the particle size can lead to a significant enhancement in mixing rates. Conversely, when particles are small relative to the plume's turbulent eddies, the model's predictions remain accurate. In cases where the plume and surrounding gas have identical particle densities, a different mixing phenomenon arises, characterized by a different periodic fluctuation pattern and a distinct mixing mechanism. In such cases, the mixing rates can be estimated using a modified expression derived from energy balance considerations. A comprehensive database of experimentally and numerically determined mixing coefficients was developed, encompassing a wide range of parameter values. In cases where the plume density exceeds the surrounding gas density, the model's predictions for mixing coefficients agree well with the database's results across a broad range of parameter values. In this study, we examine how this strain influences the spin texture in these bilayers, specifically within the leading layer, under external magnetic fields. Our findings indicate that strain can induce a spin bending effect, analogous to the magnetoelastic flexomagnetic effect, in addition to altering the spin rotation. We also identify conditions under than a certain threshold, the spin texture will be entirely determined by the strain pattern, while above that threshold, the spin texture will be determined by both the strain and magnetic field. Furthermore, we show that strain can produce a significant anisotropy in magnetic response. Ultimately, our research provides insights into the spin, strain, and their interplay in ferromagnetic thin films.
