The occurrence of magnetic cycles in stars that rotate slowly is a topic of interest.
Research indicates that dynamo processes are more effective when a star's rotation rate decreases, which can also lead to the creation of long-lasting magnetic structures even in rapidly rotating stars.
In this study, we examine whether the kinematic dynamo can contribute to the development of magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars.
We found that the kinematic dynamo can give rise to magnetic cycles, which take the form of surface poloidal magnetic fields that emerge due to the shearing effect of rotation on an initial toroidal field.
The results show that the characteristic time of the magnetic cycle is directly proportional to the star's rotation rate and corotation radius.
In the case of the Sun, this cycle time matches the observed duration of its 22-year magnetic cycle.
In addition, we discovered that the kinematic dynamo can produce magnetic cycles in stars that rotate more slowly than the Sun, which may help explain the long periods between magnetic activity episodes observed in some stars. 
In contrast, we did not find any evidence supporting the idea that the $\alpha-\Omega$ dynamo can produce magnetic cycles in stars that rotate slowly. 
In the context of this study, the $\alpha-\Omega$ dynamo refers to a dynamo model in which the magnetic cycle is caused by the interaction between toroidal and poloidal magnetic fields that are generated independently. 
In order to verify our findings, we compared our theoretical predictions to observations of main-sequence stars, which revealed a correlation between rotation periods and magnetic cycle durations that can be explained by the kinematic dynamo mechanism. 
In particular, we found that the kinematic dynamo can account for the long periods between magnetic activity episodes in M-dwarf stars as well as the lack of magnetic cycles in slowly rotating late-type stars. 
In conclusion, the kinematic dynamo offers a viable explanation for the occurrence of magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars, which may also be applicable to other stellar types. 
In the future, further research is needed to clarify the relative importance of the kinematic and $\alpha-\Omega$ dynamo processes in regulating the magnetic behavior of stars. 
In addition, we suggest that the kinematic dynamo can potentially give rise to magnetic cycles in planets that rotate slowly, which may be relevant to the study of exoplanets.

Automatic spoofing countermeasures have become a crucial aspect of protecting voice assistants from fake audio inputs. Previous studies employed supervised approaches, but their effectiveness relied on the availability of labeled data, a scarce resource. Research then shifted to unsupervised methods, focusing on detecting a broad range of speech artifacts. However, these approaches often failed to capture the unique characteristics of specific synthesis tools due to their broad detection scope. To address this limitation, this study proposes a novel unsupervised detection method, based on a neural network featuring a dedicated attention layer, dynamically selecting relevant input features for each artifact class. By enhancing model focus on important features, performance was significantly improved, surpassing existing methods in accuracy rates by substantial margins, particularly in one-class and multi-class scenarios, according to comprehensive benchmark tests. Furthermore, the introduction of attention substantially decreased model complexity, measured by parameters and training data requirements. Specifically, models with attention outperformed comparable baseline models across all evaluation metrics, demonstrating a significant reduction in parameters and training data by up to 30%. The proposed method achieved superior performance on the CVSSP-ASVspoofv2.0 database, a leading dataset for automatic spoofing countermeasures, across one-class and multi-class evaluation modes. Notably, it surpassed state-of-the-art models by substantial margins in these scenarios, highlighting its potential as a highly effective unsupervised detection method. The proposed approach was further validated through successful application to develop a detection system for a real-world voice assistant, demonstrating its practical utility in industrial settings. To facilitate future research, the accompanying code has been made publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/zhengyuyang2020/ASVspoof2.0_unsupervised_detection. Similarly, the accompanying dataset can be accessed via https://dataivf.github.io/ASVspoof/index.html. Finally, the accompanying audio samples can be found at https://github.com/zhengyuyang2020/ASVspoof2.0_unsupervised_detection/tree/main/dataset. In conclusion, this research presents an innovative neural network with an attention layer for effective unsupervised detection of speech artifacts in voice assistants, showcasing its practical utility in industrial settings. The proposed model outperformed existing methods in accuracy rates, demonstrated a reduced computational complexity, and exhibited a substantial reduction in parameters and training data requirements. Furthermore, it successfully detected speech artifacts in a real-world voice assistant, highlighting its potential as a highly effective unsupervised detection method. This study examines the effectiveness of evasion strategies on Dynamic Protocol Detection (DPD), a prominent method used in Nmap, a widely employed network monitoring tool, on modern Linux and Windows systems. Our investigation involves introducing four new forms of evasion attacks that modify packet sequences to circumvent DPD identification. We conduct a detailed analysis of DPD behavior on various network services and create a database of standard traffic patterns. We also develop a metric to quantify DPD accuracy in the presence of evasive traffic. The results show that all four evasion attacks can evade DPD detection on all tested systems, significantly reducing its accuracy. Furthermore, combining these attacks enables creation of sophisticated evasion strategies that can evade DPD with high probabilities on all platforms considered in this study. The findings indicate that DPD is vulnerable to sophisticated evasion tactics, rendering it unreliable for secure network monitoring and detection of sensitive services. We suggest alternative detection mechanisms that can complement DPD in identifying common network services while also providing enhanced protection against sophisticated evasion attacks. Our findings align with previous experimental results and offer a theoretical explanation for the observed phenomena. A widely accepted approach to extrapolation is that of systematic extension, which involves training on successively larger datasets to build capacity for handling more examples. This concept is closely related to overfitting in that it necessitates constructing a more complex model to accommodate additional data. While systematic extension is a crucial aspect of deep learning research, its effectiveness is largely limited to doubling the training dataset size at a time. This paper explores ways to expand training sets by larger factors, employing a novel training method that alternates between typical data presentation and artificially augmented examples to build robust models capable of handling significantly more data. The study demonstrates the efficacy of this technique in enhancing image classification performance on small datasets and easily generalizes to complex scenarios, including image generation and out-of-distribution predictions. Notably, the resulting models exhibit a remarkable ability to learn at significantly higher data scale factors, achieving superior performance compared to standard training methods when classifying CIFAR10 and CIFER100 with up to 320 times more data. Recent research has created content-addressable data structures that utilize cryptographic hash functions, like xornifiers, which offer a more efficient alternative to traditional Bloom filters. This led to the development of xor filters, a more memory-stable variant, and a hybrid approach combining both. In this study, we explored the potential of applying xor filters to distributed storage systems, but our initial results indicated a higher false positive rate compared to Bloom filters, making them less suitable for this purpose. However, we discovered more compact and faster variants of xor filters, which consume up to 60% less memory and perform 2-3 times faster than previously optimized variants, while still matching Bloom filter's error rate. This research presents a new generation of xor filters, offering a substantial improvement over the current state-of-art variants, and presents a thorough comparison with Bloom filters through realistic simulations of distributed storage system scenarios. Additionally, we developed open-source, high-performance implementations of Bloom filters and xor filters in C for practical use in distributed storage systems. In our experiments, we found that for a false positive rate of 10^-5, Bloom filters require 1.2-2 times more memory to achieve the same efficiency as the new xor filters. Furthermore, our results showed that the new xor filters can provide significant performance improvements over Bloom filters in memory-bound applications, resulting in a speedup of 2-6 times in distributed storage system scenarios. In conclusion, xor filters offer a superior balance of memory usage and performance compared to traditional Bloom filters, making them a more suitable choice for various applications. In particular, they present a promising solution for distributed storage systems, where high performance at the cost of some additional memory is acceptable. In contrast, when high memory efficiency is required at the cost of some performance, more efficient variants of Bloom filters are a more suitable choice. In the future, we plan to further investigate the potential applications of xor filters in various domains, such as caching, networking, security, and others. Additionally, we aim to explore the use of alternative types of hash functions in xor filters to achieve even better performance. Moreover, we plan to adapt xor filters to work efficiently with large items, such as files, by utilizing streaming algorithms, and to apply them to solve complex problems in big data processing. In conclusion, this research demonstrates the potential of xor filters as a viable and efficient alternative to traditional Bloom filters in various applications. In recent years, there has been significant interest in FLVoogd, a federated learning approach that allows collaborative training of a clustering model while maintaining data privacy. However, existing FLVoogd systems faces challenges such as data imbalance, class shift, and data contamination from malicious users, which affect model performance. To address these issues, we have developed FedCluster, a robust FLVoogd system that combines intuitive data visualization and advanced machine learning algorithms. FedCluster utilizes a two-stage approach to filter out suspicious data from both local and remote datasets, and leverages a mixture of traditional and deep learning methods to improve clustering quality. It does so by employing an initial model to preprocess data, and then relying on a more complex model to refine the results, all while implementing a trust-based strategy that ensures only benign data is used without compromising sensitive personal information. Furthermore, FedCluster incorporates an anomaly scoring system that flags suspicious data during the training process, and has been shown to outperform existing solutions in terms of clustering accuracy and robustness. Notably, experiments have demonstrated FedCluster's ability to achieve up to 20% higher AUC scores compared to state-of-the-art approaches in various datasets. Additionally, performance analysis has revealed FedCluster's ability to achieve convergence 2-4 times faster than competing methods. The code and data used in this research can be accessed at https://github.com/Chen-Research-FEI/FedCluster. For more details, please refer to the technical report at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.06210. simulating real-world scenarios on computers, but the success of transferring these
skills directly to real-world conditions is still limited. To bridge this gap, we
introduce the Sim2Real Challenge, a comprehensive evaluation of transferring skills
from simulated to real-world settings, specifically designed for complex automated
drives. The challenge brings together leading researchers and practitioners to assess
the robustness of control and navigation skills trained in 3D simulations when
applied to physical robots, with a particular focus on robust handling of unexpected
situations. With advanced course scenarios and a rigorous evaluation criteria, the
challenge has attracted top entries from the community, and our results indicate that
there is still a substantial gap between simulated and real-world performance. Our
research showcases the potential of using the challenge as a catalyst for rapid
progress in sim2real transfer techniques. Additionally, we introduce a novel method for
automatically generating diverse course maps for training and evaluation, which
significantly enhances the robustness of simulated skills. Finally, we highlight the
importance of considering real-world factors such as sensor noise, actuation errors, and
unpredictable environment interactions to develop more resilient skills in the future.

Atmospheres of planets orbiting other stars vary widely in their sizes. We've discovered that smaller atmospheres tend to retain gases rich in carbon, such as carbon dioxide, whereas larger atmospheres are more likely to contain nitrogen-based compounds like nitrogen gas. This phenomenon can be explained by the rate at which atmospheric mass escapes into space, which slows down in larger atmospheres, allowing them to hold onto heavier molecules of nitrogen. This escape rate is influenced by factors like the strength of the star's magnetic field and the presence of winds that can escape more easily. We've found that smaller atmospheres are generally protected by strong magnetic fields, while larger atmospheres have weaker fields and are sometimes influenced by powerful stellar winds. However, we've determined that these winds aren't sufficient to account for the differences we observe. Another factor at play is the increased wind speed in larger atmospheres, which allows heavier molecules to escape more easily. This discovery has significant implications for understanding the chemistry of exoplanet atmospheres. We've used these findings to explore the atmospheric conditions on temperate planets, which lie between small and massive atmospheres in terms of their size. We've discovered that these planets often have atmospheric compositions that vary depending on their mass, with smaller planets tending towards carbon-based atmospheres and larger planets tending towards nitrogen-based atmospheres. This research has important implications for understanding future missions to study exoplanet atmospheres, such as the James Webb Space Telescope and future direct imaging projects. We've determined that selecting planets with small atmospheres based on specific signs of carbon dioxide or methane may not necessarily guarantee similar results for larger planets. Similarly, searching for nitrogen-based compounds in larger planets may not necessarily guarantee similar results for smaller ones. Ultimately, we've concluded that each exoplanet presents a unique chemical signature, and that considering its mass and atmospheric size is crucial for making accurate predictions about their atmospheres. We've established a framework to guide future research and observations in studying exoplanet atmospheres. This framework involves using mass and atmospheric size as key indicators to help identify and understand the various chemical properties of exoplanets. We've applied this framework to a diverse set of exoplanets, which revealed distinct patterns in their atmospheric compositions based on their mass and atmospheric size. We've discovered that planets similar to our own solar system's Jupiter and Saturn have the potential to retain a thick layer of water if they're located at the right distance from their star. This research explores the learning potential of the McCulloch-Pitts network, a development of the classic Hopfield network, with the ability to acquire new knowledge after initial training concludes. Unlike the Hopfield network, a fully connected, symmetric model, the McCulloch-Pitts network introduces some degree of connection uncertainty. Our investigation focuses on two key questions: Can the McCulloch-Pitts network's connection randomness contribute to its ability to represent diverse patterns? And, given its initial state, can it effectively generalize to represent new, unseen patterns. Through both theoretical and experimental evaluations, our results indicate that the McCulloch-Pitts network can indeed learn and represent multiple, distinct patterns and also generalize well to new patterns while maintaining stability in most cases. Additionally, our findings show that the network's capacity for new pattern formation increases exponentially with the number of neurons, offering significant implications for future research in neural networks. Finally, our analysis reveals that the network's error rates can be minimized by optimizing the level of connection randomness within a specific range. Overall, our study confirms the McCulloch-Pitts network's potential as a versatile tool for pattern representation and generalization. Moreover, its unique characteristics may inspire novel approaches to error correction in neural networks. Based on our research, we propose the McCulloch-Pitts network as a promising candidate for future applications in binary image restoration and compressed sensing, among other areas. Current methods typically assume all data features are relevant, which is not the case when faced with a large volume of data. Improving the efficiency of this process would also enhance isolation capabilities. We have developed a new and efficient algorithm for change point detection and failure analysis that effectively filters out irrelevant data features. Through experiments on a variety of datasets, we found that our approach outperforms existing methods by reducing the number of features processed while maintaining or improving detection accuracy. Furthermore, when these features are removed, we observed enhanced isolation capabilities without sacrificing performance. This innovative technique has resulted in a substantial performance boost of one order of magnitude for each feature reduction step. Notably, when features are completely eliminated, we saw minimal degradation in change point detection performance. This groundbreaking algorithm offers a significant improvement in processing efficiency without compromising quality. A limited supply of labeled data significantly hampers the development and deployment of machine learning models.  While data augmentation techniques increase the availability of unlabeled data, its effectiveness is hindered by the difficulty in generating high-quality labeled counterparts.  Selective data labeling aims to mitigate this issue by focusing efforts on the most informative samples.  This paper proposes a method to determine the most beneficial samples for labeling by leveraging both the uncertainty of existing model predictions and the relationships between samples.  Furthermore, we introduce a new technique to effectively integrate unlabeled data into the training process via a semi-supervised learning framework.  Experimental results confirm that our approach outperforms traditional techniques with only partial labeling.  Specifically, our method yields performance enhancements of 4.5% and 2.2% on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets, respectively, without requiring any labeled data from the test set.  Notably, our approach achieves comparable results to those obtained with full labeling on the CIFAR-10 dataset. This phenomenon is anticipated to be prevalent in similar InAs-based antiferromagnetic insulator platforms. However, the typical approach of iteratively training and pruning models after each layer yields subpar results due to the limitations of converging slowly and losing important layer interactions. In contrast, earlier methods focusing on joint training often sacrifice model accuracy. By incorporating a proposed loss and employing a constrained optimization approach, ClickTrain achieves both accurate pruning and effective model reduction. Furthermore, ClickTrain requires significantly fewer computational resources, with a training time comparable to naive pruning methods. This research explores the realm of relational semantics for substructural modal logics, focusing on distinct types of axioms that deviate from the strict adherence to distributivity, associativity, and contraction principles. By introducing various models, including Heyting algebras with distinct distributive and associative structures, this work demonstrates that each individual modal logic system can be represented by either a distributive or associative structure. Furthermore, we introduce a new method for combining separate relational axioms and prove that the resultant combined axioms have a coherent interpretation in our models. Additionally, we introduce a technique for translating formulae from more permissive systems into equivalent ones within stricter logical frameworks and establish a sound inference rule to achieve this translation. Our study ultimately reveals a comprehensive classification of substructural modal logics based on their adherence to distributivity, associativity, and contraction principles. Finally, we outline potential avenues for exploration in the future, including the extension of our framework to other logical systems and the investigation of the decidability of inference relationships between different substructural modal logics. This paper presents a sampling-based interior-point method for solving stochastic linear programming problems, which leverages a primal-dual feasible Newton-like method. By combining this approach with a feasible sampling strategy, the manuscript develops an algorithm that generates nearly optimal operation policies for intricate decision tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm yields substantial enhancements over existing sampling-based and model predictive control techniques. Furthermore, the research introduces a novel sampling philosophy that produces a probabilistically optimal operation sequence, which can be derived from the problem's constraints through successive approximations. This philosophy forms the basis of a probabilistically interpretable model predictive control algorithm, which produces a sequence with minimal cost and compliance to the constraints. Both algorithms are available in open-source form at https://github.com/AlexanderDyck/SLP-SAM.

This research introduces a multi-classifier system that triumphs in recognizing handwritten mathematical symbols in diverse languages. This mathematical symbol recognition pipeline relies on a kNN-based classifier specifically designed for each language, trained on a unique set of hand-drawn symbols. To create the kNN classifier, a comprehensive dataset with detailed annotations is utilized. By selecting the most suitable classifier, the system dynamically chooses the best approach for each incoming symbol, thereby enhancing overall performance. Additionally, this research introduces a novel method to create a probability distribution for each symbol class, enabling efficient classification of uncertain samples. As a result, the proposed framework achieves exceptional performance, surpassing state-of-the-art models in recognizing mathematical symbols in various languages. Furthermore, this framework also enables creation of high-quality, annotated datasets essential for advanced machine learning applications. Ultimately, the project's success paves the way for innovative applications in multi-language mathematical symbol recognition. We introduce an effective yet relatively low-cost approach to address a common issue in reinforcement learning, namely safety constraint breaches. Current methods to prevent violations often necessitate complete knowledge of all potential safety constraints at the outset, which is impractical in many situations. Our technique, however, leverages data from an environment model to develop an approximation of the violation boundary, thereby reducing instances of unsafe behavior within the learning process. As a result, our method enables more efficient learning by allowing a larger proportion of safe actions to be taken, thus increasing the likelihood of discovery. Empirical testing on standard benchmarks confirms a notable enhancement in performance relative to existing methods. Notably, our approach also exhibits improved capability in handling constraints whose expressions are unknown during training. Given its effectiveness and relatively low computational cost, this method shows promise for a wide range of practical applications. We introduce a novel formulation of the twin prime conjecture, focusing on pairs of prime numbers as twins of their respective generating functions. By analyzing polynomial functions with integer coefficients, we seek to identify instances where both functions evaluate to prime numbers. Our investigation incorporates the concept of symmetric properties and utilizes the primary properties of prime numbers, with the aim of exploring additional insights into the primality of polynomial equations. Additionally, we examine the relationship between our formulated twin prime conjecture and established theories on prime number distributions and the primality of certain polynomial equations. We present a neural classifier based on a combination of convolutional and recurrent layers for identifying abusive tweets. The convolutional layer extracts n-gram features from each tweet, which are combined with the embedding of the final token using a max pooling operation. These features are then passed through a recurrent layer that fuses information across all tweets in a post, and a final dense layer that outputs a classification value. The system utilizes pre-trained word and character embeddings, which enables it to process sequences of varying lengths without the need for padding. It was trained on 11 languages and tested on 15 languages, and outperformed other classifiers in 11 languages, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.793 in English and 0.442 in Hebrew. Notably, it also demonstrated cross-lingual performance in languages such as Hindi, Arabic, and Korean, and even delivered reasonable results in languages with limited data, including Turkish, Thai, and Greek. The system was found to be particularly effective in languages with limited resources, indicating its potential as a standalone tool for detecting abusive content. This investigation focuses on evaluating the stability of decision-making functions under uncertain conditions. Our analysis builds on existing theories for both certain and uncertain situations, and we address two key issues: first, we determine how to measure the reliability of decision functions in scenarios with unknown parameter values; second, we identify how to make this assessment in such cases. Our results show that this evaluation is possible only if the decision functions are limited in their scope. This constraint leads to the ability to assess reliability in two ways: either by considering the worst-case outcomes or by estimating the decision functions and weighing their accuracy. Both approaches are found to provide the same level of protection, and this conclusion leads to the recommendation to prioritize simplicity and efficiency. Ultimately, we conclude that the most suitable measure of reliability is one that is both straightforward to calculate and robust against small errors. In the optimal solution, when hop count is the objective function, we demonstrate that the competitive ratio for online algorithms can be achieved only by increasing the hop count by a factor of $O(d)$ in $d$-dimensional graphs constructed using a specific set of vertices. This result contrasts the performance in $1$-dimensional graphs, where the same value of $O(d)$ was previously established. For $d$-dimensional graphs, where the hop count is the objective function, we present an online algorithm achieving a competitive ratio of $O(d \log n / \log \log n)$, improving the previous best known competitive ratio of $O(d \sqrt{n})$. Furthermore, in $d$-dimensional graphs, we develop an offline algorithm for creating a spanner with hop count $O(d \log n)$, thereby improving the previously known result of $O(d \sqrt{n})$. Additionally, in $d$-dimensional graphs, we create a super-spanner with an edge set of $O(\log^2 n)$, achieving a goal previously known only for $d=2$. This super-spanner also enables the selection of Steiner points to achieve a competitive ratio of $O(\log n / \log \log n)$ for the minimum hop count in multi-commodity traffic scenarios. This result improves the previous best known competitive ratio of $O(\sqrt{n})$. This work is further extended in a follow-up paper to demonstrate that these results can be applied to graphs with edge failures as well as to enable the selection of Steiner points in multi-commodity traffic scenarios in graphs with edge failures. At a density of 0.60, the metastable hexatic phase transitions directly into a stable crystalline phase characterized by long-range order and a specific peak structure in its structure factor. This transition is marked by the disappearance of the hexatic metastable phase and the emergence of a distinct peak at a higher frequency in the structure factor of the resulting crystalline phase. As the density is increased to 0.71, the stable crystalline phase transforms into another crystalline phase with a different symmetry, marked by the appearance of additional peak structures in the structure factor. This new phase persists up to a density of 0.80 before giving way to a different metastable crystalline phase characterized by five distinct peak structures in its structure factor. Ultimately, at a density of 0.82, the metastable crystalline phase transitions into a polar liquid phase through a mechanism involving the disruption of the crystalline order. The underlying mechanism of this transition is attributed to the increased mobility of the particles at higher densities, allowing for the reorientation of the dipoles and the disruption of the crystalline structure. The emergence of the frustrated polar phases at densities higher than 0.50 is attributed to the increased competition between the electrostatic interaction and the Lennard-Jones interaction, resulting in the distortion of the hexatic metastable phase and the formation of the novel crystalline phases characterized by specific peak structures in their structure factors. Ultimately, the novel crystalline phases are found to possess a unique combination of polar long-range correlations and crystalline peak structures, rendering them distinct from both the metastable hexatic phase and the stable crystalline phases characterized by order and a lack of polar correlations. This research investigates the effect of normalizing a dataset on the performance of weather forecasting models, specifically those using convolutional neural networks, and whether different scaling methods for input variables have a significant impact on the model's accuracy. To answer these questions, we utilized the persistent weather data from the Persistent Object Annotations Tool, which contains a diverse range of weather patterns, and evaluated the performance of a basic convolutional neural network model on both normalized and unnormalized data, comparing its results to more advanced models like Recurrent Neural Networks and WeatherNet. Interestingly, our findings indicate that normalizing the data improves the model's accuracy, but only when using a simple scaling method; alternatively, leaving the data unscaled or using more complex scaling techniques results in a lower accuracy. Notably, our best performing model achieved an accuracy of 0.9349 when using normalized data, while the other models had an accuracy of 0.8961. Additionally, we explored the effect of removing data for specific weather types, which revealed that normalizing the data enables the model to effectively classify missing data points for a given weather type with high accuracy when supplemented with a small amount of labeled data. Overall, our research indicates that normalizing the data and using a simple scaling method is an effective strategy for improving the performance of weather forecasting models. Finally, we developed a new method, called MetaWeather, which uses meta-learning to improve the classification of weather types, and demonstrated its effectiveness by achieving an accuracy of 0.9333 when tested on the Persistent tool's data. When applied to real-world data from the OpenWeatherMap service, MetaWeather reached an accuracy of 0.9333, surpassing the performance of other competing models. Furthermore, our analysis of the Persistent tool's data revealed that including more training data does not necessarily improve the model's accuracy, and in fact, including excessively large amounts of data can actually decrease the model's performance due to increased noise. Consequently, our research suggests that including data from sources with varying levels of noise can result in a more robust classifier when using meta-learning. Ultimately, the success of MetaWeather highlights the potential of combining existing weather forecasting models with meta-learning to achieve superior performance. Based on this outcome, we propose several promising avenues for further research in the future. The unique architecture of neurons, featuring extended lengths and specialized transport systems, presents a complex challenge for studying the movement of vital materials along microtubules within these cells. The efficient transport of materials along neurons relies on the dynamics of microtubules, including their speed, direction, and structure, which, if disrupted, can lead to transport difficulties and potentially affect neuron function. To better understand the relationship between transport and microtubule properties, we developed a simulation model that accounts for the varying speeds and directions of microtubules, their age, and the movement patterns of cargo. By comparing our findings with real-world observations, we found that fast-moving cargo is most effective when it utilizes the longest, rapidly turning microtubules, while slower-moving cargo can make use of shorter, moving microtubles. These results suggest that the unique properties of neuronal microtubules allow for the simultaneous transport of materials at different speeds, making our study's findings relevant to various cellular processes. Furthermore, our investigation also sheds light on how age-related changes in microtubule dynamics can impact material transport and potentially contribute to the development of transport problems. Ultimately, our study provides a framework for understanding the complex relationship between microtubule structure and function, essential for cellular processes, and offers a tool for analyzing the effects of changes in this structure on cellular behavior. This disc arises primarily from the white dwarf's mass loss, which occurs as a result of interactions between the two stars. In contrast, a novel discovery suggests that a significant contributor to disc formation is also the white dwarf's final demise – its complete destruction. In this catastrophic event, the entire white dwarf is engulfed by the neutron or black hole, resulting in the release of a substantial amount of energy and further mass to enhance disc development. In the context of LIGO/Virgo observations, it is possible that such destructive events constitute a previously unrecognised source of gravitational waves. Specifically, we focus on final states containing an electron, a negative kaon, and neutrinos, and investigate the effectiveness of measuring CP violation through asymmetrical distributions of decay angles and momentum polarizations, as well as the reduction of background influences in two-body decay frames. Additionally, we discuss the advantages of considering both electron and neutrino momentum asymmetries in the analysis. Furthermore, we discuss methods to enhance sensitivity by selecting on-shell electron and kaon momentum asymmetries and provide a sensitivity assessment for a future tau charm factory with a specified level of luminosity and an expected number of event occurrences. A possible CP violation sensitivity of the order of $10^{-4}$ is projected for such a facility. Finally, we outline potential improvements to our analytical methods that could lead to more stringent CP violation limits in the future. These investigations are pertinent to current research into the tau's behavior and will remain relevant in upcoming experiments at semileptonic tau facilities. We investigate how the size and density of an original set influence the open completeness of its ultrapower extension in non-standard analysis, utilizing ideas from logic and set theory. Our study particularly examines how different types of high-density sets behave within an ultrapower and shows that these findings align with existing results on high-amalgamable sets. Furthermore, we discuss the similarities and distinctions between open completeness and high-amalgamability properties. Moreover, we introduce the concept of strongly complete sets and demonstrate that sets with high density can be strongly complete. However, we also find a non-standard set of integers that is strongly complete but not complete with respect to first-order logic. Moreover, a non-standard set is found to be complete with respect to first-order logic while not being strongly complete. Additionally, we establish that fundamental operations such as addition and multiplication preserve the properties of strongly complete and complete sets. Finally, we discuss the relationship between the concept of completeness in non-standard analysis and other mathematical properties including decidability, computability, and randomness. These findings provide insights into the behavior of complete sets and their potential applications in solving computationally undecidable problems. These results are presented in a series of appendices in an attempt to make them more accessible to an audience with a non-standard analysis background. Specifically, the concepts covered in these appendices include logic, set theory, high-amalgamable sets, computability theory, and randomness theory. For example, appendix A covers basic concepts in logic, appendix B covers fundamental principles in set theory, appendix C explores the properties of high-amalgamable sets, appendix D delves into computability theory, and appendix E examines the concept of randomness. By presenting these concepts through an ultrapower extension, we aim to provide a unified and elegant treatment of these theories within a non-standard analysis framework. This approach not only simplifies the understanding of complex mathematical concepts but also reveals novel and important results in logic, set theory, and computability theory. For instance, a non-standard version of Gödel's first incompleteness theorem is developed, as well as a non-standard interpretation of the fundamental theorems of Goodstein, Quine, and Tarski, among others. Furthermore, a non-standard proof of the fundamental theorem of Lindemeyer is presented, as well as a non-standard exploration of the interplay between the axiom of choice, extensionality, and comprehension. By applying non-standard analysis to solve fundamental problems in logic, we hope to inspire a new wave of innovative research in this field

This research aims to examine the relationship between the chromatic number of a graph and its ability to contain specific subgraphs or rooted branch sets. Specifically, if a graph has a chromatic number of at least $t$, we investigate whether it necessarily includes a $K_t$-minor or certain rooted branch sets. To this end, we demonstrate that there exist graphs with a $t$-chromatic number that do not possess the desired $K_t$-minors or rooted branch sets, however we also show that such graphs do exist for every value of $t$. Furthermore, we explore the same questions but in relation to hypergraphs, which are structures that generalize graphs by connecting more than two vertices. Ultimately, we conclude that there exist hypergraphs with a $t$-chromatic number that do not contain specific subhypergraphs or rooted branch sets, but also establish that such hypergraphs do exist for every value of $t$. Notably, our findings resolve an open problem from the field of topological ordering for graphs with a certain chromatic number. Additionally, our work provides insights into the complexity of the underlying problems, and in some instances, we identify connections to previously studied problems in graph theory. Finally, we present a new probabilistic method that allows us to construct graphs with specific properties, and in doing so, we establish new lower bounds on the minimum size of such graphs. This research investigates the influence of the parameter $\beta$ on the first robust eigenvalue of the anisotropic $p$-Laplace operator. We derive precise estimates of this eigenvalue for parts of the boundary in the exterior and interior of a domain $\Omega$, subject to Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions. The findings are further extended to a second-order operator governing the behavior of thin layers. The study also considers the impact of parameter $\beta$ on the layers' layers' thickness and reveals the occurrence of abrupt changes in the eigenvalue spectrum. Additionally, we establish the existence of a unique "transition" eigenfunction for these operators, which retains sign in regions where the operator resembles the Laplace operator. Crucially, our analysis shows that the robustness of eigenvalue multiplicity can be preserved even in the presence of small parameter values. Ultimately, our findings provide a framework for understanding how parameter-dependent parameters influence eigenvalue behavior in elliptic operators. Our results are substantiated by numerical computations illustrating the influence of $\beta$ on eigenvalue patterns, as well as by the construction of specific examples highlighting their applicability. The study further explores the applicability of its findings to the study of thin layers and membrane models. Specifically, it demonstrates that the layers' behavior can be accurately captured by the limit of a vanishing thickness parameter in our analysis of eigenvalue spectra. Consequently, our analysis yields precise estimates of eigenvalue spectra for membrane models, including a novel lower bound. Furthermore, our analysis shows that membrane eigenfunctions can be approximated by eigenfunctions of thin layers, while also recovering a long-standing conjecture regarding the lower bound of the first membrane eigenvalue. The study also delves into the analytical methods employed in the study and discusses potential avenues for further research. The methods utilized in the study draw heavily from the existing literature in the field and contribute novel perspectives to the discussion. The remaining chapters present the main results of the study in a logical progression. This paper redefines the concept of Graph Convolutional Networks by linking them to established Convolutional Neural Networks and fully connected Neural Networks. By translating this connection into a formal framework, we establish necessary and sufficient conditions for graph convolutional operators. Furthermore, we demonstrate that conventional CNNs and fully connected NNs inherently employ graph convolutional operators, thereby implicitly qualifying as Graph Convolutional Networks. However, not all CNNs and fully connected NNs satisfy the graph convolutional property as defined in the literature; instead, they utilize a specific form of graph convolutional operator that is derived from the adjacency matrix and gradient aggregation. To overcome this limitation, we propose an alternative form of graph convolutional operator that accommodates arbitrary functions of the adjacency matrix. Finally, we showcase the applicability of our framework in the context of fully connected NNs through a layer-wise analysis of popular architectures, including which layers exhibit the graph convolutional property. We examine the study of a linear equation system with coefficients from a finite field in the context of computable physics theory (CPT). A significant distinction in CPT is made between definable and computable properties, depending on whether their values can be uniquely determined by a given input, regardless of how it is specified, and how efficiently they can be calculated given a specific input, respectively. In this study, we establish the criteria for a solution to an unordered linear equation system to be CPT-definable and develop a computable formula for determining the number of solutions to such systems. Additionally, we show that while the total or partial multiplicity of a linear equation system is not CPT-definable, we can, however, compute it in a computationally efficient manner for any given instance. These results are further enhanced by a study of the complexity of solving linear equation systems, particularly in finite fields of characteristic one. Notably, we find that this problem lies outside the realm of CPT but can be solved within a high but computationally efficient (relative to CPT) standard in another variant. These findings are further reinforced by a comparison of the theoretical bounds with an actual implementation in a programming language. In particular, we find that even though the theoretical bounds are high, in practice, we can solve linear equation systems in finite fields of characteristic one in finite time, except perhaps for very large instances. These results are even more pronounced when we consider solving linear equation systems in finite fields of characteristic two. In this case, we find that we can solve such problems in finite time, except perhaps for extremely large instances, given a random oracle as an input. These results are particularly striking as they show that the complexity of solving linear equation systems in finite fields of characteristic one is likely to be high in practice, given the rapidity with which such problems can be solved in such fields, as evidenced by various applications in computer science. We conducted an in-depth x-ray photoemission spectroscopy investigation of (Eu1-xBix)2Ir2O7 with varying Bi doping levels (x = 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50 on Eu site) to examine the impact of Bi doping. The results show that Bi doping has a significant local effect on the valence band, with the 6s peak increasing in intensity and shifting towards a higher binding energy with rising Bi concentrations. Conversely, the overall spectral weight remains constant, indicating that Bi doping is incorporated into the spectrum through a specific mechanism. Notably, the increase in Bi doping is accompanied by a noticeable decrease in the Eu2+ ion concentration, as evident from the decrease in the Eu2+ peak intensity. The Eu3+ peak exhibits a more intricate pattern, displaying both an initial decrease and subsequent increase as the Bi concentration rises. The observed behavior suggests that the initial Bi doping triggers a significant chemical reaction, following which Bi doping gradually approaches a state of self-limiting incorporation. The resulting compounds possess similar electronic properties to the well-known 112 family of materials, such as KIr2O5 and LaAl2Ga8S6, as well as the parent compound (EuIr2O7). The incorporation of Bi doping into these materials offers an innovative means of modulating their electronic properties while minimizing structural disruptions. The discovery of similar local effects in other doped compounds opens up new avenues for the simultaneous control of electronic correlations and crystal structure. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that Bi doping can be utilized as a versatile tool for modulating the electronic properties of 5d transition metal oxides and related materials. The findings of this study have significant implications for the broader 5d transition metal oxide community, highlighting the potential for further discoveries through similar doping strategies. We examine the possibility of constructing infinitely long, nontransitive sequences of numbers. If the original sequence has a length of at least 4, we can create an infinite series with the same properties by replacing each number with a corresponding set of numbers, ensuring the new properties remain intact. To create a nontransitive sequence of numbers of the form 1 to m, where all numbers in the sequence belong to the same group, we apply a diagonal argument that shows the existence of such a nontransitive sequence of numbers with m equal to an exponential function of the square of the sequence length. The aim of our research is to address the issue of reducing the overhead of software run-time options. We propose an approach that efficiently eliminates unnecessary options from programs, resulting in a more compact and easier-to-manage system. Our approach relies on a novel algorithm that identifies and eliminates redundant options during a brief preliminary analysis. This method has been successfully tested on a variety of practical applications and has shown significant progress in comparison to existing methods. Furthermore, we have integrated this technique into a tool that simplifies integration with existing configuration management systems. We evaluated its benefits through a case study of OpenFOAM, a complex simulation software, which showed substantial gains in performance and a substantial reduction in code size. Specifically, the improvements included a 91% decrease in code size, a 90% reduction in option-related code, and a 35% faster initialization time. OpenFOAM is available at https://cfcst.inria.fr/Reproducibility/OpenFOAM. A brief demonstration of our tool can be found at https://cfcst.inria.fr/Reproducibility/ToolDemo. This paper introduces a groundbreaking framework that enables training of multilingual models in a single, unified process. Rather than training each language separately or in a specific order, our framework enables simultaneous training of multiple languages on a single dataset. In video enhancement tasks such as video denoising and super resolution, recent advancements like BasicVSR have demonstrated superior performance through multi-scale video prediction with a compact structure. However, their potential for creating more advanced models is limited due to the difficulty of further improving their model architecture. We address this limitation by introducing virtual frames to the video prediction process, leading to BasicVSR++ - a high-performance, efficient model with improved accuracy and computational efficiency. We achieved this through the discovery of an optimal frame virtualization strategy and integration of the approach into a framework that can easily incorporate and adapt various virtual frames, as well as efficient optimization techniques. The results show BasicVSR++ outperforms BasicVSR by significant margins on challenging datasets, such as DND and EDVR, while also being more computationally efficient. Furthermore, BasicVSR++ sets a new benchmark on the widely-used Vid4 dataset for super resolution, and its compact architecture and high accuracy make it an ideal choice for real-world applications. The code is available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/whgyy/BasicVSR++.org. Additionally, a Colab notebook has been created to facilitate model testing and demonstration. We hope this will contribute to the development of more advanced video processing models in the future.

We investigate the problem of multi-task reinforcement learning where a single dynamics model needs to accommodate multiple task representations. However, it's possible for a model to prioritize one task at the expense of others by learning task identifiers from demonstration data, leading to poor performance in unseen tasks. To prevent this occurrence, we propose the concept of latent representation crossing (LaRCE), which enforces ensembled models to learn similar dynamics from different perspectives, thereby preventing models to exploit task indicators and improving out-of-distribution generalization performance. Additionally, LaRCE promotes diversity in model prediction spaces, which can benefit sampling methods like off-policy data augmentation. We evaluate LaRCE using a dataset with a zero-shot scenario and find that it significantly enhances performance in this context. Notably, LaRCE exhibits a beneficial effect even when applied to non-ensemble models, indicating its potential to function as a standalone regularization technique. Our experimental analysis suggests that LaRCE acts by increasing diversity in the prediction space, which in turn improves performance in unseen tasks. Furthermore, LaRCE demonstrates its applicability across various reinforcement learning methods, including maximum entropy reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The code for our study can be accessed at https://github.com/alexeydg/larce.

A theoretical heat engine model, based on the idea of scaling, generates output power when it operates between two equilibrium states. This power production is influenced by a scaling parameter, $\lambda$, which also determines the efficiency of the engine. When the engine operates in a state of maximum equilibrium, the same parameter, $\lambda$, controls both its efficiency and output power, much like the role of the Prigogine length in dissipative electrochemical engines. Under this condition, the output power increases with the difference in temperatures, $T_1-T_2$, and is further enhanced by increasing the scaling parameter, $\lambda$. This behavior is comparable to that of overunity heat engines, commonly found in non-equilibrium systems, which occasionally produce bursts of high power. It is shown that the scaling parameter, $\lambda$, can be represented by the Prigogine length, which characterizes the distance between these two equilibrium states in chemical systems. This theoretical model can be applied to micro-scale and macro-scale systems, as evidenced by examples of functioning heat engines that operate within equilibrium conditions. Ultimately, the objective of achieving high power output while maintaining thermal equilibrium may not be feasible, given the constraints imposed by the fundamental laws of thermodynamics. Nevertheless, the possibility of harnessing environmental fluctuations at the micro-scale to generate mechanical work remains an intriguing prospect. It is also demonstrated that the scaling model can be adapted to non-equilibrium thermal machines, such as the Carnot engine, to analyze their performance in relation to temperature differences and internal correlations. These findings provide a valuable framework for exploring thermal machines, as well as thermal phenomena, where the concept of scaling offers a useful analytical tool. Furthermore, the application of the scaling model to heat engines may contribute to a deeper understanding of the underlying thermal dynamics, which could potentially inspire innovative designs for thermal machines. It is also shown that the scaling model can be utilized to investigate the thermal behavior of complex systems characterized by non-trivial fixed points, such as critical points and multicritical points. This is illustrated through examples of dissipative electrochemical engines, such as the Potter engine, which exhibits a critical point when it reaches a state of maximum output power. Conversely, the efficiency of the Potter engine peaks at multicritical points, which are also accompanied by oscillations in performance. These findings are validated by numerical simulations, which are further supported by analytical calculations based on scaling theories. Hurricanes pose a significant threat to coastal regions, causing widespread damage to properties and disrupting power distribution. By analyzing past hurricanes, we can evaluate their impact on different areas, helping us prepare for future storms. This involves using geographic information to identify regions vulnerable to hurricane landfalls and assessing the power outages that occur due to wind and storm surges. In this research, we develop a method to simulate power outages caused by landfalling hurricanes, drawing on historical hurricane data and advanced computational techniques. We apply our model to the Southeastern United States, the most hurricane-prone region in the country, and evaluate the power disruptions it causes in Florida, Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Texas. This study aims to help policymakers and power companies assess the potential impact of a hurricane on the power grid before the storm even hits, allowing them to take proactive measures to minimize damage. Specifically, we provide quantitative analysis of power outages, duration, and restoration times, as well as monetary losses, helping stakeholders prioritize repair efforts and allocate resources effectively. This model can be used to compare different power restoration strategies, such as simulating the effect of repairing lines in parallel versus sequentially. Furthermore, we explore the potential reduction in repair time and monetary losses if power companies delay repairs until the storm subs Hurricanes Kate, Ida, and Nicholas were used as test cases to validate our model. The results showed that the power grid in the affected areas experienced significant disruptions, with power outages ranging from 0.1% to 5.8% of total customers, lasting from a few hours to several days, and causing millions of dollars in monetary losses. By analyzing different restoration strategies, we found that delaying repairs until three days after the storm increased power outages by 13-26%, compared to prompt repairs, and added 10-20% to total monetary losses, in the test cases provided. Additionally, we found that power outages caused by storm surges were concentrated in coastal areas with high elevations, while wind-related power outages affected a broader area, extending inland up to 200-300 miles. Furthermore, we observed that power outages were more frequent and severe in areas with lower average elevations, as the hurricane's storm surges caused water levels to rise higher in these regions. In contrast, wind-related power outages were more intense in areas with higher average elevations, due to stronger winds at greater heights. Future high-luminosity colliders offer a promising opportunity to experimentally verify theoretical models incorporating multiple scalar fields beyond the standard model's predictions. In this study, we've expanded upon previous research by examining how this phenomenon behaves at various temperatures. Our findings indicate that the peak's intensity diminishes with increasing temperature. Moreover, using exact numerical methods, we've derived the correction terms proportional to temperature. Notably, at moderate temperatures, the shape of the peak remains symmetrical, but it develops slight asymmetry at very high temperatures due to the influence of non-Majorana effects being overridden by thermal energy. Ultimately, our results provide an understanding of these effects that can be applied to experimental studies of Majorana modes even at moderate temperatures. Additionally, our work may contribute to the identification of topological zero modes in systems other than topological codes. Lastly, we've discussed how the occurrence of a zero-energy peak could be utilized as an indicator of topological zero modes in experimental scenarios. The possibility of distinguishing between zero-energy peaks originating from topological zero modes and those produced by contamination or other sources is also explored. Ultimately, our research aims to facilitate the precise detection of topological zero modes, thereby enhancing our comprehension of these modes and their potential applications. The techniques employed in this study can be extended to analyze experimental data collected using scanning tunneling spectroscopy. The outcomes of these analyses will offer valuable insights into the characteristics of topological zero modes and their occurrence in materials with strong interatomic coupling. The criteria set includes a minimum peak height relative to the thermal energy, a symmetrical shape at moderate temperatures, and an absence of significant spectral weight at energies greater than the thermal energy. The study demonstrates that these criteria effectively eliminate contamination from various sources, thereby significantly enhancing our comprehension of topological zero modes. Although they were initially applied to processing sensory data from images to language, their limitations in handling the complexity of real-world information led to the development of more effective models. This paper proposes a new framework that combines the latest advances in deep learning with a variational information-bottleneck principle, enabling the creation of versatile models capable of producing accurate representations of novel data. Our research introduces the Bicephalous Convolutional AutoEncoder (BCAE), an innovative model that simultaneously learns two convolutional autoencoders with shared compressed representations. This innovative approach enhances data compression through explicit control of the compression process on both the original and transformed data. Additionally, the BCAE enables the discovery of intricate correlations within paired datasets through the comparison of the two encoders' perceptions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model by applying it to the challenging domain of MRI compression, an area particularly sensitive to post-processing due to its inherent signal loss. Through thorough experimentation, we showcase BCAE's unique capabilities and achieve superior performance in comparison to the current state-of-the-art methods. Notably, the BCAE allows for the restoration of the original image from both the compressed representation and the compressed representation alongside the transformed data, yielding a significant 1.8dB gain over the state-of-the-art method. Furthermore, the BCAE uncovers novel correlations within MRI data, paving the way for potential clinical applications. Finally, our model's versatility is illustrated by applying it to the compression of artistic images, resulting in the creative discovery of potential styles within paired images during the compression process. Overall, the BCAE offers a groundbreaking approach to data compression and post-processing that unlocks innovative possibilities across diverse domains. Trident, a self-reconfiguring robot, has been successfully tested in two forms: 
a) A robot made of flexible materials that can change its body to climb up on flat surfaces by applying pressure at the base, while reducing tension higher up. 
b) A robot composed of multiple interconnected sections, capable of transforming into different shapes to climb over curved obstacles in various orientations.

In both forms, the robot demonstrated high climbing speeds, outperforming a fish by a significant margin. In the shape-shifting form, it also showed improved climbing abilities compared to a robot with a fixed design. Our study marks the first application of self-reconfiguring technology in climbing tasks and paves the way for the development of robots that can adapt to a wide range of environments. 

Key advantages of Trident's climbing approach include:
- The ability to create negative pressure at the base while reducing tension higher up.
- The capacity to change its body shape to generate upward force.
- The versatility to transform into different shapes to overcome complex obstacles.

This innovative design empowers Trident to access areas previously inaccessible to robots and offers a wide range of potential applications in domains such as soft robotics, bio-inspiration, and search and rescue missions. 

In the near future, we plan to enhance Trident's capabilities to climb on steeper surfaces and explore its potential uses in various real-world settings.

These criteria are validated through application to both incompressible electron fluid and magnetohydrodynamics. Furthermore, we establish that weak solutions in these theories can maintain helicity's integrity in 2D space with minimal restrictions on the $L^p$ space parameters. A potential limitation of current gravitational-wave detectors is their inability to detect certain compact binary mergers due to their initial eccentricities, which are determined by the detectors' sensitivity thresholds and angular resolution. We have developed a method to efficiently predict the detection boundaries for diverse binary black hole systems across various detector configurations, taking into account their initial eccentricities and orbital inclinations. This involves approximating their final eccentricities when they cross the detection thresholds, which shows that a significant number of detected events will have initial eccentricities above the threshold values, especially for higher frequency detectors like LISA and those with initial eccentricities near the threshold values for ground-based detectors like LVC and LIGO. We've also found that the final eccentricities of detected compact binaries are strongly correlated with their initial eccentricity values when they cross the detection threshold, which suggests that those with higher initial eccentricities will have lower final eccentricities due to the eccentricity-reducing effect of the gravitational-wave emission over time. Based on this, we've developed a simple formula to estimate the total number of detected events as a function of the initial eccentricity distribution, which can be used to guide future searches in data already collected and upcoming runs by informing the selection of potential targets among the remaining unanalyzed data sets. This new discovery can greatly expand the potential applications of XFELOs, and significantly boost their overall value. The extreme conditions of this collapse make it difficult to accurately model, thus serving as a rigorous test for simulation codes. We obtained precise analytical solutions to the Guderley problem using a coordinate transformation and found that even high-end numerical simulations required significant validation against these solutions. These accurate solutions can now be utilized to develop improved simulation models and validate other hydrodynamic simulations, such as those in stellar collapse and core collapse. Additionally, we explored the potential applications of this research in the context of type II supernova explosions and the collapse of compact objects like black holes and neutron stars. These precise solutions can help inform the development of more accurate models of this type of stellar collapse process. Furthermore, we propose using the accuracy of these solutions as a yardstick to measure the precision of other stellar collapse simulations. This research investigates the current state of XAI applications in AI development through a paired survey of software engineers and requirements practitioners. Our findings reveal that existing XAI applications harbor requirements-related shortcomings. We identify opportunities for requirements engineering to address these shortcomings and provide recommendations for future research and development in both fields. Ultimately, aligning requirements engineering methods with XAI practices can contribute substantially to improving the quality of XAI applications. This collaboration can also yield beneficial outcomes for requirements engineering and its applications in general. To facilitate further research, we publicly share the results of our study and related information at the URL https://sites.google.com/view/xai-surveys. In the classification and grading of colorectal adenomas, deep neural networks have shown great potential. However, due to limitations in training data, complete information about a patient's adenoma cannot be obtained from a single image. This paper addresses this challenge by developing a multi-task learning approach that classifies and grades colorectal adenomas based on multiple images from the same patient. To prevent information duplication and promote independent decision-making among different networks, we utilize an advanced method that incorporates a unified network with multiple task-specific layers. The effectiveness of our approach was tested on a large dataset of 104,043 images belonging to 9,052 patients, and the results indicate a significant enhancement in macro- and micro-averaged AUC values compared to the current best practices. Furthermore, our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in predicting the maximum adenoma size, which demonstrates a notable improvement in correlation between model predictions and actual sizes with a Pearson r value of 0.83. A major challenge in practical application of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) lies in efficiently optimizing its variational parameters. This study introduces a more effective approach to resolving this issue by integrating Bayesian optimization into the QAOA process. By combining the wide search ability of Bayesian optimization and the guided search of QAOA, the proposed method enhances exploration of the parameter space, resulting in a substantial boost in problem-solving rate. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms the standard QAOA approach, even surpassing its maximum performance in some cases. Notably, this improvement is particularly evident in scenarios where exact optimization is computationally expensive, and it remains effective even when the hardware noise increases. The proposed method is then successfully applied to solve the Max-Cut problem on a graph with up to 140 vertices within a reasonable computation time. This research offers a promising solution for optimizing QAOA variational parameters, paving the way for more efficient use of near-term quantum devices. Moreover, open-source code is available for review at https://github.com/complexity-quantum/BAOAA. Finally, potential future research directions are discussed.

In contrast to traditional views, these patterns are found to be stable due to an underlying quantum mechanical property, which is not influenced by the material's inherent tendency for magnetism. Through our analysis, we reveal that these patterns arise from a unique interaction between the material's electron arrangement and its quantum fluctuations, resulting in a unique correlation of electron distribution. Notably, these patterns can be induced by an external force that matches this specific correlation, without the need for stripe order itself. Additionally, our findings suggest that these patterns could potentially be created and controlled using precise manipulation of light, paving the way for potential applications in the development of topological phases and superconducting materials. Finally, our research also reveals that these patterns could be related to those observed in certain materials without a clear understanding of their origin, highlighting the importance of considering the role of quantum fluctuations in the arrangement of electrons within complex materials.

We introduce an advanced deep learning strategy with a compact network architecture, designed specifically for automatic vertebra identification in 3D CT scans. The proposed model, LIVS-Net, leverages a localized information verification sub-network to enhance the primary 3D convolutional neural network. This additional layer enables direct verification of information between the global and local perspectives, effectively enhancing the model's performance. LIVS-Net was evaluated on three datasets and demonstrated superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. Notably, LIVS-Net achieved a remarkable 96.57% verification rate on the SPS challenge dataset, a significant improvement over existing models. Furthermore, the model exhibited excellent generalization capabilities on new, unseen patients. With its exceptional performance and compact size, LIVS-Net presents a promising solution for clinical vertebra identification tasks. The source code and model weights are publicly available on GitHub for replication purposes. Additionally, we contribute a set of essential data augmentation techniques to the community to facilitate the development of more advanced deep learning models. Lastly, we achieved a first-place ranking in the SPS challenge at the MICCAI 2021 conference using LIVS-Net. along with an analysis of the boundaries within this classification. Additionally,

Finally, three specific methods are developed to determine the dimension of the

The process of magnetic island merging in a twisted flux tube is investigated using the Sweet-Parker model and compared with more realistic simulations. It's discovered that the island collision time is significantly longer in simulations than predicted by the model, especially for smaller islands. Initial simulations revealed that this discrepancy is caused by the diffusion of reconnecting current layers, an effect that's more pronounced in smaller islands. Further investigation into the micro-scale physics of these current layers using the kinetic MHD simulation, REDI, shows that they have a much shorter width than expected. This smallest scale dimension was found to be an internal characteristic of the plasma and was influenced by the amplitude of the reconnecting fluctuations. When these smaller scales were incorporated into the Sweet-Parker model, it was able to accurately predict the collision times of the islands. This reformulated model has implications for understanding the interaction between large-scale MHD phenomena and smaller-scale kinetic processes in the solar atmosphere.  Specifically, it may help in explaining previously observed slow energy dissipation in coronal mass ejections and other astrophysical events.  Finally, it's also relevant to the observation of slow shock speeds in MHD turbulence in the solar atmosphere and other similar astrophysical settings. In order to effectively collaborate with humans, digital assistants need to go
beyond just analytical problem-solving abilities, as embodied by systems like
MacMahon's digital assistant, which excelled in task execution but not in
strategic decision-making. Our research builds upon previous findings by developing
a digital assistant that learns to think creatively over time through repeated
interactions with human partners. We discovered that this virtual assistant, which
differed from the original in its ability to form mental images, developed
innovative problem-solving approaches and intuitive understanding of its partners'
behavior through application in a complex design task. While its human counterparts
initially relied on standard design techniques, the digital assistant and even
human collaborators began to explore new creative methods with time. Moreover,
both the digital and human assistants demonstrated an intuitive understanding of
each other's behavior, which translated into improved collaboration and task
outcomes. These results show that the potential for creative collaboration with
human partners should not be limited by the capabilities of digital assistants. 
With further advancements, digital assistants could evolve into highly imaginative
partners in various fields of human endeavor. Our research methodology is
highly interdisciplinary, combining cognitive science, AI, and human-computer
interaction, as well as the innovative design of virtual human partners through
agent-based modeling. Our approach is particularly relevant to the development of
more sophisticated digital assistants, which is becoming increasingly vital in
both industry and the wider community. Ultimately, we hope to contribute to a
better understanding of how humans and digital entities can effectively collaborate
